lead: Adults who are deaf or severely hard of hearing in both ears can now also qualify for reimbursement of a second hearing implant. <entity id="org:zbo-zorginstituut-nederland">Zorginstituut Nederland</entity> announced this yesterday. Children were already reimbursed for a so-called cochlear implant in both ears. But adults were only entitled to this if they were deaf due to meningitis, or if they were both deaf and blind. Other adults who are severely hard of hearing or deaf could only get one device reimbursed. For their other ear they therefore often wear a hearing aid. But for some people this does not work well enough. The Zorginstituut reviewed various scientific studies and concludes that a second device is of added value. For example, people can better distinguish sounds in a noisy room. This in turn makes them more self-reliant and less quickly tired, the Zorginstituut states. The reimbursement has applied since 27 October 2026. However, each case is assessed individually to see whether someone qualifies, says professor Hearing & Implants Wendy van Huinck of Radboudumc in Nijmegen. For this, the so-called "residual hearing" in the ear that does not yet have an implant must be "bad enough", Huinck says. The Zorginstituut expects sixty to one hundred patients per year. The Oorfonds is pleased that more people can get a second implant. "This has been a point of discussion for years", says Eddy de Ridder. "Whereas one implant is much more awkward than two, because with one you only hear on one side." Hearing rapidly deteriorating Alonda van Toor (59) is hard of hearing, already has one implant and wants "very much a second". Van Toor carries the DFNA9 gene. People with this condition hear well until about the age of forty, after which their hearing suddenly deteriorates sharply. In 2021 she received her first implant because hearing aids no longer helped enough. "I hardly heard anything anymore." The implant has changed her life. "Now I can have a one-on-one conversation well again." Electronic beeps A cochlear implant is fitted through an operation, says professor Huinck. "Electrodes are placed in the cochlea of the ear. These stimulate the nerve endings of the auditory nerve." Depending on where the electrode is placed, the person then hears a high or low tone. This sound is electronic and therefore sounds different from what people without hearing problems are used to. Patients with an implant often have to practise for months before they understand the sound, says Huinck. "Your brain has to learn to understand again. At first the sound may seem like beeps. Slowly you start to recognise sounds again. For some people this goes quickly, for others more slowly." Van Toor is now completely used to her first implant. But she still runs into things. On the left she still has a hearing aid and hears almost nothing. "If someone to my left says something, I have to turn my head. Socially that is difficult." And on the street she cannot tell well which direction a car is coming from. "I am very watchful about that." She expects that a second implant will further improve her life. That is also only logical, says Van Toor. "I did not get two ears for nothing."

title: Hormone-disrupting pesticide to be banned
lead: A widely used pesticide containing a hormone-disrupting substance may no longer be used. The College for the Authorisation of Plant Protection Products and Biocides (Ctgb) has decided this. It concerns the fungicide Pitcher from manufacturer Adama, which is widely used in agriculture and horticulture. This product contains the substance fludioxonil, which is harmful to people, animals and nature. 21.000 kilo Fludioxonil is hormone-disrupting, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) concluded in a 2024 study. Hormone-disrupting pesticides have not been permitted in the European Union since 2009. Ctgb's withdrawal of the plant protection product follows a court ruling last summer. The judge ruled that Pitcher should not have been authorised and that the product must therefore be removed from the market as soon as possible. A Ctgb spokesperson says that with current knowledge the product would not have been authorised. "It rarely happens that the authorisation of products is withdrawn after a reassessment." The case was brought by environmental organisation Pesticide Action Network (PAN). Sjoerd van de Wouw, a researcher at PAN, believes the withdrawal has taken "bizarrely long". "Only since 2018 has it been assessed whether substances are hormone-disrupting or not. But by then fludioxonil was already authorised on the market, and a substantive assessment only came in 2024." The organisation points out that in addition to Pitcher, 23 other pesticides containing fludioxonil are used in the Netherlands. "It is a widely used product," says Van de Wouw. A Ctgb spokesperson states that hormone disruption has been part of the assessment of products since last year. This procedure focused on Pitcher, the spokesperson says. Therefore the withdrawal applies to that specific product. "It is being studied what this ruling means for the authorisation of other products." Each year around 21.000 kilos of fludioxonil are used in the Netherlands. For example, in dip treatment of bulbs and tubers and in the cultivation of perennials and floricultural crops. "Farmers and residents near agricultural areas in particular are heavily exposed to this product," says Van de Wouw. 300 products. But residues have also been found on all kinds of vegetables and fruit. In an analysis by the <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit</entity> (NVWA), fludioxonil was found on more than 300 of the just over 2200 products tested, from potatoes and strawberries to tomatoes and grapes. "Of the hormone-disrupting substances, fludioxonil is the one most often found as a residue on vegetables and fruit," says Van de Wouw. "When consumed, it mainly poses a risk to pregnant women and young children," says Van de Wouw. He points to a broad range of risks. "All kinds of cancers, Parkinson's, asthma, allergies and cardiovascular diseases," says Van de Wouw. The manufacturer of Pitcher has been asked for a response. "We were not directly involved in the lawsuit between PAN and Ctbg. So we are taking note of the ruling and will accept it," says Jan-Willem van der Klugt, bulb manager at Adama. The use of Pitcher will be prohibited from May 2027.

title: Podcast De Dag: Trump's problems
lead: US President Trump has been hit hard in the midterm elections. Thanks to the blue tsunami, the Democrats now have both a majority in the House and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>. What does this huge Democratic victory mean for Donald Trump? Listen here: you can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Enjoying it? Be sure to subscribe. American expert and lawyer Kenneth Manusama explains in the podcast De Dag what the Democrats can do with that majority. Because the demands are clear: America must become more affordable, the Iran war must stop, and the deployment of ICE agents must change. President Trump immediately threatened to use his veto if, in his view, things go in the wrong direction. But Trump also has to make sure that the Republican party continues to stand behind him. Respond? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editors: Rosanne Sies Final editing: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: Suspects Tarwekamp: plan went from stealing bridal gowns to arson
lead: Greater clarity about what exactly preceded the devastating explosion in a flat on Tarwekamp two years ago. That is what the court in The Hague tried to obtain this afternoon from the four suspects who were heard on the first day of the hearing. Six people did not survive that explosion. This morning the main suspect Moshtag B. was already heard by the judges. B. was questioned about statements from himself, the three other suspects and those of his ex-girlfriend. It was her bridal fashion shop that the attack with heavy fireworks and about 175 litres of petrol was aimed at. Possessive and jealous: In the interrogation of the main suspect and the statements of his ex-girlfriend, it emerges that she initially felt pampered in the relationship. He often took her out to eat, gave her many gifts and a monthly allowance. Later in the relationship Moshtag B. became possessive and jealous because he thought his girlfriend was cheating. So he regularly hung around her home and her bridal shop, and Moshtag B. cloned her phone, allowing him to read along with her messages on social media among others. He also reportedly forbade her from associating with other men and required her to take a lie detector test. Shortly after she had ultimately ended the relationship, the devastating explosion took place at the bridal fashion shop on Tarwekamp. Months of contact: That the main suspect felt his honour was harmed and wanted to financially ruin her had already emerged earlier from a reconstruction by NOS. But how exactly that was to happen was long unclear to co-suspects Mourad B., his cousin Ilias B. and Adil A., as the trio stated in their interrogations today. Those interrogations revealed that they had been in contact with the main suspect for months before the eventual explosion on 7 December. They explained how for a long time they did not know exactly what they were supposed to do, and on whose orders. They stated that since August they had met several times in various combinations to discuss plans. Mourad B. was the first to be involved by the main suspect, whom he knew from Roosendaal. Moshtag B. reportedly explained that he wanted to carry out an attack on a bridal fashion shop on behalf of an organisation. From stealing dresses to arson: But what kind of damage they were to cause exactly remained uncertain for a long time and was regularly a topic of conversation among the suspects. For example, Mourad B. claimed that initially it would be about stealing bridal dresses from the shop to then sell them. Suspects also said they would cause damage in the bridal shop by smashing tiles or applying paint to the walls. In the autumn the preparations took off and they bought items for starting a fire. The suspects also researched via ChatGPT which substance burns best and bought jerrycans. There was much discussion about how much petrol was exactly needed. In addition, they searched for torches that would spread the fire and the suspects talked about acquiring Cobra's, heavily illegal fireworks. These were ultimately reportedly bought by Ilias B. Sets of black clothing were also purchased which the suspects could wear during the attack. 170 litres of petrol: They first put on that clothing on 30 November. Then police by chance found a white Ford Transit van at a shopping centre in Oosterhout, with Mourad B. and Ilias B. dressed in black. They were waiting there for Adil A., who had dropped out of the job. Police found the men there with fourteen jerrycans containing 170 litres of petrol. Despite suspicions of an attempted attack, they were released the next day. A week later Mourad B. and Ilias B. went to Tarwekamp with new clothing and jerrycans of petrol, where they caused the explosion in the early morning. According to Moshtag B. he did not know they would use so much petrol. He himself was in London at that time. He had followed his ex-girlfriend there. At the end of the interrogation he told how he learned of the attack. "I woke up and the first thing I thought was: 'is this Tarwekamp?'. Only when I saw her car and the aerial photo did I know it was there."

title: Up to 30 percent fewer livestock farms expected as a result of nitrogen plans
lead: More animals per farm, 10 to 30 percent fewer livestock farms in the Netherlands, and an agricultural sector better in balance with what our country can bear. This is what the nitrogen plans of <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">minister Van Essen</entity> of Agriculture will lead to, according to Wageningen researchers. They also state that the plans do not endanger food security. "The nitrogen package is very far-reaching for the farming families involved," emphasises lead researcher Petra Berkhout of Wageningen University directly. "At the same time, shrinking the livestock sector is necessary to meet nature and environmental goals, and it is crucial that governments can grant permits again. If part of the livestock farmers stop, that also creates space and opportunities for the farmers who continue." Berkhout and colleagues carried out the research on commission from the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity>, as often happens with far-reaching cabinet plans. The Wageningen University study is a first, rough analysis of the economic impact on farm businesses of the nitrogen plans as Van Essen presented them in June. Many details had not been worked out in those plans and there were still many uncertainties. In the nitrogen bill that Van Essen presented yesterday, he deviated from his earlier plans on a few points - after a summer of demonstrations by farmers and intensive talks with the agricultural sector - but the bulk is unchanged. Substantial investments For dairy farmers, the targets they must meet in the future are the most concrete. These concern, for example, the amount of ammonia they may emit and requirements for the amount of grassland per cow. In a sample of dairy farmers, the researchers found that less than 5 percent of dairy farms already meet the requirements of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. That means many livestock farmers must invest heavily to meet what the cabinet asks of them. There is admittedly a nitrogen fund to help livestock farmers with this, but Berkhout expects that even with that support a considerable share of livestock farms will not survive, including in sectors other than dairy farming. "If we look at all sectors of livestock farming, we expect even without the nitrogen plans that about 10 percent of all farms will stop between now and 2035," says Berkhout. "As a result of the nitrogen plans, we expect 10 to 30 percent additional farms to stop in that period." In total, this is expected to mean 20 to 40 percent fewer livestock farms in 2035. Scale enlargement "Whether you can continue depends on how much fat you have on the bones," says Berkhout. She expects that large farms will more easily stay afloat, because they can usually invest more. "Compare it to making your home more sustainable. Someone with a higher income can more easily buy a heat pump than someone who earns less." The nitrogen plans therefore further encourage scale enlargement, the researchers expect. "In 2000, a dairy farm had an average of 51 cows, now it has 114," says Berkhout. "An average pig farm has 3,900 pigs and an average poultry farm has 45,000 laying hens. Those numbers will increase." Berkhout does not necessarily see scale enlargement as something negative. "The most important thing is that livestock farms comply with the law and produce our food as cleanly as possible. Costs for extra environmental investments often land on the farm rather than in the price of products. So it is quite logical that farmers want more animals to earn back the costs." At the same time, this does not mean that all small or medium-sized farms will disappear. "There is always a diversity of farms and that will remain so," Berkhout expects. "Small farms are often already less intensive or have additional sources of income, such as a farm shop. If they meet the standards, such farms can also continue to exist in the future." More than we eat ourselves The researchers conclude that food security is not endangered by the nitrogen plans. "The plans mainly affect the number of animals we keep in the Netherlands. We do import some beef, but for all other animal products we produce much more than we eat ourselves," says Berkhout. With the presentation of the nitrogen plans yesterday, in which not all details have been worked out and there are therefore still uncertainties, this research is not outdated according to Berkhout. "Things may still change, especially in the zones around nature areas, but the overall task for agriculture to reduce ammonia emissions by 42 to 46 percent has not changed. In broad terms, our conclusions therefore still hold."

title: Three men jailed for multi-million fraud with fake returns at Amazon
lead: Two men aged 30 and 32 from Hoogeveen and a man aged 34 from Emmer-Compascuum have been sentenced by the court in Assen to prison terms for defrauding the web shop Amazon. The three made millions with fake returns. They did this by ordering expensive items such as phones, smartwatches and other electronics and then sending the parcels back empty. They filled the boxes with worthless materials that matched the weight of the original shipment. As a result, Amazon processed it as a return and refunded the purchase amount. By chance The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> came across the three by chance. The 30-year-old main suspect was arrested in Hoogeveen in early 2023 after a shooting. In a warehouse, officers then found drugs and shelves full of luxury goods. Not long after, it became clear that a great many shipments were being sent back to Amazon from the man's address. The police soon discovered that he was not acting alone. In the house of a fellow resident they found more evidence of so-called 'refund fraud' in the form of cash, goods still packed in boxes, phones, computers and shipping labels. The man from Emmer-Compascuum also turned out to have accounts with the web shop through which many items were ordered and returned. In addition, he had money counting machines, shipping codes, empty envelopes, set squares and a barcode scanner at home. Demand of 2,5 million The man from Hoogeveen was sentenced to almost three years (35 months) in prison. His 32-year-old fellow resident must serve 20 months behind bars. The man from Emmer-Compascuum received a sentence of 10 months, of which 5 are suspended. In addition, he must perform 480 hours of community service. Amazon is also claiming total damages of around 2,5 million dollars from the three fraudsters, RTV Drenthe reports. The multinational can still take the matter to the civil court for that.

title: 'Human rights organisations are breaking off cooperation with the Court under American pressure'
lead: At least twenty human rights organisations have since last year significantly restricted or completely halted their cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC), based in The Hague. That is what emerges from a survey by investigative platform Investico and German medium Süddeutsche Zeitung of one hundred non-profit organisations, in cooperation with weekly De Groene Amsterdammer. Many NGOs no longer dare to work with the Court as a result of the sanctions the United States imposed on the Court in February last year. For example, several human rights organisations have stopped cooperating because their contracts with American funders forbid it. Several organisations have quietly stopped their work, Investico writes. This includes large organisations such as Human Rights Watch. Restrictive sanctions The Court is being hit hard by the sanctions, as research by news agency AP also showed earlier. US President Trump introduced those penalties by decree, after the Court issued arrest warrants against, among others, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, for war crimes and crimes against humanity. That sanctions package consists of financial penalties and visa restrictions for people who help the ICC with its investigation into American nationals and allies of the US, such as Israel. Because of the sanctions, staff no longer have access to their property and assets in the US, such as money they hold in an American bank account. They also may no longer buy anything from American companies or use their services. Recently <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>-Trump added to that with new financial measures that will largely take effect next year. In a video message, foreign minister Rubio said the US will prohibit "transactions with this rogue court". No evidence, no investigations The organisations with strong local networks are indispensable in preparing criminal cases, because they provide, among other things, evidence, eyewitness accounts and new forms of evidence with which the Court can proceed. They are also often the first on the ground and can share specialist expertise on local legislation. "They are a very important part of our work", says former chief prosecutor Fatou Bensouda to Investico. "They do not investigate for us, but they do provide us with tips, which allows us to find ways to substantiate evidence." Bensouda worked for the ICC until 2021 and was herself hit by American sanctions when she was placed on a blacklist in 2020. What does the International Criminal Court do? The International Criminal Court investigates, prosecutes and tries persons accused of human rights violations and serves as a complement to the national courts of member states. The Court investigates, among other things, genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. All countries in the European Union are obliged to carry out decisions of the Court, because of the Rome Statute. The Court is not recognised by all countries in the world. For example, the United States, Israel, Russia and Iran do not recognise the Court. The number of organisations that have halted cooperation may be higher. According to Investico, many NGOs refuse to speak openly with journalists about the consequences of the sanctions. A number of organisations did so. Save the Children Netherlands says it is having difficulty finding a new form of cooperation. The platform Forensic Architecture says it is reconsidering its working relationship with the ICC. Fear of more sanctions Investigations that at first glance have nothing to do with the United States or Israel are also being affected. "For example, a European organisation that conducts investigations in East Africa, the Middle East and Ukraine was forbidden by an American donor to use its money for the Court", Investico writes. European organisations that do not fall directly under the sanctions have also halted cooperation. "We cannot accept the risk of being sanctioned ourselves, and of all our other work being endangered as a result", a German NGO tells the researchers.

title: From Ukraine to Iran: Democrats' victory will have worldwide impact
lead: The resounding election victory of the Democrats in the midterm Congressional elections will have a major impact not only in the US but also abroad. Such a drastic reversal of the balance of power in Washington cannot go unnoticed in countries such as Ukraine, Iran and Israel. The difference will only become clear once the newly elected American members of Congress actually begin their work. That happens on 3 January. Then the election winners in the Capitol will take up powerful positions: the House of Representatives, <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and also the influential foreign affairs and intelligence committees in Congress are all expected to get Democratic chairs. That is why Trump will become what Americans call a lame duck: a crippled president. He will no longer have the comfortable relationship with a cooperative Republican majority in Congress. The Democrats will likely block his domestic political agenda and vice versa. A political stalemate looms. Still a lot of power. It is a well-known pattern in American politics that a lame-duck president shifts his attention to foreign policy. This is often seen as an attempt by the president to build his political legacy during his last two years in the White House. The American constitution gives the president a great deal of power in the area of foreign policy, a power Trump has already used extensively, for example by attacking Iran and imposing high trade tariffs on many countries. What can Congress do about that? And what will the rest of the world notice? Ukraine and Russia. This spring Trump stopped virtually all financial and military aid to Ukraine, leaving the country unable to defend itself against the Russian missiles and drones that claim victims there daily. And last month Trump lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel, by his own account to do something about high fuel prices in the US. The move went very much against Ukraine's wishes, because diesel sales fill the Russian war chest. Many members of Congress, including many Republicans, are angry about Trump's course toward Moscow and Kyiv. Congress could resume aid to Ukraine with a new law and stop imports of Russian fuel. Several Republicans in the current Congress are also outspoken supporters of that. Republicans in the new parliament will probably join them as well, if only to distance themselves from Trump's warm ties with Putin. If supporters of such a law secure a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate, Trump cannot even block the resumption of aid to Ukraine with a veto. Iran. "We must stop the war in Iran immediately," said the presumed Democratic chair of the new Congress, Hakeem Jeffries, to CNN. Trump did not ask Congress for permission to start the war in Iran, even though that is formally required. In the months that followed, the Democratic minority in Congress submitted several resolutions to force him to back down. One of them was adopted with the support of some Republicans, but was subsequently ignored by Trump. The new Democratic majority in both chambers has the power to restrict defense spending. With that, they could gain some grip on the war against Iran. Despite Democrat Jeffries' firm language, Congress cannot end the war on its own. However, the Democrats can prevent Trump from escalating on a large scale by simply not allocating money for it. The question is whether the Democrats will do that. Because Iran seems determined to keep the Strait of Hormuz in its grip and thereby keep gas and oil prices high on the world market. Some members of Congress may think that argues for continuing the war. An American capitulation there could also turn against the Democrats. So there is a chance Trump can still win Congress over on this point. Israel. Mainly because of the genocidal violence in Gaza and the close ties between Trump and Prime Minister Netanyahu, support for Israel among Democrats has fallen sharply. Under their leadership, Congress could halt the billions in American military aid to Israel. Just before the elections, Trump himself promised to do that, starting early next year. He said Israel does not need that aid and can henceforth pay for American weapons itself. It was a last-minute attempt to take the wind out of the Democrats' sails and came too late to make a difference. But with that statement in hand, it may become even easier in Congress to restrict direct aid to Israel. On the other hand, the Democrats remain deeply divided over Israel. When Democrats in Congress proposed halting aid to Israel last summer, less than half of their own representatives voted in favor. Even after the elections, there will be Democrats in Congress who want to spare Israel. The Democrats may reach a compromise among themselves and adopt a less far-reaching measure, such as halting the supply of heavy bombs to Israel or imposing sanctions on the country for the expansion of Jewish settlements on the West Bank. Humanitarian aid programs. Last year Trump stopped about 5 billion dollars in aid via USAID, which forced large foreign aid programs against hunger and for the prevention of diseases such as Ebola and AIDS to be shut down. Although the Democrats cannot undo those actions by Trump and cannot revive USAID, they can use laws to resume part of the foreign aid.

title: Finding a majority for the tax plan remains a complex puzzle for the minority cabinet
lead: It is still uncertain whether <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> will succeed in getting the tax plan for next year through parliament. Tonight in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> it appeared that many political maneuvers are probably needed to find a way out. Because the minority cabinet did not succeed in finding a majority in advance, the parliamentary groups now have the lead. Governing party D66 wants to talk with opposition parties Pro and Volt about their proposal to change the plans so that the tax on wealth goes up, in order to be able to lower the tax for workers. With the support of these parties, a majority for the tax plan in both the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Eerste Kamer</entity> is within reach. "I understand the direction," said D66 MP Oosterhuis about the proposal from Pro and Volt. But according to coalition partner VVD, such an amendment to the tax plan is in conflict with the coalition agreement. "It is unthinkable that this proposal in this form would be supported by one of the coalition parties," said VVD MP Van Eijk about it. Besides conflicting with the coalition agreement, such a 'millionaires tax' is according to her bad for the investment climate and therefore bad for the Netherlands. The CDA considers the opposition parties' proposal "going too far". MP Van Dijk also sees "that there are a number of points in it that touch on what we agreed in the coalition agreement". She could not yet say whether her party could support it. But her <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">fractievoorzitter Bontenbal</entity> said yesterday that he is not happy that the cabinet is "gambling" on a majority for the tax plan. He accused the VVD of an overly rigid attitude on taxing wealth. In the Tweede Kamer a small majority can still be found, but in the Senate it is still far away. Business transfer In total, Pro and Volt want to shift 1.5 billion euros from the tax on labour to the tax on wealth. Part of that, 180 million euros, must come from abolishing a tax-favorable scheme for transferring a business. The minority cabinet's coalition agreement states precisely that this scheme should be left untouched. Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity> made clear that he has "gone deep" with his proposal. He accepts that income tax for workers goes up, but with his amendment proposal it is somewhat less. "It is an attempt to make it fairer. Everyone must contribute, not only workers." He is willing to negotiate the precise details. Divided votes If the proposal from Pro and Volt is amended so that it no longer conflicts with the coalition agreement, it could still be the key to a solution. The coalition parties do not rule out that they will vote in a divided way, although CDA MP Van Dijk said that this is "certainly not the intention". During the votes, the amendments proposed by the MPs are voted on first. If such an amendment is adopted, it immediately becomes part of the tax plan. Only after that is the entire plan voted on. It is possible that parties vote against an amendment but still support the final tax plan. In the corridors a scenario is circulating that the VVD votes against the part of the tax plan on the higher wealth tax, but accepts that the proposal gets a majority with the support of D66 and CDA anyway. That would save the tax plan and the coalition. In the debate, the coalition parties did not respond to questions about this. In the coming days much can still be negotiated and therefore the plans can still change. The votes on the tax plan are scheduled for next week Thursday, 12 November.

title: German politician found dead in hotel room
lead: In Germany, 55-year-old politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel room. Aiwanger was deputy premier and minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-ez">Economische Zaken</entity> in the southern state of Bavaria. Yesterday he was due to give a speech in Berlin, but because he did not feel well he had cancelled. When Aiwanger, the national and regional chairman of the conservative party Freie Wähler, could not be reached later, his body was found in the Berlin hotel room. No cause of death has been made public. The police are conducting an investigation. Aiwanger was a successful pig farmer when he entered the political stage just over twenty years ago. In 2002 he joined the Freie Wähler. Six years later, in 2008, Aiwanger and the party entered the Bavarian state parliament for the first time. This was not the end for the Freie Wähler. In 2018 the CSU (sister party of the CDU of Chancellor Merz) and the Freie Wähler formed a coalition and Aiwanger became minister of Economic Affairs and deputy premier of Bavaria. Antisemitic pamphlet Despite these successes, Aiwanger's political career suddenly hung by a thread a few years later, after a revelation by the Süddeutsche Zeitung. The German newspaper wrote in 2023 that the farmer from Lower Bavaria had written and distributed an antisemitic pamphlet during his secondary school years. Aiwanger denied having written the pamphlet, but did admit that "one or more copies" of the pamphlet had been found in his schoolbag. Not long after, Aiwanger's older brother, Helmut, said he was behind the pamphlet. The controversy did not die down after this confession. Former classmates of Aiwanger stated that the politician had on several occasions given the Hitler salute in the past. Even so, the scandal did not bring down Aiwanger politically. A few months after the revelation, the Freie Wähler achieved the best election result in Bavaria's history. Under his leadership, Freie Wähler also made large gains in the local elections in Bavaria this spring. Shock The sudden death of Aiwanger is being met with shock. Markus Söder, Bavarian minister-president and CSU party leader, speaks of an "absolute tragedy". "We are all deeply shocked." The chair of the Bavarian state parliament has also responded. Ilse Aigner (CSU) speaks of a "great loss for the Bavarian state parliament and for all of politics in Bavaria". Aiwanger leaves behind two children and a girlfriend.

title: Brussels does not expect better times with Trump: 'Not worse would already be a win'
lead: Nobody thinks that the Republican election defeat in America will suddenly make everything better in the strained relationship between the US and the EU. That is what diplomats in Brussels say, on condition they may speak anonymously. "Not worse would already be a win," says one, somewhat bitterly. " Keep calm and carry on ," says another. Carrying on with what he is doing is exactly what the American ambassador to the European Union is also doing. The European Commission cannot get energy prices down, he sneered yesterday on X, a few hours after the election result came in. He then called for a longer postponement of European climate rules, which will also affect the American energy sector. The ambassador did not mention that energy prices are partly so high because of the war in Iran, which President Trump started with Israel in February. In Brussels they have by now become used to this way of communicating. And the expectation is that the Americans will continue in the same vein. Optimists and pessimists Still, there are optimists and pessimists. The optimists point to the devastating results for President Trump and his initial, moderate reaction in which he says he wants to work together with the Democrats. From this they draw hope for the future that everything will remain as it is, or that the American president, under pressure from a Democratic Congress, may even be somewhat less hard-line abroad. The pessimists, on the other hand, are holding their breath. Now that Trump is losing so much power at home, he will direct his anger at the EU and NATO, they think. American presidents have a lot of room to go their own way in international affairs. Support for Ukraine For example regarding the war in Ukraine. In <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and the House of Representatives there is strong support for Ukraine. Yet Trump has repeatedly taken Russia's side recently. For example, he concluded a diesel deal with President Putin and accused President Zelensky of not wanting to make peace. This offers little hope, the pessimists fear, for the negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States taking place next week in Abu Dhabi. Still, some politicians hope that the American Congress can help Ukraine more, such as German Foreign Minister Wadephul and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. They express the hope that the new Congress in the US will continue to support Ukraine and put more pressure on Russia. Withdrawing troops from Europe At NATO, they are mainly looking at the American plan to withdraw troops from Europe. The details of that are expected next month. Pessimists fear that Trump will use the review to punish European countries that, in his view, contribute too little to NATO and have not supported him sufficiently in the Iran war. Currently there are around 80,000 American military personnel in Europe. According to some American media, the Americans are considering withdrawing up to a third of those troops. But the optimists think it will not go that far and that everything will be handled in good consultation. In 2020 Trump also wanted to remove 10,000 soldiers from Germany. Congress also opposed that at the time. Ultimately, Trump's successor Joe Biden halted the plan. Too much damaged In Europe they think Trump will go his own way wherever possible. German Chancellor Merz expects Trump to use presidential decrees to bypass Congress, he said yesterday. That is why in Brussels they are also not counting on lower import duties or on the reversal of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. Whether the optimists or the pessimists will be proven right remains to be seen. But on one thing almost everyone agrees: the relationship between the EU and the US will never be the same again as before Trump. Too much has been damaged in recent years. So the motto is: keep going and stand on your own feet as quickly as possible. Become independent in all areas where the EU still needs the US, such as defence, tech, energy and the economy. That will be a matter of trial and error. "These interim American elections must not distract Europe from protecting its own interests," said French Foreign Minister Barrot yesterday.

title: House of Representatives wants to retrain a civil servant facing cuts to become a teacher
lead: A majority in the House of Representatives wants civil servants at the Ministry of Education who are being cut to be able to voluntarily retrain as teachers or lecturers. Governing party VVD will ask <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> today to work out a plan for this. The idea is in any case supported by coalition parties D66 and CDA and opposition parties JA21 and 50Plus. The VVD is putting forward this proposal in response to the cabinet plan to cut 25,000 national civil servants over the coming nine years. By 2035 some 16 percent of the approximately 160,000 (full-time) civil servants must be cut, as State Secretary Van der Burg for Agile Government announced at the end of October. 'Two birds with one stone' The party says that at the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap</entity> (OCW) civil servants work "with enormous passion" for education. VVD MP Kisteman thinks the cabinet can "kill two birds with one stone". "The announced cuts are a good opportunity to have these dedicated people voluntarily retrained, at the government's expense, for a job in education", said Kisteman. Civil servants could be given a weekly study day to retrain. This is not the first time an attempt has been made to get national civil servants into the classroom, mainly to reduce the teacher shortage. The idea is that a move from education civil servant to school is less complicated, because they have a lot of knowledge in that field. It could also encourage civil servants to start a different career and become career changers. In 2008 a pilot was launched to help fifty national civil servants move into a job at a secondary school. They received an extensive introduction period and training, and a possible drop in salary would be supplemented for a few years. Setback The project turned out not to be a success, as the <entity id="org:sociaal-economische-raad">SER</entity> concluded in a report in 2011. Schools were not keen on career changers with too little pedagogical experience. The feared drop in salary also proved a considerable hurdle. The national civil servants turned out to be afraid of losing their permanent job at the ministry and were not convinced that their new employer could offer the necessary stability. It is not yet clear whether the 25,000 national civil servants will be forced onto the street, because State Secretary Van der Burg is still going to work out his plan, and that will come in spring 2027. The Ministry of Education does have over 400 million euros in the budget to tackle the teacher shortage. Today or later it will become clear whether the cabinet will get to work on the retraining plan for national civil servants.

title: New institute for Defence to keep the Netherlands safe with faster innovations
lead: To keep the Netherlands safe, Defence wants to innovate faster and on a larger scale. A new institute is meant to play a role in this. <entity id="person:derk-boswijk">Staatssecretaris Boswijk</entity> of Defence has presented the National Institute for Defence Technology (NIDT) at the barracks in Stroe. Companies and start-ups can register there for an assignment. The institute hopes to bring knowledge and techniques together in this way. That is badly needed, Boswijk said at the opening. According to the state secretary, the war in Ukraine shows how quickly the battlefield is changing. "Drones, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and autonomous systems are changing the way war is waged", said Boswijk. The new institute is not looking for a new type of drone, he says. "Because that could be outdated again tomorrow. We are mainly looking for new ways of collaborating, experimenting and scaling up." 350 million euros From 2028, the NIDT will receive 350 million euros per year to contribute to those innovations. The goal is to innovate, produce and scale up faster, more flexibly and more in the home country where necessary. The first assignment that companies and start-ups can apply for concerns protecting the North Sea. The threat there has been felt for longer, the state secretary says, due to Russian spy ships and the shadow fleet sailing around there. "It is one of the busiest seas in the world and forms the gateway to the Rotterdam port. Above and below water lie fibre optic cables, wind farms and offshore installations that are crucial to our economy and security", says Boswijk. Therefore, the institute is not waiting until it is fully operational in 2028, but the first assignment has already been issued now. Not only defence companies can register for it, but also start-ups, universities and other knowledge institutions.

title: Bomb threats on European flights again, plane aborts flight to Rome
lead: As earlier this week, a series of European flights has again been hit by bomb threats. A plane travelling from Dublin to Rome made a stopover at a French military base in Évreux after a bomb threat. The aircraft, belonging to the Irish airline Aer Lingus, landed safely. The 115 passengers and six crew members are fine, say the French authorities. They are now off the aircraft. Bomb experts were deployed to examine the plane. Évreux lies about 100 kilometres northwest of Paris. British Minister of Transport Heidi Alexander says that her <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> takes bomb threats seriously, but according to her, in this case there is a "series of malicious hoax threats". Also in Poland and Bulgaria This morning a suspicious report also came in about a flight by LOT Polish Airlines, from Warsaw to Brussels. Belgian media report that the federal <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> ruled shortly afterwards that security measures were not necessary. The aircraft landed as planned at Brussels Airport. Similar reports come from Bulgaria. There, bomb warnings reportedly came in about three aircraft: two of them landed in Sofia, the third in Plovdiv. This happened under escort of Bulgarian fighter jets. The Czech police say they received reports about four flights, all of which landed in Prague. "We assess the risk as low," the police said on X. It has now reportedly become clear that no explosives were found on any of the aircraft. Furthermore, a bomb threat is reported about a Finnair aircraft travelling from Helsinki to Rome. Under escort of the Italian air force it landed safely in the Italian capital. Another Finnair aircraft also faced a bomb threat; it landed from Helsinki in Vienna as planned. In Bucharest, according to the BBC, a flight from Milan that a bomb threat had been received about also landed. It was a Wizz Air aircraft with nearly 200 people on board. In recent days several bomb threats have also come in about European flights. On Tuesday at least seven flights were affected. No explosives were found, but air traffic was disrupted. Now a larger number of flights is involved; again, as far as is known, no explosive has been found. About possible bomb threats concerning flights via the Netherlands, nothing has been reported. What is being said? Aviation expert Joris Melkert says that many reports also come in that never make the news, partly to prevent people from getting the wrong ideas. "It is always a question of how serious a report is. That depends on: where does it come in, what is being said? Ultimately it can be decided to inform the crew so they can make a precautionary landing." If the report is taken seriously, according to Melkert it is obvious not to land at a busy airport. "Then you choose a remote airfield, or a military air force base that is easy to secure." Hybrid warfare Who is behind the reports is still under investigation. European officials regularly point out that Russia, and to a lesser extent Iran, is guilty of hybrid warfare on European soil. The Chair of the European Commission, Von der Leyen, said earlier that it increasingly does not stop at threats. Arson, sabotage and attempted assassinations regularly occur. It is far from always clear who is responsible, but many incidents can be attributed to Russia.

title: Brabant carnival gets an ambassador in The Hague: 'A tremendous honorary post'
lead: CDA MP <entity id="person:inge-van-dijk">Inge van Dijk</entity> has today been appointed the first Ambassador of the Brabant Carnival. The idea is that the folk festival will in this way get better attention in national politics. At 11.11 a.m., how could it be otherwise, Van Dijk was officially appointed. "A tremendous honorary post," she calls it. Earlier this year she was approached by the Brabant Carnival Federation (BCF). "Of course you can't say no to a task like that." The BCF hopes that with the appointment it will get more attention in national politics for the social and cultural significance of carnival. Van Dijk grew up in the Brabant region De Peel and also has an affinity with the festivity. "Carnival is instilled with the cradle milk there, it started already at primary school. The annual parade, celebrating with the neighbourhood association, it's all part of it." Regulations Brabant is proud of this festive culture, she says. At the same time Van Dijk knows that many carnival associations, just like other associations in the country, run into problems with organisation. "It concerns regulations, permits and a shortage of volunteers, for example." It is Van Dijk's task to keep asking for attention for that in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. "If nobody does that, it will only become harder." So the Eleventh of the Eleventh event in <entity id="org:gemeente-tilburg">Tilburg</entity> next week is hanging by a thread, because the local hospitality sector and the municipality disagree about admitting minors to the festivities. This story is not a standalone one, Van Dijk says. "We see one event after another being cancelled. Because the organisation can't reach agreement with the municipality, or because it becomes too chaotic due to a jumble of rules. We have to prevent that." And so the conga line reaches the Binnenhof, writes Omroep Brabant. "Remember: in The Hague they don't know carnival. I have missed a lot of carnival celebrations because I simply have to work. It just doesn't live here." Still, according to the MP it is important to "keep certain cultural events high on the agenda of our society". "So that people continue to recognise themselves in them."

title: Battle for ECB presidency, 'one of the most influential people in Europe'
lead: Decades after Wim Duisenberg took office as the first president of the European Central Bank (ECB), Klaas Knot may once again bring a Dutchman to the helm of the bank. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> officially put him forward yesterday as the Dutch candidate . The contest seems to be mainly between two people: Klaas Knot and the Spaniard Pablo Hernández de Cos. "Although it is actually not a two-way contest, because these appointments always have to be seen in a broader context," says ABN Amro economist Jan-Paul van de Kerke. Two other important ECB positions are also becoming vacant: that of the German board member Isabel Schnabel and that of the Irish chief economist Philip Lane. "Those positions go into a big lottery and all factor into the decision on who becomes the new ECB president," said Van de Kerke. Notable detail: should Knot become the new president, Frank Elderson, the current Dutch ECB board member, will probably have to leave. "It is unlikely that one country would supply two board members to the ECB's executive board, and that also weighs in the choice of the new president," says Van de Kerke. No dark horse It could be that another candidate emerges who is chosen at the last moment over these two favourites. For example, Christine Lagarde was also not one of the big favourites for the post before her appointment as ECB president. "But the situation is now fundamentally different," says chief economist of ING Germany, Carsten Brzeski. When the French Lagarde was appointed, the appointment of the German Ursula von der Leyen as president of the European Commission played a major role. "President Macron is said to have proposed her so that Lagarde could take the position of ECB president," says Brzeski. "But no such deal is on the table at the moment. There is no sign of a dark horse at present." Where the ECB president comes from should not really matter, but should Knot get the job, economists say it could have positive consequences for the Netherlands. "In practice it can indeed have advantages," says Van de Kerke. "Why do we want Rutte as head of NATO? It gives you a small informational advantage over other countries, because the line is shorter." Brzeski also lists the advantages. "We must not forget that with that role you are one of the most influential people in Europe." The ECB president takes part in various important EU meetings with heads of government, among others. Will it be a hawk or a dove? Still, one should not overestimate what a Dutch ECB president could mean, says Van de Kerke. "It is largely about image and network benefits." Jakob de Haan, professor of political economy at the University of Groningen, also looks at the appointment. "It should not matter for policy whether there is a Dutch president or not." The ECB must ensure that prices remain stable and inflation is kept under control. To this end it can, among other things, raise or lower interest rates. "The perception is that a southern European is more inclined to favour lower interest rates than a northern European," says De Haan. This contrast is also called the difference between doves and hawks. The Spaniard Coz is seen as a dove: someone who is less quick to raise interest rates, as opposed to the Dutch Knot, a hawk who intervenes more quickly. De Haan thinks that image is unjustified. "In the past, Knot has almost always supported decisions on purchase programmes." With rising inflation and the sky-high French government debt , the new ECB president faces a difficult task. "Let us hope this does not escalate further, but should the ECB end up in that situation, Knot is exceptionally well suited to respond," says De Haan. A decision on who will become the new ECB president is expected in mid-December.

title: Gas and oil prices fall, lowest petrol price since July
lead: After months of rising prices, the gas price has dropped sharply in recent days. Since the midterm elections in the United States, the price of gas has fallen to about 88 euros per megawatt hour, a drop of 15 percent. Especially in October, the European gas price kept rising. The peak came last Friday, when the price came close to 104 euros per megawatt hour. The 100 euro per megawatt hour threshold had been broken a few days earlier, which had not happened since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The oil price is also falling. This was already slightly visible at the pump before the American elections, but was reinforced by the election result. The price of a barrel of oil dipped below 100 dollars yesterday for the first time in over a month. Today the advisory price for a litre of petrol at the pump has fallen to below 2.50 euros. That is the lowest level since July. The price of diesel has also fallen. It is currently 2.647 euros per litre. That is almost 18 cents below the record of mid-September, when the price was 2.824 euros. Delay Pump prices lag behind the oil price. In the Netherlands the effect is also somewhat smaller, because a large part of the petrol price consists of excise duty and VAT. Petrol and diesel are also still much more expensive than at the beginning of this year. The drop in the gas price also does not show up on the energy bill right away. Energy suppliers do not pass on the price drop immediately. They often wait to see whether the drop continues, especially when they paid a high purchase price. People with a dynamic contract already see the price drop. Effect of the election result uncertain Fuel prices this year were strongly influenced by the war in Iran, which involved the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. In February, before America and Israel started that war, the gas price was still below 30 euros per megawatt hour. It is still very uncertain what effect the American election result will have on the war and therefore on the oil price.

title: Large-scale military deployment in Jakarta over wiretapping scandal and power struggle
lead: Amid a major wiretapping scandal, many thousands of soldiers have been mobilised in the Indonesian capital Jakarta. Tensions have risen sharply over what appears to be a power struggle between President Prabowo Subianto and his predecessor Joko Widodo. The army has placed 21.000 soldiers on heightened state of readiness. Military vehicles are among other things standing on the square in front of the presidential palace, Indonesian media report. Senior police officials were arrested this week on suspicion of wiretapping President Prabowo. One of the suspects is Listyo Sigit, who is known as a confidant of former president Widodo. The impression has arisen that Listyo was keeping an eye on the current president Prabowo on behalf of Widodo. Firing squad The presidential palace calls the tapping of Prabowo's phone treason. If Listyo and the other top officials are found guilty, they could be executed by firing squad. The confrontation between the Prabowo camp and the Widodo camp is also erupting in another way. The son of former president Widodo, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, is currently still vice president, but it is uncertain whether that will remain so. The High Court has ruled that Gibran's secondary school diploma is not valid. There appears to be a majority in parliament for a parliamentary inquiry into the authenticity of his diplomas. In the most extreme case, the vice president could be removed from office. Former president in court today The vice president's father had to appear today in a court in Jakarta. Former president Widodo had to testify in a defamation case he has brought against people who accuse him of forging his school diplomas. This case is separate from the political uproar over his son's diplomas. The former president was cheered by hundreds of supporters on arrival, news agency AP reports. The authorities say thousands of police officers and soldiers have been deployed to keep order around the court. There have recently been many protests in Indonesia. According to the national authorities, the mobilisation of the more than 20.000 soldiers is not directly related to the political tensions surrounding the wiretapping scandal. The army leadership states that this is a "regular deployment" to safeguard Indonesia's national security. Some of the troops are also said to have been placed on readiness for upcoming military exercises. Prabowo's popularity has plummeted Critics fear that President Prabowo will crack down hard on demonstrations and unrest. His popularity has plunged in recent months, polls show. The economy is performing poorly and there is growing discontent over Prabowo's centralisation of power. Prabowo was a general under dictator Suharto, who ruled Indonesia for more than thirty years. Prabowo won the presidential election in 2024 by a wide margin. He had lost to Widodo twice before. In the election two years ago, Prabowo was in fact backed by Widodo, whose son was appointed vice president. But relations between the two now appear to have reached boiling point.

title: France protests again for higher wages, government wants to prevent unrest
lead: On the large nationwide protest day in France, riot police in Lyon charged demonstrators and used tear gas. Some protesters chanted anti-police slogans. Some of them were dressed in black and wore face coverings. A secondary school near Toulouse was set on fire. In Paris, pupils and other demonstrators faced the police after they had blocked a street with rubbish bins. In a suburb of the capital, rubbish bins were set alight. The fire brigade quickly brought the fire under control. The large demonstration in Paris began this afternoon at 15.00. In various cities, including Marseille, Lyon and Nantes, demonstrators already took to the streets this morning. According to French interior minister Nuñez, 270,000 people are currently taking part in protests at 180 locations across the country, not counting Paris. This is what the demonstrations look like at this moment in Paris: Demonstrators walk through the streets waving flags. They demand higher wages, changes to the budget plans and more investment in education. Preventing unrest: The trade unions expect 40,000 to 80,000 demonstrators in Paris to take part in a protest march from Place de la République via Boulevard Voltaire to Place de la Nation. The march began at 15.00. A demonstration straight through the city, from Bastille to Concorde, was banned by the prefect. Because of the protests, the Eiffel Tower, among other sites, is closed to the public. The Louvre is open, but some rooms are closed, according to the website. Dozens of schools across the country have been occupied by pupils, and a large part of the staff in secondary education is on strike. Public transport is not running or is running irregularly in many places, and there are actions in healthcare. The authorities want to prevent the protests from again descending into chaos like on 17 October, when the protest day completely got out of hand and massive destruction was caused. Around 70,000 police and gendarmerie officers have been deployed.

title: Graffiti sprayers force Amsterdam metro to a standstill, entire carriage covered in graffiti
lead: Footage has been published on YouTube showing an Amsterdam metro being blocked at a station with a bicycle on the tracks. Then about twenty people sprayed the metro train completely with graffiti. Passengers were still on board at that moment. It appears they could not get off because the doors were pushed shut. The incident took place last Saturday evening on Henk Sneevlietweg in Amsterdam Nieuw-West, the Amsterdam transport company GVB reports. Quite shaken. It is not clear who is behind the incident. In the footage the perpetrators are masked and wear hoods. The incident took place on 31 October, Halloween, and the title of the YouTube video is 'Amsterdam Nightmare'. "Our driver was quite shaken by the incident," a spokesperson for the transport company says. "We can imagine that for passengers too this was a frightening situation." The footage was uploaded by an account called 'Locos Worldwide'. Over the past five years it has posted fifteen videos showing graffiti on train and metro carriages. Not only in the Netherlands, but across Europe. The videos appear to have been made in Copenhagen, Madrid and Paris, among other places. The Amsterdam metro train could not continue driving after the action. Even the windows at the driver's position were covered in paint. The GVB calls it a "serious form of vandalism". The transport company also says the safety of passengers and staff has been endangered. "Not only has a metro been defaced, but a bicycle was also thrown onto the tracks. That carries major safety risks," a spokesperson says. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> also strongly condemns the actions of the group of graffiti sprayers. "I can imagine that it was very frightening for those on board," a spokesperson for the Amsterdam police says. An investigation has been started. Cleaned up. Passengers were helped out of the metro by the GVB. The metro train was cleaned on Monday and is back in service on the timetable. The GVB will try to recover the costs from the perpetrators. Footage of their action has been preserved and will be handed over to the police. The transport company spends many millions a year on the consequences of graffiti and vandalism in general.

title: Podcast De Dag: The Hague grapples with an open marriage
lead: The tax plan has kept The Hague's politics busy for months. Normally almost a rubber stamp, it is now a source of much political debate. The question of whether to seek a majority from left or right divides the minority cabinet. And after a debate yesterday, there is still little prospect of clarity. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. What makes this tax plan so complicated? Political reporter Roel Bolsius explains it in the podcast De Dag. The coalition parties have now agreed that in the extreme case, they may all vote differently on the tax plan, in the hope that a majority will come into sight in such an open marriage. <entity id="person:rob-jetten">Premier Jetten</entity> remains consistently optimistic that his <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> will finalise the tax plan in the coming week. Reactions: email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial team: Rosanne Sies Final editing: Rosanne Sies

title: Verwey-Jonker Instituut applies for suspension of payments, bankruptcy looms
lead: The renowned Verwey-Jonker Instituut is on the verge of bankruptcy. The independent research bureau says it is suffering too much from budget cuts and the rise of AI. The institute has applied to the court for suspension of payments. The Verwey-Jonker Instituut in Utrecht has existed since 1993. The bureau researches and advises on socio-societal issues, such as domestic violence, prejudice and discrimination, and bullying in the workplace. The foundation says it has been hit hard by cuts to research budgets and can no longer pay its own bills. The Verwey-Jonker Instituut also reports that technological developments are getting in its way. It sees that its clients increasingly use AI instead of engaging researchers. Cheaper premises, smaller board To reduce costs, the Verwey-Jonker Instituut moved to cheaper premises and its board was reduced. This has not helped enough. Leadership at the bureau has also been turbulent recently. Last year an interim director was appointed who left again this spring. He is now being replaced by the chair of the supervisory board. The research bureau wants to continue its activities where possible, but a trustee must now determine to what extent that is feasible. Ongoing research will be completed this year as far as possible, but a different solution will have to be found for longer-running studies and collaborations with other organisations. The institute is named after Dr Hilda Verwey-Jonker (1908-2004), the first graduate sociologist in the Netherlands. In 1932 she obtained her doctoral degree. She was then active in politics and sat on the board of the Social Economic Council.

title: British comedian Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
lead: British comedian Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault. The court in London has just ruled to that effect. It concerns one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Brand is expected to receive a prison sentence, and the judge will pronounce sentence on Monday. He has been taken into pre-trial detention. The 51-year-old Brand was charged with seven sexual offences: three counts of rape, three counts of assault and one attempted assault between 1999 and 2009. He has always said he is innocent. Last year, in a video on Instagram, Brand said that in his younger years he had been a fool and a sex addict, "but what I never was is a rapist". 'Sexual predator' "A relentless sexual predator", is how the public prosecutor already described Brand last month. According to the prosecutor, Brand has a "random and insatiable desire for some form of sexual contact". In a packed courtroom today, more became clear about what took place during that ten-year period. Six women had reported him anonymously. "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually abuse women", writes chief detective Andy Furphy of the police in a statement. "As his fame grew, so did his sense of superiority." Not even a minute Brand has been found guilty, among other things, of assaulting a woman in a bar in London in 2004. Brand and the victim were not even talking at the bar for a minute when he grabbed her breasts. He is also guilty of assaulting a woman in a radio studio, where he fondled the victim's face, breasts and buttocks. The third conviction for assault dates from 2009, when he unsolicited pushed his face, nose and mouth into a woman's crotch. Brand has also been found guilty of rape. In 2009 he had sex with a woman by mutual consent, before anally raping her. "He hurt me and injured me, and when I asked him to stop, he didn't", the victim stated before the court. 'No one is above the law' "I hope this conviction clearly signals that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful he or she may be", said Furphy. The police expect that more victims will now dare to come forward. The long list of allegations does not end with these convictions. Two other women also accuse Brand of rape, and that investigation is ongoing. There is also a civil case against Brand in the United States, also for rape. He is alleged to have forced an extra into sex during the filming of the movie Arthur. Controversial Brand built his career with films such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall (2008), Despicable Me and Get Him to the Greek (2010). He has also presented various programmes on British radio and television. He is also known for his controversial stand-up comedy, in which he does not shy away from subjects such as drug use. He has also written a book about, among other things, his years of addiction to drugs and alcohol. Today the Briton is mainly active online as a podcaster, for example with his podcast Stay Free with Russell Brand. He also shares videos on YouTube, where he has millions of followers. In his videos he regularly discusses conspiracy theories. He also gained some fame through his marriage to pop star Katy Perry between 2010 and 2012.

title: Iron wire strung across bike paths, police investigating: 'This goes beyond mischief'
lead: In Den Bosch, youths strung iron wire across bike paths in two places. The police are investigating . No one has been arrested yet. "This goes beyond mischief, so we hope the boys will come forward", says a police spokesperson to Omroep Brabant . One woman fell over the iron wire last weekend, the broadcaster writes. She was slightly injured. In another place, an alert motorist was able to remove the strung wire in time. Residents of the Maaspoort neighbourhood are shocked. "You don't want to think about it if you're cycling there with your little one", says a man who regularly cycles through the neighbourhood. Another man, who lives a bit further on, says he is paying extra attention after the incidents. "If my children have to cycle to school, I tell them that too." Eggs Residents say there is more nuisance from wayward youths. For example, they reportedly throw eggs and kick doors. The police are familiar with those stories. The police are investigating the incidents with the iron wire falls and have the suspected perpetrators on camera. It possibly involves two minor boys. "We have camera footage that helps us", the spokesperson said.

title: Rubber boat carrying migrants set out from the Netherlands into the North Sea
lead: The rubber boat that was pulled from the sea near Breskens last Saturday set out from Dutch territory. That is what the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> (OM) reports. The OM does not disclose exactly where the boat set out. But according to Omroep Zeeland, the people on board were not hypothermic when they were found. According to various sources the broadcaster spoke to, the migrants probably boarded east of Breskens. It is not yet clear what the intended final destination was. People smuggling On board the rubber boat were 36 Afghan migrants and two suspected people smugglers from Sudan. Of the 38 people on board in total, six were minors. The two Sudanese men have been arrested and are suspected of people smuggling. On Tuesday the investigating judge ruled that they will remain in custody for another two weeks. Disturbing situation On Saturday at around 06.00 the Royal Marechaussee received a report of a disturbing situation on the North Sea, near the Zeeland-Flemish coast. When the coast guard and the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> arrived at the rubber boat, it was adrift, as the engine was missing. The small boat was towed to the marina of Cadzand, where the migrants were taken off board and checked by ambulance staff. The search for the boat's engine off the coast of Cadzand is still ongoing. Watch the footage of the rubber boat at sea here:

title: Man (26) from Roermond arrested after driving into police car, officer injured
lead: A man (26) from Roermond was arrested this afternoon after a police chase from Belgium. The man reportedly drove into a police car in the Limburg town of Echt. An officer was injured in the process, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. Belgian officers chased the man because he ignored a stop sign. The Dutch police joined in the chase. Around 15.00 hours the man drove at high speed in the opposite direction into one of the police cars. The driver then tried to flee on foot, but officers were able to apprehend him. "Unknown substances" were in the vehicle, a spokesperson tells L1 Nieuws . The police are still investigating this. Wreckage The injured officer has been taken to hospital for a check-up. How the officer is doing has not been announced. The collision happened on the Loperweg in Echt. The road was then closed. According to the police, the damage was extensive.

title: Paraguayan president Peña steps down after massive protests over bank freeze
lead: After days of massive protests, President Peña of Paraguay has stepped down. Paraguayans took to the streets furiously earlier this week after the digital bank Ueno was placed under supervision. Since then, millions of residents have been unable to access their money. The 47-year-old Peña came under fire because of his ties to the bank. For example, he was still a shareholder until last year. Residents therefore demanded his resignation, a call he has now answered. "Dear compatriots", says Peña in the video message. "Today I speak to you at one of the most difficult moments of my life." He says he is stepping down so as not to endanger stability in the country. Massive protests His departure does not come as a surprise. The country has been in turmoil since Ueno was placed under curatorship by the Paraguayan central bank. This was done because of serious financial problems. The bank reportedly has less than half of the required minimum equity and too little money to meet direct payment obligations, according to the financial regulator. The bank is also suspected of having taken too much risk when granting loans. For example, Ueno reportedly lent money to owners of persons affiliated with the bank, while guarantees or collateral were lacking. To prevent the bank from collapsing, all deposits and banking transactions have been blocked. About 3 million customers cannot access their money as a result. That amounts to about 60 percent of the adult population of the Latin American country. Demonstrators took to the streets en masse: "President Santiago Peña and his party have stolen all our savings!", shouted one of the demonstrators in the capital Asunción. Earlier this week the opposition also expressed fury at Peña and demanded his resignation. Members of parliament accuse Peña of conflict of interest, inadequate financial oversight, misuse of pension funds and cover-up practices in connection with the banking crisis. In his statement he offered apologies, but did not take responsibility for the chaos that arose. He said his priority is ensuring that savers get their money back. "Behind every deposit lie years of effort, sacrifice and family plans", said the president. Impeachment procedure Although Peña seems to be leaving voluntarily, his resignation still has to be officially accepted by the Paraguayan Congress. The chance of that happening is small. Shortly after he announced his departure, parliament voted unanimously to start impeachment proceedings. If that procedure is continued and he is formally removed from office, he loses his immunity and special protection as a former head of state. That means he is no longer protected from criminal prosecution. Santiago Peña came to power in 2023 as one of the youngest presidents in Paraguayan history. His right-conservative Colorado party has governed the country almost without interruption since 1947. Peña was previously minister of Finance. Following his resignation, vice president Pedro Alliana is expected to take over from him.

title: Emotional statements from Tarwekamp victims: 'Affects me every second'
lead: "I felt the ground being pulled from under my feet", says a woman when she read that Sunday morning that there had been an explosion at Tarwekamp. She lives in Greece with her three children; her 44-year-old husband worked in The Hague. He did not survive the disaster. Due to the heavy explosion at a bridal fashion store and the subsequent collapse on 7 December 2024, six people lost their lives in the Hague neighbourhood of Mariahoeve. Today is the second of nine court days in total in the trial. Based on written statements, survivors of the disaster and relatives of the victims spoke. Better half "When I contacted the manager of the apartment building and he confirmed that his apartment had been completely destroyed, I fell to my knees and cried as I had never cried in my life", the wife continued in her statement. "V. was my better half, my companion, my fellow traveller. His loss affects me every second of my life." "Everything has changed", writes V.'s brother in his statement. He also represents the parents of the Greek man. "I am trying to understand it all so that I can get over it, but that is impossible." V. financially supported his parents. "Where we had hoped for a new future, everything is now gone." Escaped via a tree branch One of the survivors is a then 8-year-old boy from a Chinese family . The boy lost his parents and sister in one blow. He came out of the building almost unharmed, with a scratch on his face and a small wound on his foot. He was woken by a loud bang, the judge said in his statement. "He first thought he had fallen out of bed. He had the feeling he was in a dream in which he was falling", according to his statement. The boy then heard his father shouting for help and saw that there was a fire. He managed to escape via a tree branch. Outside he met a firefighter, who took him to an ambulance. He saw that his house was no longer there. "The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> said: 'We did our best, but they are no longer alive'. The boy was shocked and asked: 'All three?' The police confirmed that. Then his eyes turned red." According to an aunt, he stayed strong when he was told that his family had not survived the disaster. Only when he realised he would also have to go to another school did the tears come. "He probably realised then that he would have to miss not only his father, mother and sister, but also his friends." A 31-year-old man from Voorburg also lost his life. At that moment he was staying with a female friend at Tarwekamp, who did survive the disaster. The sixth victim has not been made public. Slot machines The owner of a café at Tarwekamp described how the slot machines had saved him. "They hung over us like a bridge. Otherwise everything would have collapsed on top of us. A female friend he was with in the café that morning was also rescued. She was in a coma for five days afterwards. She said that early that morning she heard three bangs. "At the first one I thought of fireworks, at the last one I thought Russia was attacking us. We held each other's hands." Eventually the man managed to free himself. How she herself got out of the rubble she no longer knows exactly. Her fine motor skills have been affected, she does not sleep and she is afraid of the dark. She also has panic attacks and flashbacks. The truth "I find what happened terrible", responded Mourad B. (31). He is suspected of carrying out the attack. His nephew and presumed co-perpetrator Ilias B. (25) said: "Every day I go to bed with it and get up with it." According to the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity>, Moshtag B. (35) ordered the attack. He allegedly wanted to destroy her bridal shop out of revenge against his ex-girlfriend. He is also suspected of stalking, threatening and abusing his then girlfriend. Her victim statement revealed that the explosion had financially and mentally ruined her. "I am trying to make the best of it." Adil A.
