In 2018 the two countries still agreed to negotiate faster. When Japan imposed economic measures against Russia in 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, Moscow broke off talks completely. Last August Putin visited one of the disputed islands for the first time. He tasted caviar in a fish factory, promised the hospital to replace a rusted-through ambulance and had a drone shown to him at a school. "Just like a holiday resort", he told residents about the sunny weather. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called his visit "completely unacceptable". Monument Subsequently Russia unveiled in Khabarovsk a 15-metre-high monument of a Soviet soldier smashing a Japanese border marker bearing the symbol of the Japanese emperor. Tokyo immediately demanded that Russia remove it. That relations between Tokyo and Beijing have also deteriorated considerably plays into Moscow's hands. On the day of Putin's visit to Iturup, Etorofu in Japan, the Russian and Chinese ambassadors referred in a joint letter to their struggle against "Japanese militarism". Meanwhile their navy ships and bombers are increasingly exercising together around Japan. Moscow and Beijing also call Japan's defence buildup a "joint threat to world peace". When Japan announced new economic sanctions last month, Moscow threatened countermeasures. Later that month the Russian security service reported that it had arrested a journalist from the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun in Sakhalin on suspicion of espionage. He was transferred to Moscow. According to Russia experts, this is a form of "hostage diplomacy". A quarter of the profit Japan Tobacco's share has meanwhile lost nearly a third of its value. The company had expected in 2026 to derive well over 10 percent of its turnover and a quarter of its operating profit from Russia. At the end of September it had assets there worth 1,500 billion yen, about 8.5 billion euros. The company is currently investigating the consequences. Japan Tobacco has been active in Russia since 1999 and, with a market share of about 40 percent, is the largest cigarette maker there. After the invasion of Ukraine the company announced it would make no new investments, but it kept making and selling cigarettes. Other Japanese companies, such as Toyota and Nissan, did withdraw. Putin is now using a 2023 arrangement that allows Russia to place assets of companies from "unfriendly countries" under its own management. In September that also happened with the Russian activities of Swiss Nestlé. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said at the time that Moscow was taking into account the "increasing involvement of unfriendly countries in direct hostilities against us". After Russian state intervention, company assets regularly end up in the hands of people close to the Kremlin. Japan Tobacco already paid tax in Russia, but it is still unclear whether the company can still transfer its profits to Japan and whether Moscow can use that money for the war. Two weeks ago the Japanese and Russian foreign ministers met at the G20 in Atlanta, for the first time in about five years. Foreign minister Motegi demanded the release of the journalist. His Russian counterpart Lavrov only wanted full talks again if Tokyo withdraws its "unfriendly policy".

title: Another migrant boat off the Belgian coast, eleven people clung to a buoy
lead: For the second day in a row, a boat with migrants has been spotted off the coast of Belgium. Belgian media report this. Two people were in a boat off the coast of Ostend. Eleven other migrants had clung to a large buoy in the North Sea. The Maritime Rescue and Coordination Centre, the reporting point for accidents at sea, received a report around 17.40 hours, according to the Flemish broadcaster VRT, of a small boat with two migrants on board. It could be located thanks to a helicopter and four rescue boats. "The NH90 helicopter then carried out a reconnaissance flight, during which it found eleven people on a buoy in French waters", says Dries Derudder of the Agency for Maritime Services and Coast (MDK) to the VRT. Hypothermia One of the two people on board showed signs of hypothermia. The pair told the emergency services that eleven people were still in the water. It is not known whether they were originally on board or why they may have left the boat. The group had clung to a large black-and-yellow buoy in French waters. Such a buoy shows ships on which side they must pass. Both the VRT and HLN say it is not clear whether there are any injured among the rescued migrants. Bobbing off the coast for hours Yesterday a migrant boat was also located off the Belgian coast. The migrants had themselves called in the emergency services. The boat bobbed for hours off the coast of Nieuwpoort; the nearly thirty people on board did not want to be taken off the boat. In the afternoon the boat crossed the border with France. The group of migrants was taken off the boat during the night at their request and brought to Dunkirk, the VRT reports. "They had already been travelling for twenty hours and many people were completely exhausted and hypothermic", says a police spokesperson to the Flemish public broadcaster. According to the VRT, the group consisted mainly of Afghans.

title: Missing 13-year-old girl from Berlin found dead in house next to seriously wounded 22-year-old man
lead: A 13-year-old girl from Berlin who had been missing since last week Tuesday was found dead yesterday in an empty house in the village of Altglietzen, close to the border with Poland. The police also found a seriously wounded 22-year-old man there. He has been taken to hospital in critical condition and is being guarded there by the police. The Berlin police say they assume that the man is responsible for the abduction and murder of the girl Lisa. German media write that the man attempted suicide when the police entered the house. Officers reportedly found him with a life-threatening gunshot wound. He is in intensive care. 113 Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking helps, and you can do so anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113. The Public Prosecution Service (OM) reports that, like the girl Lisa, he comes from the Berlin district of Marzahn-Hellersdorf. He has no criminal record, but since August 2025 two investigations have been running into him for obtaining and possessing images of child abuse. For example, during a house search in March 2025, 900 "incriminating files" were seized from the man. Later, "a large number of other alleged child pornography items" were also found on his mobile phone. 'Mama misses you' Lisa's case has gripped Germany for days. The girl left her parents' home at around 7:15 a.m. last week Tuesday to go to school. According to her sister, she was texting a friend on the way, but the contact suddenly stopped, three minutes after she had left her house. She never arrived at her school. That same afternoon the police issued a missing person notice with a photo of Lisa. Her mother also appealed for people to look out for her daughter. On social media she wrote: "Mama hopes you come home safe and sound. Mama misses you so much." Massive search Neighbourhood residents distributed flyers about the disappearance in the following days, and the police deployed a helicopter and search dogs. Last Saturday more than 200 officers went door to door in the neighbourhood where Lisa lived. On Sunday a police chief said that a crime was being considered. Shortly afterwards, Lisa's body was found by chance in the empty house. According to German media, the police had received a report from the homeowner that unauthorised persons had entered the vacant property. Once inside, officers found both Lisa's body and the 22-year-old seriously wounded suspect. Lisa's discovery was a coincidence The police had no indication that Lisa would be there, a spokesperson says. "In the end it was purely by chance that this break-in led to her discovery," said a press spokesperson for the OM in Berlin to German media. According to the OM, an autopsy has been performed on Lisa's body, but no cause of death has yet been determined. It is also still unclear when she died. There are no indications that the suspect and the victim knew each other. The police say they assume Lisa was a random victim. The investigation of the empty house and of the man's home in Berlin is still ongoing.

title: Pensions for healthcare, construction, metal and technology sectors up slightly
lead: For pensioners from healthcare, construction, and the metal and technology sector, pension payouts will rise slightly from 2027. Retired healthcare workers will see their payouts rise by 0.75 percent. In construction, pensioners will get 0.8 percent more, and former metal workers 0.82 percent. Pension funds Zorg & Welzijn, BpfBouw and PMT announced this today. These are the three largest pension funds that switched to the new pension system at the start of this year. The funds face uncertainty in the financial markets. On the stock market there is optimism this year about the performance of tech companies, but the American attack on Iran has caused unrest and fluctuations. New pension system. In the new pension system, pension payouts of pensioners will, more than in the old system, move with the investment results of a pension fund. If those results are good, pensions can be increased faster than in the old system. If investments do less well or poorly, it can more quickly happen that pensions are not increased or, in an extreme case, reduced. To prevent a reduction, pension funds do keep a buffer. In addition, younger employees are invested in riskier ways than older employees and pensioners. That risk now differs by age group is visible in the figures. For example, 35-year-olds at PMT see their pension pot return 10.7 percent so far this year. Someone close to retirement age sees their pension assets decrease slightly by 0.3 percent. On the other hand, the assets of older employees and pensioners are better protected against stock market fluctuations than those of young people. At most pension funds, the return for pensioners is now only paid out for a third. This too should help ensure that in a bad investment year, pensions cannot be raised or must be lowered. The remaining return carries over to the following year. In 2028, a third of the (hopefully higher) return will again be used to increase pensions. Distributing reserves. Last year, among others, pensioners of PFZW, PMT and BpfBouw received a substantial extra increase due to the switch to the new system. In the new system, pension funds need to hold much fewer reserves, and a large part of those reserves therefore flows into personal pension pots, which pensioners will see immediately (after the final calculation) in their pension payouts. On 1 January 2027, another 37 funds will switch, with 2 million pensioners. Pension adviser AON recently calculated at the request of NOS that they may hope for a substantial increase in their pensions. This applies to, among others, retired civil servants, retail workers, transport workers and bank employees. An increase of between 12 and 25 percent is very possible for this group of pensioners. Then by far most Dutch people who are members of a pension fund will have been moved to the new system. No later than 2028 all pension funds must have switched to the new pension system.

title: Republican submits motion to remove US Defense Secretary Hegseth
lead: The Republican congressman Thomas Massie wants to remove US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth from office. He had already announced that he wanted to start an impeachment procedure against one of the most prominent people in the Trump administration. Whether the proposal will also lead to Hegseth's departure is still an open question. Massie read his resolution aloud in the House of Representatives, where for the first time since the midterms there was a session again. The Republican from Kentucky accuses Hegseth of abusing his power and exceeding international humanitarian law in Iran. He also points to his role in military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. He calls the minister "a threat to the Constitution", who is guilty of "serious crimes and misdemeanors". Massie is known as a major critic of the Trump administration. With the motion against his fellow party member he wants to pressure Trump to replace him, he indicates. That would be better for the Republican party than waiting to see what the Democrats will do after their win in the midterms. 'No worries' Trump says he will continue to support Hegseth. In a response the president calls Massie an "ice-cold loser", with "a lot of hatred in his heart". He is referring to Massie's lost primary election. He lost to the Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, who takes over his seat in two months. Hegseth himself says he is not worried about the attempt at an impeachment procedure. He has announced that he will hold his first press conference in more than half a year on Tuesday to go further into the threat. "If we want to question the military actions of the Trump administration, I will gladly do so all day long." Vote The vote on the proposal in the House of Representatives could already take place on Wednesday. A majority is achievable if a handful of Republicans also vote for removal alongside Democrats, and that possibility exists. But for an actual impeachment, support from two thirds of <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> is still needed afterwards. That will be a much bigger challenge, even if the Democrats have a majority from January. Two years ago the impeachment procedure for Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas failed at that stage. That was only the second time the House of Representatives voted for the impeachment of an American secretary. William Belknap had the honour in 1876. He resigned himself before he could be removed from office.

title: Iran war turns expected decline into new record year for coal
lead: Burning coal leads to unhealthy air pollution and emits greenhouse gases that warm the earth, more than oil and natural gas do. When people make plans to tackle climate change, they first want to get rid of coal. Yet in practice that proves difficult. Never before did the world use as much coal as last year. This year the record seems set to fall again. Coal replaces natural gas Five years ago countries at the climate summit in Glasgow still promised to reduce. At the climate summit in Turkey, countries are gathering again this week and must conclude that it still has not come to that. At the end of last year the International Energy Agency (IEA) still forecast a slight decline. In September the organisation had to revise this. It now estimates that coal use will rise by just over 1 percent. Other research also sees an increase, but a slightly smaller one. The Iran war gave coal a big boost. This conflict led to a huge disruption of energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. That hardly affects coal, but it helps the fuel via a detour. Because of the disruption, less liquefied natural gas, or LNG, passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Worldwide there is less for sale and the available gas is more expensive. That affects the choices of companies. To generate electricity you can use both natural gas and coal. "Gas and coal power plants can therefore compensate for each other", says Daan Walter, researcher at energy think tank Ember. "When gas prices rise, you prefer to burn coal." That is not possible everywhere. You must have coal power plants that have room to generate extra electricity. Two countries where that clearly happened were Pakistan and Bangladesh. "Pakistan is not receiving LNG supplies from Qatar", says Walter, "so coal goes up. Why? Because they had a lot of coal power plants built by China." Previously those ran for a limited number of hours, so they could easily step in. Also in the Netherlands Elsewhere, Poland, South Korea and Japan partly swapped natural gas for coal. The Netherlands also burned more coal than in both 2024 and 2025. In The Hague this already led to tentative discussion about the future of coal power plants that from 2030 are legally no longer allowed to burn coal. According to Walter, not every increase was due to high gas prices. In Vietnam and India drought led to hydroelectric plants producing less electricity. Emerging countries in particular also use more electricity year after year and have to generate more and more. When you see how sharply gas prices rose, Walter finds the extent to which countries switched rather meagre. Walter expects the current revival of coal to prove temporary. In the European Union, coal use has been declining steadily for years. After Russia's large-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the gas price rose to astronomical heights. At that time European countries used more coal to generate electricity for a while, but after that shock the decline simply continued. Short-term effect "In the short term, countries throw in some extra coal for now, because then the lights don't have to go out", says Walter. "In the long term we throw solar and wind energy at it." Now too he expects renewable energy to gain ground after the shock, compared with both gas and coal. When the peak will come exactly is hard to say, but in the long term analysts expect a worldwide decline in coal use. Last year, however, was once again a warning for countries that importing energy makes them vulnerable to its loss or to price shocks. Countries with large amounts of coal in the ground know they can rely on that. They also appear to be investing more money in coal. According to the IEA, investment in coal has not been this high since 2012, mainly in China. According to Walter, you must look closely at exactly what is being invested in. China is still building coal power plants. Although they will run less and less, he expects. China increasingly uses them as a 'backup' when there is no wind or sun. Hardly any investment is going into coal mines. According to Walter this illustrates that investors realise the revival will be short-lived. "It is a kind of sugar rush for coal power plants. We can now turn them up for a while and earn money, because gas is expensive", says Walter. "But they all know that after the sugar rush comes the crash. Then you don't want to have invested in new coal mines."

title: Iran war leads to dip in fossil fuel emissions
lead: High prices at the pump, concerns about low gas reserves and political unrest. The Iran war caused an unprecedented disruption of energy markets. Partly because of that shock, the world will emit slightly less CO2 this year from burning coal, oil and natural gas. That is according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists. The scientists do not expect a break in trend but a short-lived dip. "A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging", says Pierre Friedlingstein, one of the researchers involved, "but a decline partly caused by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution." Blow to oil use Oil use is decreasing in particular. At the start of this year growth was still expected, but emissions are expected to be 1.9 percent lower. Emissions from natural gas also fell, but only to a limited extent. "That is logical", says Jilles van den Beukel, energy expert at The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies. The war was most disruptive for oil. "For gas only LNG (liquefied gas, ed.) has been hit. And that is only a limited part of the gas supply." The Iran war did not lead to a single energy shock. The problems changed over the course of the year, says Van den Beukel. Initially there was mainly a shortage of crude oil because it could no longer get out through the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Gulf states and the United States are increasingly succeeding in getting crude oil onto the world market. In recent months the crisis has mainly affected oil products such as diesel. Ukraine damaged Russian refineries and oil products from the Middle East are reaching the world market less. The other refineries simply could not make any more diesel, kerosene and petrol. "What has also played a role recently is high prices for tankers", says Van den Beukel. "There is a shortage of tankers because they have to sail ever longer routes." Decline despite Trump In the European Union, fossil emissions are expected to fall by 1.5 percent. More surprising is that other blocs are also seeing a decline. Although China by far remains the largest emitter, due to the enormous amounts of coal it burns, its emissions have barely increased since 2024. This year scientists expect a decline of 0.9 percent. After a brief increase, US emissions are expected to fall by 1.3 percent. That is remarkable, since President Donald Trump has scrapped virtually all American climate policy and is heavily investing in fossil fuels. But even Trump seems unable to stop the decline in coal in his country. Emissions from burning coal did increase worldwide, as the only fossil fuel. Coal was barely affected by the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and was a 'safe haven' for many countries. Read more about the unexpected record year for coal here: Solar panels and wind turbines are also experiencing strong growth again in 2026. However, it stands out that the International Energy Agency (IEA) expects less capacity to be added than last year despite the energy shock of the Iran war. It is the first time in 21 years that the increase is not breaking a record. The IEA attributes this mainly to a change in rules in China. Still, it is strong growth. In rich countries the increase in renewable energy is steady, but the IEA no longer expects feverish growth. Quite different is what is expected in the coming years in Southeast Asia and Africa. The costs of solar panels in particular have fallen so much that it is becoming increasingly attractive for people in emerging countries. They sometimes invest without governments making policy for this. Pakistan is a good example. "One of our analysts was on holiday there", says Daan Walter, researcher at energy think tank Ember. "Next to the fish cart at the local market there are simply solar panels. You take them home and put them on your roof with an instructional TikTok video." A Bloomberg journalist noted that solar panels in Nigeria are becoming increasingly popular as wedding gifts. Without the rise of renewable energy, the world would now be using 8 percent more fossil fuels. At the same time, the hunger for energy is enormous, especially in emerging countries. The researchers at the Global Carbon Project think that after the dip, fossil fuel use will nevertheless start rising again. "Accelerated deployment of solar and wind energy, batteries and electric vehicles is reducing emissions in dozens of countries and is outpacing emissions growth in many more", says Glen Peters, one of the scientists involved. "But the changes are not yet enough to reach a peak in global emissions."

title: Booker Prize goes to M. John Harrison, oldest winner ever
lead: The Booker Prize goes this year to British writer M. John Harrison. He wins the prestigious literary prize for his book The End of Everything , a satirical story about a post-apocalyptic Great Britain. It is the first time the literary prize, worth 50,000 pounds, has gone to a science fiction story. Harrison himself stresses that he does not want to be confined by that label. "I think this book, and now also this prize, shows that it is entirely possible to write a book that mixes not just two, but three or four genres together", he said during a press conference after the award ceremony. A touch of optimism The End of Everything is set in the near future, after a catastrophe has disrupted society. The story revolves around a beachcomber on the Channel coast who finds an object that changes shape. Harrison is praised for his writing skill, but also his humour. According to jury chair Mary Beard, the author views "the politics of today through the lens of the future". "It is a book that turns you upside down. It brings a wry smile, but despite its subject it still leaves you with a touch of optimism", said the jury. At 81, the author is the oldest winner of the Booker Prize. That record had been held since 2019 by the then 79-year-old Margaret Atwood .

title: 'US aircraft withdrawn from second British base due to Iran threat'
lead: The US is removing aircraft from a second British air force base, The Wall Street Journal writes. Sources tell the American newspaper that the decision was made because of the threat from Iran. It concerns RAF Mildenhall, near Cambridge. Tanker aircraft stationed there are being removed. Two will depart this morning already for bases in Germany, others will follow later, the paper reports. Early last month the US already hastily withdrew bombers from the Fairford base. That base was possibly a target of terror suspects a few days earlier: five men were arrested because they behaved suspiciously near the base. Several more arrests followed later. The reason is unclear. It is not clear what the precise reason is for also withdrawing aircraft from Mildenhall. The WSJ does not know whether there is a specific threat or whether it is more about the general threat from Iran. Security has been tightened at a third base, Lakenheath. A British defence spokesperson does not wish to comment on the newspaper reports. It is policy not to comment on troop movements of other countries, it is said. The Pentagon was not reachable outside office hours for an explanation. Iranian target: Air force base Fairford was used by the American bombers for the attacks on Iran earlier this year. The Revolutionary Guard of that country already made clear at the time that it considers every base involved in the war a legitimate target. Fairford and Mildenhall, together with RAF Lakenheath, are the three most important airfields for the US in the United Kingdom. In total, according to British figures, around 11,000 American military personnel are stationed in the country.

title: Schools report child abuse more often, but 'recognising it remains difficult'
lead: On average, every class contains children who are dealing with abuse. Schools play an important role in recognising abuse. Suspicions are increasingly being passed on, but there is still much to be gained. That is why two years of research was carried out into the detection of child abuse at primary schools. Based on that knowledge, a digital toolkit for teachers has been created, which can be used from today. Signals at schools A large part of the week a child is at school. Teachers see and speak with children and their parents. In this way they play an important role in detecting abuse. This also became clear in a study of child torture. In children who had experienced this most severe form of abuse, there were often signs known at school. As in the case of an abused girl in Stadskanaal. She was beaten, locked in a cellar and sometimes given no food. The school saw that the girl talked less, did not play and was hungry. When she came to class with a cut on her head, the school made a report. More reports Despite their important position, few reports of child abuse come from schools, compared with other countries, it turned out seven years ago. In England and Germany it was over 20 percent of the total, in the Netherlands it was a few percent. But schools are now sounding the alarm more often. The number of reports from schools has since nearly doubled. They have also asked the organisation Veilig Thuis for advice much more often. Such advice is more accessible than making a report. The number of reports and advice in the first half of each year: The increase may be due to stricter rules. For schools, a step-by-step plan has long existed that must be used in cases of possible abuse, called the meldcode. In 2019 it was revised, to ensure that a report is always made when serious abuse is suspected. Also, more people trained to help teachers with such difficult situations are now present at schools. At least 500 primary schools and 200 secondary schools have a so-called attention officer. Acting in time Schools are therefore sounding the alarm more often, but early detection remains difficult for teachers, recent research into primary schools by the Nederlands Studiecentrum Criminaliteit en Rechtshandhaving shows. It was carried out by Veroni Eichelsheim, also professor at the University of Groningen, and Carlijn van Baak. "Teachers sometimes walk around for months or years with suspicions of abuse," says researcher Van Baak. "They try to arrange help for the family. It is often a search for what exactly is going on and when a report is needed." A shortage of knowledge plays a big role. "In training for primary school teachers, recognising child abuse, for example, is not standard content," says Van Baak. "Yet in practice it is so difficult, because it is not always visible." Fear also plays a role in reporting. "Fear that children or parents will no longer trust the teacher, or that violence in the home will increase." Another major hurdle is not found at school, but at Veilig Thuis. The organisation receives more than 100,000 reports a year and gives more than 100,000 pieces of advice. They can no longer cope with the work, they warned a month ago. "That is worrying," says researcher Van Baak. "Veilig Thuis is the only one that can link information about children together and conduct investigations. It is also the only route to mandatory help." The digital toolkit Over the two years of research, files were examined and people were interviewed. Based on this, a toolkit with and for teachers was created, using new and existing material, such as a broadcast of the NOS Jeugdjournaal. The aim is to recognise and deal with possible child abuse. "We will certainly use this toolkit," says Friso Kingma, director of Baasis, a school federation of about 2,700 pupils. "Our most important task is teaching the children things, but that is only possible if they feel good about themselves. Knowledge about abuse is therefore important." "A good moment for us to pick up the toolkit is, for example, at a recurring team meeting or a study day."

title: One million French people demand action against influential news channel CNews
lead: A petition to take one of France's most-watched news channels off the air has gathered more than 1 million signatures. According to the signatories, CNews is a mouthpiece for radical and far-right politicians. And opinion makers have repeatedly made racist statements there. CNews is "not a news channel, but a propaganda machine", according to the petition. "We have seen in the US what can happen when an influential news channel pushes a clear political agenda for years", a reference to the American Fox News and the rise of President Trump. Islamophobic This afternoon at 1 p.m., the competent committee of the French parliament will discuss the issue. It will decide whether the petition gives rise to a debate in parliament. Although the petition was launched in early June, it gained momentum at the end of October. According to French media, the trigger was the terrorist attack in Trappes, in which a Franco-Congolese man was killed. The perpetrator had racist and Islamophobic motives. Even if the petition does not end up on the political agenda, it is in any case seen as an important signal. According to critics, CNews increasingly follows the ideological course of radical right-wing parties such as Reconquête of Éric Zemmour and Rassemblement National (RN) of Marine Le Pen. Partly because of this, the channel is described as the French equivalent of Fox News. The commercial 24-hour channel would benefit if Le Pen won the French presidential elections next spring and kept her promise to further privatise the public broadcaster. That is a measure CNews has long been positive about. Devout Catholic But there is also an ideological motive. Behind the successful CNews stands the Breton billionaire and media mogul Vincent Bolloré. The right-conservative and devout Catholic entrepreneur is one of the ten richest French people and maintains close contacts with radical right politicians such as Le Pen and Zemmour. Through his media conglomerate, Bolloré has further expanded his influence on the French media landscape in recent years. So far that a verb has been coined for it: se bolloriser. For example, he owns the influential weekly Le Journal du Dimanche and StudioCanal, one of the largest film production companies in Europe. He is also a major shareholder in companies and publishers through various concerns, and Bolloré has interests in the French commercial radio station Europe1, for example. CNews was revived in 2017 and has since been called to account several times by the French media watchdog Arcom. Since the beginning of this year, Arcom has imposed a total of 300,000 euros in fines on the channel. According to the petition's initiators, the channel has been reprimanded almost 30 times since 2019. The most recent fine was imposed after statements by journalist Erik Tegnér. He is the founder of the radical right medium Frontières and is regularly invited by CNews. After the riots around the Champions League final in Paris last year, he described the violence as a "civilisation problem" and attributed it to immigration. It is an example of the many statements that, according to opponents, sow hatred. CNews rejects these accusations and says it is precisely defending freedom of expression. Earlier this year, Bally Bagayoko, the new mayor of Seine-Saint-Denis on behalf of the radical left party La France Insoumise (LFI), was compared to a monkey by a guest during a live broadcast on CNews. The French public prosecutor's office has launched an investigation. CNews says the statement was taken out of context. Expulsion order Another controversy surrounding CNews concerned the Russian media personality Xenia Fedorova. Before she regularly joined CNews in 2025, she was director of the French branch of the Russian state propaganda channel Russia Today (RT). That channel was banned in the EU after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. At CNews she grew into a regular guest and an outspoken defender of the Kremlin's positions, and she regularly criticised Western support for Ukraine. Last July the French ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> issued an expulsion order against her for spreading Kremlin propaganda and disinformation. According to the authorities she poses a threat to public order and French interests. She is under house arrest. Canal+, the media group of which CNews is part and in which Bolloré is a major shareholder, called her expulsion an attack on freedom of expression. In France there are also voices calling for CNews to be kept. Several parliamentary petitions state that the channel contributes to the diversity of the French media landscape. "The channel is watched by millions of viewers and offers debates and analyses that enrich the range of available news reporting", according to one of the petitions.

title: 'Trump effect' at universities: more international students than agreed
lead: After years of a decline in the number of new international students, slightly more have started a degree at a Dutch university this year. Umbrella organisation UNL thinks that due to "developments in the United States" more students are choosing a European degree. Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, he has introduced various measures that frustrate higher education. For example, he tightened checks on visa applications, openly quarrelled with several universities and tampered with academic freedom. International students are therefore more often choosing a European degree, the figures show. Both from within the 30 countries of the EEA (European Economic Area) and from outside it, more people came to the Netherlands: 800 more Europeans and 300 more from outside Europe. Especially from Asia, relatively considerably more students came. Higher than agreed The figures are higher than universities have agreed. To limit the number of international students, it was agreed that a maximum of 16.766 international students per year may begin a degree in the Netherlands. This academic year there were, according to provisional figures, 17.600. Around 600 more students began a technical programme. The rise comes after three years of declining interest from abroad, due to the discouragement policy of programmes and the government. This is intended to counter Anglicisation, keep more housing available for Dutch students and not spend Dutch tax money on international students. Numerus fixus tightened To limit inflow, several universities are lowering the numerus fixus that applies to English-language versions of programmes such as psychology, economics, business administration and political science. Chair Caspar van den Berg of the Universiteiten van Nederland says this keeps the inflow "well balanced". "We urgently need international talent, certainly in priority sectors such as technology," he says. "At the same time, universities have agreed to cap international inflow. We are therefore taking targeted additional measures." The Interstedelijk Studenten Overleg is opposed to a numerus fixus. "Every student must have the freedom to follow the programme of their choice," a spokesperson said in a response. If inflow is nevertheless limited, ISO believes it is essential that students have a say in that decision. Fewer students In total, 40.800 new students started a university programme this year. In total, 330.000 students are now enrolled, 2000 fewer than last year. Forecasts from the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">OCW</entity> still indicate that the number of students will decline in the coming years, to just over 300.000 in 2032.

title: Talks on war in Ukraine begin in Abu Dhabi, Europe on the sidelines
lead: In Abu Dhabi talks have begun on ending the war in Ukraine. In a first round, Ukraine spoke with the European representatives this morning together with the American envoys. Afterwards the main meeting followed with only Russia and the US. In between, the American envoy Witkoff said in a statement that "close coordination" between the US, Ukraine and European allies should lead to "lasting peace, including support for robust security guarantees". He then began the consultation from which the Europeans were not welcome. It is the first time since February that Russia is directly talking with Ukraine. Breakthroughs are not expected: at previous meetings agreements were made on exchanging prisoners, but a ceasefire proved unworkable. The Kremlin so far maintains the position that it will continue fighting as long as Ukraine does not give up at least the entire Donbas region, including the parts the Russian army has not yet occupied. For Kyiv that is non-negotiable. Read here more about what is at stake: For the first round of talks this morning, the Ukrainian delegation and the American envoys Kushner and Witkoff met with representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, France and Italy. Delegations from NATO and the EU also took part. For the meeting with the Russian delegation those participants are not welcome: Moscow insisted on trilateral talks with only Ukraine and the American mediators. European interests at stake In Europe there is fear that the Americans, under Russian pressure, may also put European interests at stake. Although Witkoff did say in his statement that Ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity are of great importance, his boss Trump said this weekend that to achieve peace the borders of Ukraine "will take a somewhat different form". The American president also said he was willing to talk with the Russians about the broader European security arrangements. In response, German foreign minister Wadephul said that "as far as Europe is concerned, new European security arrangements are unnecessary". The first meeting this morning with the European delegation was, according to the Ukrainian chief negotiator Oemerov, intended to align priorities with allies. He named as main themes an end to the fighting, future security guarantees and economic recovery. Simultaneously, Ukrainian minister Sybiha of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> met his American counterpart Rubio in Paris. There he stressed the importance of "diplomacy and de-escalation". Russian attacks on the country continued today as well. Attacks were reported across the country on energy infrastructure. In several places power went out as a result. There is hope that the talks can build on the recent humanitarian truce in the occupied city of Olesjky, which enabled the evacuation of hundreds of residents. A Kremlin spokesperson already called that "an isolated situation that cannot simply be translated into the broader process". The idea is that the talks in Abu Dhabi will last two days.

title: Cabinet aims to preserve Moerdijk, future of village not yet certain
lead: If it is up to the cabinet, Moerdijk will continue to exist after all. In a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> state secretary De Bat writes that the expansion of the port and industry, for which the village had to make way, may be more limited. But no definitive choice has been made yet. The national government does not want to look for extra space near Moerdijk for new circular businesses. According to the minister, that scenario is "feasible". For the expansion, areas elsewhere in the Netherlands "that are reserved for that purpose" would then have to be used. Around Moerdijk, about 200 hectares are still needed. Liveability Before the decision on the village's future is finally made, De Bat wants more clarity about liveability in the area. The central government, the <entity id="org:provincie-noord-brabant">provincie Noord-Brabant</entity> and the municipality of Moerdijk must jointly investigate whether the expansion of industry will not lead to too much (noise) nuisance. The outcome of this study will still take a while, a spokesperson says. A year ago the municipality announced that the Brabant village of Moerdijk must make way for the expansion of the nearby port and industrial area. Since then the 1100 residents have been in uncertainty. In May it became clear that there might be a possibility of preserving the village. That scenario has now been examined, De Bat states in his letter.

title: Dense fog across the Netherlands also produces beautiful pictures
lead: The dense, low-lying fog of this morning causes some inconvenience, but also produces many beautiful photos. Via the mailbox of NOS Ooggetuige the whole country passes by. In NOS Weer, weather presenter Willemijn Hoebert addressed the question of why we see fog less often nowadays than in the past:

title: Even without a cabinet, Israel's opposition can already make its mark
lead: The new Israeli parliament, the Knesset, is being sworn in this afternoon. While coalition negotiations led by opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot have only just begun, he can already use the new balance of power in parliament before a new government is formed. The parties opposed to Netanyahu have a majority with 67 of the 120 seats in the new parliament. Of these, 19 seats are held by the Arab parties. Although some opposition leaders in Eisenkot's camp do not want to form a government with the Arab parties, they can still work together in parliament. The Knesset is an independent state body that can function separately from the government. Replacing the parliamentary speaker: At the top of the opposition bloc's agenda is replacing the current speaker, Amir Ohana, of Netanyahu's Likud party, with someone from Eisenkot's party. This would give the opposition more control over the parliamentary agenda and the handling of bills. It is customary for the new speaker to be elected only when a new government is formed. But the vote can be brought forward if at least 61 members of parliament request it in writing. All opposition parties have by now indicated that they want to replace the current Knesset speaker. Investigation into 7 October 2023: The next step is setting up a so-called 'Organisation Committee'. This temporary body plays an important role in organising the new parliament. Among other things, it can set up special committees that can handle bills, even before permanent committees have been formed. Eisenkot has previously said he wants to prepare legislation to establish a state commission of inquiry into the Hamas terror attack of 7 October 2023. This is an important election promise of the opposition bloc. Netanyahu has been opposing such an investigation for years. Eisenkot also wants to repeal a number of controversial legal reforms adopted under Netanyahu. For example, under his government a law was passed in March 2025 that gives politicians more influence over the appointment of judges. Eisenkot wants to reverse this law as soon as possible. He also wants to limit the term of the prime minister to a maximum of 8 years and introduce a law that prevents persons facing criminal charges from becoming prime minister. This could have consequences for Netanyahu, as several criminal cases are pending against him, although the Supreme Court could block such a law. Critics may argue that the legislation is specifically aimed at Netanyahu and is intended to exclude a political opponent. It is, incidentally, still an open question whether all the laws will be passed. Although the opposition has a majority of 67 seats on paper, that does not mean all parties will vote for every bill. The parties each have their own interests and political priorities. The coming period will therefore be a test of how united the opposition bloc can be. Netanyahu is not powerless: Netanyahu meanwhile remains at the head of the caretaker government and thereby retains some powers. Especially in the areas of defence, national security and foreign policy, Netanyahu's government retains considerable authority. In practice, this means for example that Netanyahu is still authorised to have his government approve a new attack on Iran. No majority in parliament is required for that. The threat of a new war has been hanging in the air for weeks, but the ball for now seems to be in the court of US President Trump. Eisenkot will meanwhile try to form a government as quickly as possible. Coalition negotiations officially started yesterday. While several paths to a government are possible, many election promises stand in the way. So it is an open question whether he will succeed and how stable any government under his leadership would be.

title: Report: meat sector and ministry fail to protect animal welfare
lead: That animal welfare in the meat sector is still poor is because everyone involved takes too little responsibility. That applies to the farmers, the slaughterhouses, supervisor <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">NVWA</entity> and the Ministry of Agriculture alike. That is what a report from a special committee set up by the ministry states. The system is failing, is the harsh conclusion of the report. Responsible <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> of Agriculture acknowledges that it can and must be better. "In recent times we have already taken many steps with new rules for animal-friendly livestock farming, rules for transport in warm weather and camera supervision in slaughterhouses. But more must happen." The advisory committee states in the report, titled 'Dierenwelzijn verdient beter', that companies in the sector often "subordinate animal welfare to business economic and financial considerations". As a result, lame animals are still delivered to the slaughterhouse, and pigs and chickens receive too little food and water. Mainly efficient production: The problems are structural. According to the report, the standards are unclear or inadequate. Companies focus mainly on efficient production. Financial pressure also affects farmers, "who want to take good care of their animals". Companies are willing to take animal welfare into account, "as long as the consequences for costs, productivity and feasibility" are acceptable. Moreover, the ministry acts "insufficiently forcefully", according to the report. State Secretary Erkens is presenting an improvement programme for animal welfare across the whole chain, "from farm to slaughterhouse". In doing so, he again places clear responsibility on the sector itself. Soon <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> will discuss measures to improve animal welfare. The Party for the Animals believes those plans do not go far enough and has submitted private member's bills to end unnecessary animal suffering in livestock farming and the meat sector. The intention is for debate on this to take place at the beginning of next month.

title: 12 dead, dozens injured in huge pile-up in fog in Bulgaria
lead: In Bulgaria at least twelve people have died in a major pile-up on a motorway. In dense fog, dozens of cars collided near the village of Zimnitsa. "More than seventy vehicles were involved in this tragedy," a regional governor said on the spot. "The devastation is indescribable, I have never seen anything like it." At least fifty people have been taken to hospital. A few of them are in a bad way. The traffic disaster began when a lorry hit a bus on the A1 motorway between the capital Sofia and the seaside resort of Boergas. This led to massive devastation in both directions on the six-lane motorway. "We were driving at about 100 kilometres an hour when suddenly all these stationary cars appeared. A lot of them," says an involved driver. "I braked hard, but could not stop in time." "I was still able to pull a man out of a burning car," says another driver. "When I smashed his window I heard collisions all over the other carriageway. Debris was flying everywhere." Another driver describes what he saw happen: At the moment of the collision visibility was extremely poor due to the dense fog, less than 50 metres. The fire brigade is currently still checking the wrecks to see whether anyone is still trapped. EU president Ursula von der Leyen was visiting Bulgaria when news of the collision broke. She decided to cut short her meeting with Prime Minister Radev. In a message she expressed her sympathy and admiration for the emergency services.

title: Singapore seizes American cruise ship that was to sail 'forever'
lead: The American cruise ship that was on a "years-long world voyage" has been seized by Singaporean port authorities. Due to rising fuel costs, the cruise company could not continue the voyage. Last month guests had to disembark in Cambodia. The ship has been chained up on court order, the port authority (MPA) said in a statement to Singaporean media. No further details were given on the reason for this. The vessel is now at Changi General Anchorage, a designated area for seized ships that is supervised by MPA. "The crew on board is reportedly doing well and the creditors are taking measures to ensure their welfare," MPA said. There were no guests left on board. The company behind the cruise ship, Villa Vie Residences, has not yet responded. World voyage: The luxury cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey left Belfast in October 2024 and was to take guests on a years-long journey around the world. Until it ran aground last week off the coast of Cambodia because it could no longer pay for fuel. Fuel costs in Asia had, according to the American shipping company, risen too high due to the war between the United States and Iran. To limit costs, the ship had therefore been idle in ports for some time and sailed at lower speed. Ultimately it proved unaffordable nonetheless. Per cabin, costs had reportedly risen from 1600 euros to 7000 euros per month. It would not be a "realistic solution" to pass the costs on to guests, the company wrote in a statement. There were over 200 guests and 150 crew members on board. The guests had to disembark at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville, after which the ship left the port.

title: Dead newborn baby found in rubbish bag in Belgian meadow
lead: On the edge of a meadow in the Belgian Weerst, just across the border from <entity id="org:gemeente-maastricht">Maastricht</entity>, a dead baby has been found. The body of the newborn girl was in a rubbish bag, with her umbilical cord still attached, French-language outlet Sudinfo reports. The lifeless girl was found Sunday afternoon in the bushes in a sub-municipality of Dalhem in the province of Liège. According to the mayor of Dalhem, the body was discovered by a farmer's son. "It was unusual," mayor Benoit Defauwes tells VRT. "He went to look and examined the bag with a piece of wood. In doing so he discovered the head of the newborn. He immediately called the police." The mayor then also came to the scene. The Public Prosecution Service in Liège has started an investigation into the circumstances under which the baby died. According to Belgian media, the first findings show that the baby was only a few days old. The area has been examined with drones, among other things.

title: Regulator concerned about cyber incidents: banks too will soon be targets
lead: Empty shelves at Albert Heijn, tampering with the temperature of refrigerators and freezers in various European supermarkets, a break-in at Denmark's population register, to a major crypto heist at Binance. These are just a selection of the many hacks of recent weeks. And it will not stop there, warns the <entity id="org:zbo-stichting-autoriteit-financiele-markten">Autoriteit Financiële Markten</entity> (AFM) in its annual Trend Outlook Report on the financial markets. The regulator for financial markets is very worried that a trading exchange or perhaps even a bank will soon be hacked. "It is not a question of whether the financial markets will be hit by a cyberattack, but when and how," says AFM chair <entity id="person:laura-van-geest">Laura van Geest</entity>. Smarter and better with AI "I think the increase in incidents we are now seeing, including at larger parties, is a consequence of AI becoming smarter or better," says Van Geest. "And that is also the reason we are sounding the alarm." The AFM now calls cyber incidents "one of the most acute systemic risks" for the financial sector. The regulator sees that it is no longer only about hackers demanding ransom for sensitive information they steal from computer systems. Countries are now using cyberattacks as hybrid warfare. "A lot of mischief comes from abroad," says Van Geest. It can range from very harmless, such as people no longer being able to easily call, to not being able to access your account anymore. Financial institutions as targets For now, cyberattacks on a supermarket or cooling systems are mainly painful for the affected companies. Greater social panic can break out if people can no longer access their accounts because a bank is brought down by a cyberattack. "Financial institutions are a primary target because of their central role in the financial system and their high degree of digitalisation," the AFM states in the report. The rise of artificial intelligence, AI, also makes it easier for hackers to carry out attacks. "The newest generation of AI models offers increasingly powerful weapons for detecting and exploiting vulnerabilities in security. On the other hand, AI can also support companies in improved detection of and response to cyber threats." Cash money "I think it starts with the responsibility of companies to properly prepare themselves for cyber incidents," says Van Geest. "We as supervisors cooperate, the government does too, and the Ministry of Finance." The regulator advises not to put all your eggs in one basket, but to spread the risks. "Besides, there is nothing wrong with having a bit of cash in your drawer and perhaps a second bank account," concludes Van Geest.

title: Relatives of Greek victim of Tarwekamp ask for life imprisonment: 'Future taken away'
lead: "When I tried to call him three times that day and couldn't reach him, I knew something terrible had happened." That is what the widow of the 44-year-old Greek man told the court about the day she learned that her partner had died in the devastating explosion on the Tarwekamp in The Hague at the end of 2024. This is the third of nine hearing days in total. This morning the widow, the brother and a son of the Greek man spoke about the grief the explosion has caused them. Six people lost their lives in the explosion. The 44-year-old Greek was asleep when the explosion happened. His wife was the first to speak this morning, assisted by an interpreter. Before and during her speech she was repeatedly overcome by emotion and tried to hold back her tears. Future taken away "Sometimes I think I've ended up in a very bad dream," she says. "For you these are files, for me the death of my husband is in my soul. I know this will keep haunting me until my last breath." Her husband had come to the Netherlands to work and was building a future for the family in The Hague, she said. He leaves behind three children. "That future has been taken from us, in a very harsh, violent way. In his bed, in our new home." The four suspects are also present at the hearing. Last week, on the first hearing day, they were questioned by the judge. In doing so they explained what led up to the attack on the bridal fashion shop. The widow told how her youngest son, who was seven months old when the attack was carried out, will not even remember his father. "'Papa' is a word he tries to connect to a person, but that person will be gone forever." Her eldest son, who is now 12, understands better what happened to his father. He has been anxious since that fateful day. "He sees families and knows that his is no longer complete." She too is anxious after the death of her husband. This mainly shows at night, when she thinks about the fact that her husband may still have been alive after the disaster. "I can only hope and pray that he did not suffer." She is angry at the suspects, and is frightened by her own thoughts that she wants to harm them. The widow wants them to take responsibility for their actions. That is why she asks the court to impose life sentences on the suspects. The brother of the deceased Greek man also made use of his right to speak. He told of the impact it has had on him and his parents. His brother was his guide in life and full of dreams, he says. His death has "destroyed" his parents, and his nephews and niece have had to grow up without a father because of the attack. The brother speaks of "a terrifying nightmare in the city of peace and justice." Only when justice imposes a life sentence will that peace and justice return to the city, he believes. That is why he asks the court to ensure the suspects are never released again, "so that they can never cause harm to anyone again." Always afraid The family's lawyer read out a statement on behalf of the eldest son. In it he describes how he experienced the morning of the disaster. He saw his mother hanging on the phone, crying. The family had to grope in the dark for a long time as to whether his father had survived the explosion. The boy confirms his mother's account of his fears. "I was afraid of everything, in the dark, the metro, in the car and when playing on the school playground." He is now doing somewhat better. His thoughts still often drift to things like illness, accidents and death. He misses his father. "I can't do with my mother what I did with Dad. Now that I'm getting older I have nobody to talk to man to man." "You said at the beginning that the death of your husband is a case file for us," the judge addressed the widow after the statements. "Thanks to your testimony we have got a good picture of who he was." Thereupon she broke into sobbing that lasted for minutes.

title: Rare find in Frisian restaurant: chef finds two pearls in one oyster
lead: It was a big surprise in the kitchen of a restaurant in the Frisian town of Wolvega last weekend. While preparing the oysters, two pearls were found in one oyster. Owner and head chef Jan Smink initially did not know what he was seeing when he stood at the sink. One of the cooks was working with oysters in the kitchen and found them, one larger and one smaller. "I didn't believe it at first," Smink tells Omrop Fryslân. "We were all standing around looking: how can this happen?" 1 in 15,000 A pearl in an oyster forms when the oyster accidentally takes in a parasite or a small creature. The oyster tries to get rid of it. If that fails, the oyster tries to protect itself by building layers of mother-of-pearl around the foreign particle. This process can take years. Most pearls sold in shops are cultured. The pearls from the restaurant were formed naturally, which is very rare. It is estimated that only 1 in 15,000 oysters produces a natural pearl. According to Smink, it is rare to find a pearl in oysters used for consumption. But two pearls, according to the chef, is completely unique. "The chance for one pearl would be about 1 in 15,000." Value not known At the restaurant, which last month received a Michelin star for a fourth year in a row, oysters are not always on the menu. "In this case we use them for a warm intermediate course. The oysters are first briefly steamed, which makes the shell open, and then you can quickly see what's inside," the chef says. Smink had never experienced this in his own kitchen before. "About fourteen years ago I did find one when I was tasting a fresh oyster myself." What these pearls are worth exactly is not known. Smink will certainly not get rid of them quickly. "They are now safely in a little box in my office." Pearls In the past, natural pearls have often been found in oysters used for consumption. For example, a chef at a restaurant made a similar find in 2023. In 2015 an oyster with no fewer than 21 natural pearls was found in a fish shop in the Zeeland town of Yerseke. Initially it was thought there were ten pearls, but it turned out there were more than twice as many.

title: Paul McCartney a music billionaire, and not even really thanks to The Beatles
lead: Paul McCartney is worth 1.4 billion dollars according to the American magazine Forbes, roughly 1.25 billion euros. He is thereby the second-richest artist after Jay-Z (2.8 bn) and Taylor Swift (2 bn), according to the business magazine's calculation. According to Forbes, the 84-year-old McCartney has "sung, litigated, toured and toiled his fortune together". Remarkably, it is not even his ten years with The Beatles that form the core of his wealth, but rights company MPL Communications. According to Forbes, that yields tens of millions in royalties annually. In his Beatles days McCartney was still bound to a not very lucrative contract, which according to Forbes gave him only one cent per record. "However successful we were, we got no pay rise", he told the magazine back in 2017. "It was actually a slave contract." Grease and Christmas Always the most business-minded Beatle, McCartney drew lessons from that when the British band broke up in 1970. He founded MPL to be able to buy up the rights of others. He now owns the music rights to Buddy Holly, several popular musicals and a bunch of popular Christmas songs. "Every time Blue suede shoes is streamed or an elementary school performs Grease, McCartney gets paid", Forbes summarises the business model. Also when Baby, it's cold outside, It's beginning to look a lot like Christmas or Wonderful Christmastime cannot be escaped on the radio every year, McCartney gets a cut. McCartney was thereby a pioneer for an industry that has taken off in recent years: rights to the work of Bob Dylan, Justin Bieber and Bruce Springsteen were bought up for mega sums, and widow Rachel sold André Hazes's catalogue only yesterday for an undisclosed amount. Touring In addition, over the years McCartney managed, through lawsuits and negotiations, to gain a larger share of all Beatles income. The rights are worth around 150 million each for McCartney, Ringo Starr and the heirs of Lennon and Harrison. Streams, album sales and merchandise will, according to Forbes's estimate, yield a total of 50 million dollars annually. Apart from that, McCartney also has the income from his work as a songwriter for the band: that is worth 200 million and yields 10 million annually. Touring also still brings money in for Sir Paul: performances, such as those on the Got Back tour for which he did 79 shows in fourteen countries between 2022 and 2025, yielded hundreds of millions. What helps is that McCartney still releases new music: earlier this year his newest solo album, The Boys of Dungeon Lane, appeared. 'Macca', 'Tay Tay' and Jay-Z are not the only artists who reached a billion: earlier Forbes calculated that Bruce Springsteen, Rihanna and Beyoncé are also certainly worth $1.000.000.000.

title: Eerste Kamer clears the way for culturing embryos for research
lead: Research into hereditary diseases and involuntary childlessness will soon also be allowed to use human embryos that have been specially cultured for this purpose. The Eerste Kamer has agreed to a proposal on this from D66 and VVD. It was a narrow majority of 38 votes in favour and 35 against. In <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, about a year ago, 90 members of parliament voted in favour and 59 against. The plan is not uncontroversial. Scientists want it, but critics see it as a step towards designer babies or find it indefensible to first create life and then discard it. Fundamental research Until now, scientists were only allowed to use embryos left over after an IVF treatment for research. D66 and VVD have proposed relaxing the law, because researchers would like to study the development of embryos directly after fertilisation. They expect this will help couples who are unable to have a child. The embryos left over after an IVF process are already too far developed for that kind of fundamental research. Embryos specially cultured for this purpose can also be studied at the earliest stage. This concerns the first hours and days after fertilisation. In other European countries The Netherlands is not the only country where this debate is taking place. Within Europe, embryo culturing is permitted under conditions in the United Kingdom, Belgium, Sweden and Finland. There are also countries where research on embryos is not permitted at all, not even on leftover embryos.

title: Anthropic IPO will not break SpaceX record
lead: The initial public offering of AI company Anthropic will not break any records. The company behind the language model Claude wants to go public in the short term. Today it became known that Anthropic will sell 825 million shares in total, at a much lower price than expected. The introduction price of the shares has been set at 70 to 78 dollars per share. This means Anthropic will raise at least 57.75 billion and at most 64.35 billion dollars. Beforehand, the IPO was still expected to bring in 80 to 100 billion dollars. Because of that lower price, the first major IPO of an AI company will not become the largest ever. That record remains for now with SpaceX, the space company of Tesla boss Elon Musk. It raised 75 billion dollars with an IPO in June. The introduction price of a share is set based on investor interest. That happens after the publication of a document about the company, the so-called prospectus, which must clearly describe, among other things, the future expectations and the risks. Heavy losses Anthropic published this legally required document two weeks ago. In it, it warned of the risks of AI, but also of the heavy losses the company has suffered so far. The Anthropic IPO also comes at a time when investors are less enthusiastic about investments in AI. This follows the loss of the Republican party in the Congressional elections last week. Investors expect the Democrats to introduce stricter rules for AI and to want fewer data centers, whereas the Republicans under President Trump gave free rein to these. Anthropic has not yet announced a date for the IPO. It is expected to take place still this week or otherwise next week. Ultimately, analysts expect the total value of Anthropic, including its listed shares, to come to 1.4 trillion dollars. They had previously still assumed 1.75 trillion dollars.

title: Minister sticks to decision: no funding for shelter for undocumented migrants
lead: To the frustration of undocumented migrants, municipalities, churches and aid organisations, <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is sticking to the decision to stop funding the Landelijke Vreemdelingenvoorziening (LVV). That became clear today during a hearing of the highest administrative court, the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity>. Through the LVV, foreigners who have no right to stay in the Netherlands are provided with shelter. They also receive food, the opportunity to wash and subsistence money. That is why it is also called the bed-bad-brood scheme. Often these are vulnerable people who have been in the Netherlands for a long time, cannot look after themselves properly, and have physical or psychological problems. The group of people who use bed-bad-brood is estimated at around 600. Since 2019, five municipalities have provided around-the-clock shelter: <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-groningen">Groningen</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-eindhoven">Eindhoven</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity>, but then-minister Faber (PVV) decided to end the funding as of 1 January 2025. Faber focused on return to the country of origin instead of "subsidised shelter". Since the national contribution fell away, shelter in the cities is often paid for by the municipality, which is supported in this by aid organisations. 'Inhuman and degrading treatment' The current cabinet is sticking to Faber's decision, even though judges have ruled that she wrongly stopped the funding. The court in Amsterdam ruled in May 2025 that 28 undocumented migrants had made it plausible that they cannot provide for their own bed, bath and bread. By ending the shelter, they run a high risk of "inhuman or degrading treatment", according to the court. The court in Rotterdam later reached a comparable ruling, in a case brought by sixteen undocumented migrants. Lawyers for undocumented migrants, municipalities and aid organisations argued today in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> before the Raad van State that the minister violates the European Convention on Human Rights (EVRM) by not offering shelter to this group. The state advocate, who defends on behalf of asylum minister Van den Brink (CDA), disputes this: in his view the national government does provide shelter, in the so-called freedom-restricting location (VBL) in Ter Apel. Undocumented migrants can go there, provided they are willing to cooperate in a return procedure. Shelter in Ter Apel. The very basic VBL has 232 shelter places. In the short term there is no possibility of expansion. According to several parties involved, there is not only too little space in the VBL, the shelter would also not be suitable for this group of undocumented migrants. The VBL is intended to get people to leave for their country of origin as quickly as possible, but undocumented migrants formally have no country to return to. Also, the two types of shelter have existed side by side for years, which would show that both are needed. The state advocate states that all parties involved knew the LVV would "end at some point" and that stopping it therefore could not come as a surprise. According to the state advocate, registering for shelter in Ter Apel is the responsibility of the undocumented migrants. Municipalities and aid organisations have been warning for years that vulnerable people end up on the street when the LVV stops. Stateless: Lawyer Jelle Klaas says these are people who cannot simply be put on a plane. "It is a group of a few hundred men, often with serious problems." The group is now being sheltered by municipalities or aid agencies. According to the lawyer, there are also stateless people among them, for example from the former Soviet Union, Myanmar or from a war zone. Klaas: "Suppose you flee from South Sudan, then you cannot just go to the consulate to get a new travel document. It may be that the <entity id="org:immigratie-en-naturalisatiedienst">IND</entity> says: 'You have done too little to show that you come from a war zone'. Then you have to try to gather more evidence through the people back home, and in the meantime you are an undocumented person here. There will always be people who fall between two stools. You must not let them wander the streets." By bus to The Hague: Early this morning, buses carrying undocumented migrants and other stakeholders left Amsterdam and Rotterdam for The Hague. People who no longer fit on the public gallery of the court at the Kneuterdijk followed the hearing via a livestream in a nearby church. The Protestant Church and Kerk in Actie recently called it "shameful that the state keeps campaigning against the bed-bad-brood scheme". The Raad van State is expected to rule in six weeks at the earliest, but at the end of the hearing the court already warned that it will probably take a good deal longer. How many undocumented migrants are there in the Netherlands? According to official figures there are around 20.000 undocumented migrants in the Netherlands. According to the <entity id="org:wetenschappelijk-onderzoek-en-datacentrum">Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek- en Datacentrum</entity> (WODC) the number is "with 95 percent statistical reliability between 16.955 and 23.175 persons". According to daily Trouw, that is an underestimate; after a round of inquiries among various municipalities and organisations, the paper arrives at a "much higher number". The bulk of this group provides for its own livelihood. The group of undocumented migrants who use bed-bad-brood is much smaller, however: it is estimated at around 600 people.

title: House of Representatives: consider a new formation first if cabinet falls
lead: If the cabinet falls mid-term, the House of Representatives must first debate whether it is possible to patch up the coalition or to start a new formation. Now, new elections are usually called, but a majority of the House wants to move away from what is almost an automatism. A motion on this from ChristenUnie, SGP and CDA received broad support today. Since the year 2000, only one cabinet has completed the full four years. Seven cabinets fell along the way, after which citizens had to return to the polls prematurely. According to the motion's submitters, this has led to unstable policy, which is bad for the business climate and citizens' trust in politics. In most other European countries, new elections are called less often. In addition, in the provinces and municipal councils the elected representatives always serve four years. That must also become the starting point again for the House of Representatives, the motion states. Changing the Rules of Procedure To look more emphatically at alternatives to new elections after a cabinet collapse, the House wants to change its own Rules of Procedure. These currently state that the House after a mid-term fall "can deliberate on a new formation". That must be changed to "will deliberate". In the past it was quite normal that after a mid-term fall of the cabinet a new formation took place again. In the 1960s there were even three different cabinets (Marijnen, Cals and Zijlstra) based on the same 1963 election result. Some critics then felt that this insufficiently did justice to the wish of the voter.

title: Extreme air pollution peaks again in Indian cities, despite measures
lead: Since this week a thick layer of white smog has once again settled over the Indian capital New Delhi. It is a recurring annual phenomenon. When it gets colder, the air quality in many North Indian cities plunges deep into the red. Residents increasingly suffer from respiratory complaints, irritated eyes and migraines. Lung specialist Nikhil Modi sees many complaints of this kind at his consultations, and often worse ones. On his mobile phone the doctor shows a message from a patient with pulmonary emphysema. A few days earlier the patient had come in for standard tests that showed no major problems. "His oxygen levels looked good, but a day after Diwali I got this message: that he had less than 90 percent oxygen in his blood." That is dangerously low. Patients aged 35 Last weekend Diwali was celebrated, one of the most popular Hindu festivals. Despite a court order that only less polluting fireworks could be set off, residents of the city noticed little difference from other years. Several air quality monitors indicated that air pollution during this Diwali was even higher than ever before. In the 18 years that Modi has worked as a lung specialist in New Delhi, he increasingly sees people with breathing and lung complaints come in, not only around Diwali but all year round. "Lung cancer used to be a disease of smokers around 60 years old, now we see patients around 35 years old who have never smoked a cigarette", says Modi. Most polluted city in the world In 2014 the World Health Organization declared New Delhi the most polluted city in the world for the first time. Of the 1600 cities in 91 countries, New Delhi had, according to the World Health Organization database, the highest concentration of fine particulate matter. That fine particulate matter is so small that it ends up in the bloodstream. It was the first time that measurements of air quality made big news. "Since 2014, knowledge and anger among Indians about air pollution have grown", says sociologist Vasundhara Bhojvaid. She researches the effects of air pollution on daily life. Bhojvaid also sees problems with the measurements. "It is not as if the pollution suddenly appeared in 2014, we only saw it because it was measured clearly for the first time." And where that measuring equipment stands matters, because in cities air quality is recorded more carefully than in the countryside. Bhojvaid would like to see more attention paid to the countryside, where a large part of the pollution in New Delhi comes from. Much less is known about the health effects for Indian agricultural workers. Fireworks a temporary culprit The fireworks during Diwali are mainly a temporary culprit. The rest of the year a combination of factors causes the deteriorating air quality in Indian cities. In cold air, car exhaust fumes linger longer. Dust from construction sites also leads to more problems then. This year local authorities have again drawn up rules to counter extra pollution. Older polluting cars are banned from the city centre, construction work is partly halted, and civil servants are asked to work more from home or travel by public transport. It is more complicated for farmers to do something about it. They have to prepare their land within a few weeks for a new sowing period. By setting fields on fire they gain time, but those smoke plumes drift toward the cities.
