Officially, burning fields is therefore prohibited, but on the day after Diwali alone 200 new fires were reported. Pollution refugees A new trend is that Indians who have the means leave the city during the cold months, researcher Bhojvaid observes. "It is the wealthier residents who temporarily go to the Indian mountains or even move to Europe." Pollution refugees, Bhojvaid calls them. It is a small group that is growing fast. According to Modi, these are mainly people who have no schoolchildren or job in the city. For the doctor it is not unthinkable that he himself will become such a refugee: "I have a 14-year-old child myself, and children's lungs can still recover when we move to a place with healthier air."

title: Customer rewards bond of trust with taxi driver with a house worth half a million
lead: "Over all those years I have transported thousands of people. For me it never mattered who got in; everyone deserved the same care, attention and respect." The speaker is Joeri Cools (53), a former taxi driver in the Belgian city of Ghent. The newspaper Het Laatste Nieuws (HLN) spoke with him because his care, attention and respect for his customers has brought him an extraordinary legacy. A woman who for eighteen years invariably chose his taxi left him a house worth half a million. Initially Annie was a customer like any other. She lived in Brussels, but travelled to Ghent by train every week and took a taxi from there. Bond of trust "As trust grew, she told me about her sociology studies, her youth and the social commitment she had shown her whole life," Cools told HLN. She also told him she had had three serious relationships, but marriage or children had never happened. Cools, in turn, shared his memories of his impoverished and bitter youth. "Everything that could go wrong at home went wrong. It ranged from neglect to abuse. From when I was twenty months old until I was six or seven I was in a foster family under a different name. My stepfather died in an accident, my sister is struggling with mental health problems and my brother took his own life." Their bond became so strong that on arriving in Ghent Annie always looked for Cools' taxi and got in. "'I know you, I trust you,' she would always say when she got in," Cools said. In 2021 he saw her for the last time. Two years later he stopped working as a taxi driver and lost contact with many of his customers, including Annie. Letter from notary But in September a letter from a notary suddenly lay in his letterbox. It said that Annie had died in June 2025 at the age of 81. She had spent her last years in a care home. To each of her three close friends she had left an apartment, and to Cools a property with an estimated value of half a million euros. She had already included this bequest to Cools in her will in 2011. "Because she had no family of her own, she apparently wanted to decide very deliberately where her assets would go, to avoid them being lost," Cools tells HLN. The VRT calculated that Cools must pay 358.750 euros of his inheritance to the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">belastingdienst</entity>, but if he sells the property he will still have around 140.000 euros left over.

title: Emotional victims of Tarwekamp: 'The explosion lasted seconds, the consequences a lifetime'
lead: "An explosion lasts seconds, its consequences can last a lifetime." A mother from a family that lived on the Tarwekamp described today in the courtroom what many residents and relatives still feel daily after two years. Her son called "the impact of the explosion enormous and lasting" and the daughter of the family spoke of "a life before and a life after the explosion". The nineteen victim statements painted a picture of residents and relatives struggling with post-traumatic complaints. They are also angry and sad about the attack in 2024, they said during the third hearing day of the criminal case against four suspects in the court in The Hague. Earlier, residents already told the NOS that the neighbourhood is slowly recovering, but that the court case is also bringing tension back. Great love lost This morning the mother, the brother and, via their lawyer, also the son of the 44-year-old Greek man who died in the explosion spoke. They spoke emotionally about their loss and asked the judge to impose a life sentence on those responsible for the explosion. This afternoon it was the turn of residents of an affected home and the family and girlfriend of 31-year-old Tim. He was staying with his girlfriend at the time of the explosion. She survived the disaster. He was one of six victims who died. In a statement she had read out, she said that through the disaster she lost many items of emotional value, but also "the most precious": her great love. Tim's mother and sister addressed the four suspects directly: A family that lived on the Tarwekamp told about the consequences of the explosion. They have lost their home and suffer from post-traumatic stress (PTSS) due to the attack. The father, mother and daughter of the family explained how much their lives have been thrown off balance. The daughter said she is often reminded of the disaster, and that at moments when she thinks she is slowly recovering, something happens that sends her right back to square one. Dream job and safe place lost The mother of the family had just found her dream job, but because of the explosion and its consequences can no longer work, to her great sorrow. The father also talked about the administrative consequences of the explosion. For example, they are left with a house they no longer want to live in, but which is hard to sell, and they have problems with the insurance. Their son was not at home at the time of the explosion. Since the explosion, the area where he once felt safe causes him mainly "sorrow, fear and pain". Crying with fear Other residents who spoke today described how they experienced the disaster. One woman told how she was in the building with her toddler when the explosion happened. Since then she has also suffered from PTSS. "I have become afraid of fireworks; on the last New Year's Eve I lay in bed all night crying with fear," she said. An older woman who also lived in the building told the court how she woke up from the explosion. "I looked out of my window and saw flames above the roof of the complex." She describes how new problems arose after the disaster. For example, her home and belongings were largely destroyed, and now that she is back in the home, it is hard for her to feel settled again. "It is a cold return to the Tarwekamp."

title: Call to preserve data of Q fever and post-COVID patients
lead: The government must take action to protect the data of many thousands of Q fever and post-COVID patients from being destroyed. That is the call from Jos Bosch, co-coordinator of the Post-Covid Netwerk Nederland, a collaborative project of experts by experience, researchers and doctors. The professor says a wealth of medical information risks being lost. It concerns the patient files of Q-support and C-support. The two support organisations for Q fever and post-COVID patients respectively are being dissolved. Collected data on around 36,000 patients will be deleted from the end of this week for privacy reasons, the Volkskrant reports. The Ministry of Health is consulting with C-support on the matter, confirms director Sophie Querido to the NOS. According to her, the aim is to retain as much scientifically relevant information as possible. "But for us, the protection of the patient and the person is central." Partly anonymised data According to Querido, the picture that all data will be destroyed is inaccurate. So-called 'core sets' of medical data have been compiled and will be kept. This selection will be made available to science in anonymised form. Mainly irrelevant data will be deleted, the director says. But according to Bosch, professor of post-acute infection syndromes at Leiden LUMC, anonymising the relevant data is no solution to the problem. "That severs the connection with the patients," Bosch explains. From asking new questions about the course of someone's illness or recovery to contacting someone when a new medicine is on the horizon: according to the professor, this will become impossible. "You can look back at collected data, but that is outdated again after one or two years. To learn from data, you need to be able to follow people over time," Bosch says on behalf of the Post-Covid Netwerk Nederland. Opportunity to object C-support and Q-support say that all patients have been informed and given the chance to object to the deletion of their personal data. Bosch counters that some patients are too weak to respond to this. "We are in discussion with various parties to ensure that this precious knowledge and data are not lost," the Ministry of Health says in a response. The parties involved will meet again in the coming days. C-support and Q-support are funded by the ministry but will stop at the end of this year. Besides information on covid patients and Q fever patients, the organisations also manage data on people suffering from so-called post-vaccination syndrome (PVS). These are people who, after vaccination against the virus, developed complaints similar to post-COVID.

title: Caring for someone with dementia is hard: 'You carry a lot alone'
lead: People who voluntarily care for someone with dementia experience more loneliness, psychological problems and physical problems. That is the conclusion of Alzheimer Nederland after a survey. A large majority experience one or more of these complaints as a result of providing informal care. Loneliness is the word that comes to mind for Monique Docter (55) when it comes to the care she provides to her husband. Ronald (57) has Alzheimer's disease. "You carry a lot alone. We have children and they help too, but I also have my parents and my mother has dementia. I also still work, so it's a lot of balls to keep in the air." Dementia is a collective name for a series of brain disorders. Alzheimer's disease is the best known of these. Patients struggle with memory loss and at a later stage a person has problems with thinking, speaking and acting. Docter recently put on paper how she experiences providing informal care. She did so after a colleague asked what was going on in her head. "People get emotional when they read the text." She took part in an awareness campaign. "I get many reactions to it from people who find it sad, confronting and brave." Painful choices The care for her husband is, according to Docter, hard but manageable. It has forced her to make choices. "We are also grandpa and grandma to really lovely grandchildren, but I can't look after them as much as I would have liked. That hurts quite a bit, but I have no other choice. I can't abandon my husband." Just over two in three surveyed informal carers experience mental problems. About 65 percent experience relationship problems and six in ten suffer physical complaints. Nearly three in ten informal carers indicate that they can sustain the care for at most one more year. For the so-called Dementiemonitor, over 12,000 informal carers completed a questionnaire. The sample was conducted in cooperation with research institute Nivel. The results are not fully representative of the Dutch population. Informal carers with a migration background, for example, are underrepresented. 800,000 informal carers The monitor, which was published on Dag van de Mantelzorger, according to the organisation mainly gives a good picture of how hard informal carers experience their task. Around 320,000 people currently have dementia, against roughly 800,000 informal carers. These numbers will continue to rise due to ageing, Alzheimer Nederland warns. "Caring for someone with dementia often lasts years and becomes more intensive as the years pass", says director Wiesje van der Flier. Providing care is difficult to combine with work or family life. Nearly seven in ten of those surveyed have difficulty with this. One in five working informal carers has reduced their working hours. Far fewer informal care hours The monitor is published every two years and the questionnaire has been administered since 2006. This year's results largely match those of recent years. There is one striking outlier: the number of hours that informal carers say they spend per week on care or help for their relative with dementia. According to the monitor, participants in the study spend on average 28 hours per week on this, a sharp decline compared with the studies from 2024, 2022 and 2020. At that time it was 37, 39 and 40 hours respectively. The foundation has no unambiguous explanation for this. The research does show that a larger share of dementia patients live in a care institution. That is the case for just over one in three (36 percent) of those surveyed. For comparison, in 2020 that share was about two in ten (21 percent). Constantly 'on' The husband of informal carer Monique Docter spends part of the day in a care institution. As a result, caring is easier to sustain, she explains. "It is manageable because I still have another life, but when you are together 24/7, irritations arise." According to her, that is unavoidable because she is constantly "on" and "always has to look for solutions."

title: Bird flu confirmed at company in Hierden, 70,000 ducks culled
lead: Bird flu has been confirmed at a poultry farm in the Gelderland village of Hierden. The approximately 70,000 ducks are being culled under the supervision of the <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit</entity> (NVWA). Within a radius of 10 kilometres a transport ban applies to prevent further spread of the disease. No birds, eggs, manure or used litter may be transported. Thirteen other poultry farms lie within that zone, reports Omroep Gelderland . The NVWA is investigating whether animals or products were transported to or from the farm just before the infection was discovered. If necessary, additional measures will follow. The farm was also culled twice in 2022 because of bird flu, according to the NVWA. National housing order. Since 28 October a national housing order applies to commercially kept poultry. It was introduced after three bird flu outbreaks in a short time. People who keep chickens as a hobby must also shield their birds. Visits to commercial bird premises are only permitted if necessary for the health or welfare of people or animals. Last year a national housing order was also introduced, but it was lifted again in June of this year. The number of infections had then fallen sharply, although the ministry already called the virus "unpredictable" at that time. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> is working on a plan to make vaccination of laying hens mandatory.

title: Nearly 30 influencers get a slap on the wrist for illegal health claims
lead: Three quarters of the examined influencers who advertise food supplements on social media do so with illegal claims, reports the <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit</entity> (NVWA). The NVWA examined 38 accounts on TikTok and Instagram in the spring to see whether they followed the rules. For most of them, 28 accounts, that was not the case. The number of followers of the examined influencers varied between 750 and one million. A maximum of three posts per account were examined. In nineteen posts there was even serious misleading. Not proven or misleading. Advertisements were examined for products claiming health benefits, which would for example support your resistance or make your body stronger. Among other things, advertising was made for vitamin or mineral supplements, creatine powders, electrolytes, bone broth, and ashwagandha capsules or collagen powders. In one case it concerned a supplement for children. In most cases it concerned health claims that have not been scientifically proven or health claims that were too general and therefore misleading. In two cases it concerned a medical claim. For example, a product would help against inflammation. In one case it concerned a prohibited claim about food. The advertisement said the product was low in calories, but that was not correct. Modifying or removing. The NVWA requires that the posts be modified immediately or even removed. The influencers received an official warning or a fine. If the posts are not modified, more severe measures may follow, warns the Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority.

title: First talks on ending war in Ukraine 'productive', US says
lead: The first day of talks on ending the war in Ukraine was "very productive", says US Secretary of State Rubio. He did not sit at the table himself in Abu Dhabi during the talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US. He acknowledges that there is still a lot of work to be done. It is the first time since February that Russia is speaking directly with Ukraine. Expectations of a possible breakthrough are very low. Even so, American officials say that both Kyiv and Moscow showed "a bit of flexibility" in the four-hour conversation. The talks were conducted by officials from both countries. Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council secretary sat at the table on behalf of Ukraine, and an adviser to President Putin on behalf of Russia. On behalf of the US, envoy Witkoff and Kushner, the son-in-law of President Trump, conducted the talks. 'Constructive and substantive' President Zelensky, who was not present in Abu Dhabi, calls the talks "constructive and quite substantive" on social media. Zelensky says that Ukraine wants to continue talking with the US and Russia in the coming days, but also with European representatives. Europe did not sit at the table today. However, Ukraine did speak with European representatives and American officials before the meeting. A NATO delegation also sat at the table at that meeting. European leaders have urged to be involved in the talks. They fear that the Americans, under Russian pressure, will also put European interests at stake. Ceasefire? Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov said today that Russia first wants to talk about a "future security architecture in Europe" before a ceasefire can be discussed. The EU has already indicated that it sees no point in new security arrangements and believes a ceasefire must come first. Moscow still says it will keep fighting as long as Ukraine does not give up the entire Donbas region. Ceding territory is non-negotiable for Ukraine. New talks are scheduled in Abu Dhabi tomorrow. Previous meetings between Ukraine and Russia have not produced any major breakthroughs. However, agreements were made on exchanging prisoners. That was also discussed again today, according to President Zelensky.

title: Call for action against French channel CNews leads to no political follow-up
lead: There will be no debate in the French parliament about the news channel CNews. The committee responsible for this has decided so. As a result, no follow-up will be given to a petition signed by one million French people. The petition called for CNews, France's most-watched 24-hour channel, to be taken off the air. According to the signatories, the channel is a "propaganda machine" and the French equivalent of the American Fox News; the channel is accused of giving ample room to radical-right and far-right opinion makers. The Culture and Education committee of the French <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">Tweede Kamer</entity> rejected the petition by 28 votes to 25. This means further handling of the petition is off the table. According to French media, heated discussions took place between committee members before the vote. 'Promotion instrument' Right-wing factions, including the radical-right Rassemblement National (RN) of Marine Le Pen, voted against handling the petition, while left-wing factions such as La France Insoumise (LFI) and the green party did support a parliamentary debate. Parliamentarian Aymeric Caron of the radical-left LFI was previously a journalist at iTélé, the later CNews. According to him, the channel functions as a "promotion instrument for the far right, which constantly spits venom about Muslims and immigrants." RN parliamentarian and former journalist Caroline Parmentier, speaking to the French broadcaster Franceinfo, on the contrary spoke of an "obsession with censorship on the left and far left" and accused them of wanting to silence any media channel that contradicts them. Rapped over the knuckles In recent years CNews has repeatedly come under fire from the French media watchdog Arcom, which has several times rapped the channel over the knuckles and imposed fines for inciting hatred or racist remarks. CNews is the flagship of the conservative and Catholic billionaire Vincent Bolloré. With his media group, which has interests in numerous French media and production companies, he is comparable to media tycoon Rupert Mudoch in the United Kingdom and the United States. The petition was requested via the petition site of the French parliament. That site has existed since 2020 and was created in the wake of the yellow vests protests, to give citizens more opportunities to make their voices heard. Petitions that collect at least half a million signatures are discussed by a parliamentary committee. Broader debate on press freedom Parliamentarian Alexandre Portier of the right-wing party Les Républicains chairs the Culture and Education committee. He says the parliamentary committee is not about whether or not to ban a channel. "We are not Arcom." He called for a broader debate on press freedom and media regulation in the country. There is still a possibility to put the topic on the political agenda in France. A parliamentarian can request a debate within eight days.

title: Amsterdam launches 'offensive against drug nuisance': millions for shelter and care
lead: The Amsterdam city government is allocating 6 million euros to tackle the growing drug nuisance. The municipal executive, among other things, is focusing on extra shelter places and user rooms, more cleaning, and tougher action against nuisance-causing repeat offenders. The municipal executive writes this in a letter to the city council. The city government speaks of a "worrying increase in nuisance linked to visible drug use". The number of tent camps where drug users live is also growing, there is increasing pollution and unsafe situations, and residents' sense of insecurity is growing. The executive says Amsterdammers "pay a high price for the increasing nuisance". The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> also sees this increase in the figures. In the first half of this year, the police registered 1710 alcohol- and drug-related nuisance reports, compared with 1363 a year earlier. Homeless shelter expanded In the letter, the executive speaks of an "offensive against drug nuisance in public space". To reduce the nuisance, Amsterdam is expanding homeless shelter by 274 places this winter. In addition, 37 night shelter places with user rooms for addicted homeless people are being added. They often do not use regular homeless shelters, because drug use is not allowed there. The executive will also investigate whether 250 winter shelter places can remain permanently available from April. Oosterpark neighbourhood and the H-buurt The approach focuses in particular on two "hotspots": the Oosterpark neighbourhood and the H-buurt in Southeast. In these two areas there are many users and the nuisance on the street is very visible. As a result, liveability is "under strong pressure", according to the executive, not only for residents and businesses but also for other homeless people. Among other measures, the focus there is on extra cleaning and more psychiatric nurses. The city government also wants to create more user rooms there, where addicts can use drugs under supervision. A decision will soon be made on whether the Oosterpark gets one or two user rooms. The approach to nuisance-causing repeat offenders is also being given more priority, and the agreements on clearing and cleaning small tent camps are being tightened. According to the executive, the problems on the street are difficult to solve, because they are "complex and intertwined" with each other. The municipality points, among other things, to the shortage of affordable housing and mental health care places, and to the number of homeless migrant workers, which is rising at an "unprecedented pace". Higher national contribution needed Amsterdam believes the national government contributes too little to the shelter of homeless people. The municipality receives 16.5 percent of national funding for social shelter, while according to the municipality 25 percent of the total number of homeless people in the Netherlands stay in Amsterdam. The municipality says it needs 18 million euros extra from the national government to reduce the shortage of shelter and care places. <entity id="person:femke-halsema">Burgemeester Halsema</entity> already sounded the alarm at the end of August about rising drug use and the growing number of homeless people, a problem the four largest cities, Amsterdam, <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity>, are also grappling with. The Amsterdam city government now promises to inform the city council in March next year about the progress of the approach.

title: British comedian David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct towards young women
lead: Several women accuse British comedian, actor and children's book author David Walliams of sexual misconduct. This is revealed by a joint investigation by The Guardian and ITV News . The 55-year-old Walliams denies the accusations and unsuccessfully tried to stop the British media from publishing. Walliams, known from the comedy programme Little Britain , used his power and fame to lure girls and young women into sex, the women tell The Guardian and ITV News. The investigators spoke with thirty sources. The investigative article includes the stories of two women who got to know Walliams when they were fifteen. One of these women first came face to face with the Briton, who was knighted at Buckingham Palace in 2017, at a meet-and-greet. The woman, still a minor at the time, received an autograph and left handwritten scripts with her contact details behind. Sex at seventeen with Walliams One day she was in her bedroom at her parents' home when Walliams called her. Phone calls and many emails back and forth followed. At seventeen, Walliams reportedly suggested at some point that they meet again and have sex. That happened in spring 2006, The Guardian writes, based on the woman's account. The comedian and children's book author reportedly did not use a condom. At another meeting, Walliams and the woman reportedly had oral sex. "I felt like a sex worker", the woman says about her sexual experiences with Walliams. He reportedly asked her to wait in a cafe before their meetings and only come to the apartment once he had contacted her by phone. Another woman says that Walliams approached her online when she was fifteen after she responded to a photo of him. The two exchanged messages and went for drinks in central London in August 2007. At that meeting, Walliams reportedly asked her whether she had ever had sex. Afterwards he reportedly suggested walking with her to the metro. He then reportedly pushed her against the wall and kissed her. The Briton reportedly then asked whether the woman, still a minor at the time, would come to his house. "I think I was still naive about what he wanted", the woman says. "I didn't think he wanted sex." Once at his home, Walliams reportedly kissed her again, groped her breasts and put her hand in his trousers while he had an erection. "I was not ready for sex", the woman says. Walliams eventually stopped. Inappropriate behaviour on Britain's Got Talent Walliams also reportedly behaved inappropriately at work. Behind the scenes of Britain's Got Talent, the popular talent show on which Walliams was a popular judge, his behaviour towards women reportedly caused concern. For example, Walliams reportedly contacted female production assistants of the television show. He wrote "hot" under a photo of a female employee, for instance. He also reportedly received young female fans in his dressing room. Walliams was replaced as a judge in 2022 after demeaning and sexually charged remarks about contestants made between recordings, which were captured on tape. He described one contestant as a "cunt" and said about someone else that "she thinks you want to fuck her, but you don't want to". Furthermore, Walliams was dropped by his publisher HarperCollins at the end of last year. The publisher did not comment at the time on the reasons for this decision, but according to The Telegraph it was related to an investigation into allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards young women. That investigation was carried out in 2023, The Guardian writes. At least five female employees shared their stories, the paper reports, which further writes that Walliams had a sexual relationship with a young employee of the publisher. 'I am not a sexual predator' The investigation by The Guardian and ITV News met with strong resistance from Walliams. His lawyers argued that the comedian and children's book author could commit suicide because of the publication. Nevertheless, the court rejected Walliams' request not to name him, because the investigation concerns "matters of considerable public interest". In a letter quoted by The Guardian, Walliams says he is "not a sexual predator". "I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some women I met ten to twenty years ago now say they were hurt or angry with me." Walliams denies having abused his power. "That is something I have never done."

title: Migrant boats pulled from sea close to our coast, what is going on?
lead: In recent weeks, boats carrying migrants have been spotted off the Dutch and Belgian coasts. That stood out, because nothing like it had happened off the Dutch coast before. The number of boats in Belgium also appears to have increased. What has happened? Is the smuggling route moving north? We set out the five most important questions. What has happened? Last night it happened again in Belgium. Two migrants showing signs of hypothermia were found on a boat. Eleven others were found later; they had clung to a buoy. A day earlier a boat with about thirty migrants bobbed for hours off the Belgian coast at Nieuwpoort. Eventually they ended up in French waters, where they were taken on board by the French coastguard. In the Netherlands, at the end of October, a rubber boat with 38 people was pulled from the sea near Breskens in Zeeland. As far as is known, that was the first time a boat with migrants had been spotted off the Dutch coast. Where do they want to go? The people were all supposedly heading for the United Kingdom. For years the crossing from France to England has been a widely taken route for migrants. Some want to make the crossing to the UK because, for example, they have family there. In recent years the migration flow grew to such an extent that last year the 'One in, One out' deal was concluded between France and the UK. People who now cross the Channel illegally are sent back to France. The aim of the agreement was to reduce illegal crossings and combat people smuggling. Still, people keep coming. The crossing has moved north? According to governor Koen Surdiacourt of West Flanders, people smugglers have devised a new modus operandi. Instead of sailing directly from the French coast to the UK, they travel along the coast to pick up migrants. In doing so they head both north, towards Belgium and the Netherlands, and south along the French coast. "The further apart the boats depart, the harder it is for the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> to locate them," says Surdiacourt. Is the number of boats increasing? According to Surdiacourt, it appears that the number of boats using this new route is increasing. That is partly because there are still many people waiting in tent camps in northern France for a crossing, he says. In addition, the weather is now favourable for departure. "The sea is calm, there is little wind, few waves and little current." Dries Derudder, spokesperson for the Maritime Services and Coast Agency in Ostend, Belgium, also sees this. He has already received "dozens" of reports this year. He says it is no coincidence that more boats have been spotted. "The conditions for such a crossing seem favourable." According to Surdiacourt, the end of the tourist season on the Belgian coast also plays a role. "Belgium has a coastline with a lot of social control," he says. "The dune zones are short and there are apartment blocks right on the coast." Who is on the boats? Mainly single men have been found on the boats. In many cases this probably has the same reason as why there are more men than women in asylum reception: fleeing is dangerous. The father of a family or the eldest son wants to spare the rest of the family that. Women or girls travelling alone face a greater risk of sexual abuse or exploitation than men or boys. But for men and boys too it is a "super dangerous situation", says Derudder. Because of the sea, low temperatures and flimsy boats. "It also shows the desperation of the people who undertake the venture." What is being done? The police in the Belgian town of Middelkerke are deploying extra personnel and are receiving support from neighbouring police zones and the federal police. In addition, there are extra patrols at known hotspots and a drone is being deployed to monitor the area from the air. A spokesperson for the Dutch coastguard tells NOS that there is "extra attention" for the situation and that the coastguard aircraft is "taking it into account" in patrols. No extra personnel is being deployed. That is a choice that has to come from politics, says the spokesperson.

title: Moerdijk residents are tired of the uncertainty: 'Waiting another year and a half is breaking us'
lead: The report that the Brabant municipality of <entity id="org:gemeente-moerdijk">Moerdijk</entity> may after all be preserved is not immediately leading to celebration in the village. The first reactions are cautious. Residents seem tired of the uncertainty. "The new course offers prospects, but we are not there yet," says Wilma Dirken, member of the provincial executive for Spatial Planning of the <entity id="org:provincie-noord-brabant">provincie Noord-Brabant</entity> to Omroep Brabant . The municipality of Moerdijk agrees: "It is a good first step," says a spokesperson. Liveability study Today it became clear that <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is committed to preserving the village of Moerdijk. In a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, State Secretary for Climate De Bat wrote that the expansion of the port and industry may be more limited. The village therefore does not have to be wiped off the map. The final decision has not yet been made, however. First the liveability of the village must be examined. It will therefore take another year and a half before the knot can actually be cut. "Devastating," says an older man on the street about the uncertainty it brings. "Another year and a half of waiting, that is breaking us. For years we have been kept on a string. We are worn out." He thinks it is brave of the municipal council that it was open about the plans in the spring. "But the province and the national government leave us completely in the lurch." Critical Executive member Dirken sees it differently. She was the one who hit the brakes last year when the municipality announced that abolishing Moerdijk was the drastic option. Dirken appreciates that the Rijk has looked critically at the plans. "That shows how important it is to examine major spatial questions carefully and be willing to adjust course based on new insights." At the same time, she says she understands that the prolonged uncertainty has "a big impact" on the Moerdijkers. Moving The only certainty residents have now is that the so-called Moerdijk scheme will remain in place up to and including 2029. Thanks to that scheme, those who want to leave can sell their house to the municipality. Quite a few residents would already have used it, thinks a woman who says she bought a house in the village of Zegge. She and her husband wanted to renovate the house extensively. "It would be a waste of money to still invest in this house if the village may not survive." She has made her peace with it. "It touches me, but I have accepted it. We took the step, drew a line under it, it is what it is." Her parents, whom she cares for, now live around the corner from her. She will have to drive 20 minutes from now on. "If we were one hundred percent sure this village would continue to exist, we would have stayed." Consequences for liveability Residents with a young family, she says, wonder what it means to keep living in a village where many others are leaving. Will the primary school remain? And what about club life? "The fact that people are leaving does have consequences for the liveability of the village." According to the municipal spokesperson, much still needs to be worked out. For an elderly couple of 85, that no longer matters. "By the time everything is turned upside down, we'll be dead."

title: UN chief lashes out at mega profits oil companies are 'raking in' at climate summit
lead: Fossil fuels are not only the driving force behind climate change; our dependence on them also carries high economic and security-related costs. With that message, UN Secretary-General António Guterres addressed the climate summit in Turkey. The outgoing UN leader was fierce about the record profits oil companies have made since the Iran war. "Since the conflict began, the European Union alone has incurred more than 100 billion euros in extra import costs for fossil fuels, without a single extra molecule of fuel to show for it," Guterres fulminated on the second day of the summit . According to the UN chief, the price of petrol has risen by around 26 percent in 130 countries since the war, and diesel by 38 percent. "Families, businesses and governments are paying the price. Meanwhile nine oil companies are on course to rake in more than 95 billion euros in just three months. That is more than a billion per day." A dip, but also record profits. Guterres did not name the oil companies that made large profits, but in recent months there has often been talk of the high prices at the pump that have led to substantial profits for oil producers. Last month it became clear, for example, that Shell recorded a profit of billions for the last quarter. BP also announced it had booked its highest profit in eighteen years. It has long been clear that the Iran war is seriously disrupting global energy markets. Today scientists calculated that there is even a dip visible in CO2 emissions from fossil fuels. Contrary to expectations at the beginning of this year, emissions from them this year will probably come out 1.9 percent lower. At the same time, the war was a reason for a striking record year for coal. Guterres stressed at the climate summit in Turkey that moving away from fossil fuels can no longer be a taboo. "Let us leave Antalya with clear follow-up steps," he urged the countries present. How host country Turkey views this is the question: President Erdogan this week praised the expected increase in domestic oil production. Leaders stay away. It has for years proved very difficult at the major climate summits to talk with each other about phasing down the use of fossil fuels, which is the only way to slow global warming. The previous host of the summit, Brazil, therefore developed a kind of roadmap to phase down that use. Although the UN chief praised that roadmap, it is the question to what extent the discussion about phasing out fossil fuels will go differently this time than in previous years. The fact that, alongside <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, world leaders such as President Xi of China and Indian Prime Minister Modi are staying away reveals that the discussion about phasing out fossil fuels is not at the top of the priority list for several influential countries.

title: More and faster trains: Netherlands and Germany sign rail agreement
lead: International train travel between the Netherlands and Germany must improve considerably in the coming years. More trains must run, including from new operators, and travel times must be shortened. <entity id="person:annet-bertram">Staatssecretaris Bertram</entity> (CDA) reached an agreement on this in Berlin with German transport minister Bilger. Tellingly, the state secretary did not travel to the German capital by train herself. "I would very much have liked to, but the diversions are currently so extensive that it was not possible," Bertram apologises. "That is precisely why it is important that we discuss these matters in Berlin now." The rail agreement provides for improving the most important border routes. At present you can travel by train to the neighbouring country from six places. Next month a local train from Coevorden to Bad Bentheim will be added. On that line, passenger transport becomes possible again after 87 years. These four routes must be improved: By improving these routes, more international trains should be able to run. This concerns not only connections to German cities but also further afield: to Copenhagen (via Hamburg), Warsaw and Prague (via Berlin), and Basel and Vienna (via Frankfurt). Berlin: fewer trains with fewer seats The state secretary believes, among other things, that the connection with Berlin must be better. Roughly double the number of trains run to Paris. Those trains are also much faster. Measured from Amsterdam, you can reach Paris today in 3.5 hours (500 kilometres), compared with nearly 7 hours to Berlin (660 kilometres). "Interest is not a problem, speed is," Bertram thinks. At present NS and Deutsche Bahn run only four direct trains from Amsterdam via Amersfoort, Deventer and Hengelo to Berlin. Due to long-term works, the number of trains has decreased, and next spring all direct trains will be cancelled for three months. The introduction of new train sets has in any case already reduced the number of seats per train by a quarter. That is driving up ticket prices. More competition The Netherlands and Germany also agree to offer new operators more room. GoVolta currently runs to and from Berlin daily, and European Sleeper runs a night train three times a week. These are not free of problems either: for example, GoVolta's trains were cancelled for days last week due to broken carriages. On top of that come the countless delays for which the German rail network is notorious. Last month, 44 percent of trains ran more than six minutes late. Experts at Deutsche Bahn therefore propose reducing the number of trains instead. The trains that do run could then more often arrive on time, is their idea. The demands for expansion are great, but the possibilities are limited. "You cannot simply increase the frequency," Bertram admits. Working groups from rail infrastructure manager ProRail and its German counterpart will therefore first review all bottlenecks. Still, Bertram does dare to dream about the future in 10 to 15 years. "I would like it if you then had multiple options per hour to Frankfurt or Berlin." Wishes and reality clash In terms of freight transport, the Dutch-German border routes are among the busiest in Europe. Around 45,000 freight trains run annually over the routes near Zevenaar, Venlo and Bad Bentheim. On the Dutch side, the Betuweroute was opened in 2007 to connect the Port of Rotterdam with the Ruhr area. The connection on the German side is still not finished. According to Bertram, there is no lack of urgency on the German side. "The seriousness is clear enough, but the shortages in infrastructure in Germany are gigantic." It has now been agreed to complete the connection in 'parts'. A concrete completion date is not in sight. Rail is also crucial for military transport, for example to move tanks quickly from Dutch ports to NATO territory in the east. It should become possible to run heavier trains with a length of 740 metres. All in all, it requires a great deal of patience before Dutch-German rail traffic reaches the desired level. From now on, the Dutch and German ministers will meet annually. Hopefully next time by train, Bertram said.

title: American soldier arrested in UK on suspicion of spying for Russia
lead: A soldier of the American army has been arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of possible espionage. That is what the British police report. He is a 41-year-old man. According to the police, he did this for Russia. The arrest followed cooperation between British and American authorities, the American army and the FBI. FBI director Patel says the man is accused of espionage and that this is a very important arrest. "This matter shows that cooperation is essential for the protection of our countries." "Serious allegations" The British national coordinator for counter-terrorism also emphasises the importance of the arrest. He speaks of "serious allegations". What exactly those are has not been made public. Research is still ongoing. According to a senior commander of the American army, it concerns a high-ranking soldier who was entrusted with sensitive information. The suspect was arrested in Gloucester, about 140 kilometres west of London. According to British media, he was stationed there at a NATO base. He is currently being held in the British capital.

title: Elderly residents of Rotterdam take to the streets against abolition of free public transport
lead: In <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> hundreds of elderly people have demonstrated against the abolition of free public transport for seniors in the city. They fear becoming housebound as a result. Next year most seniors in Rotterdam will probably have to pay for public transport. Only AOW recipients with an income of at most 110 percent of the statutory social minimum may continue to travel free during off-peak hours. The proposed decision is causing discontent among seniors, especially among people whose income is just slightly too high, RTV Rijnmond reports . With signs, flags and banners the demonstrators gathered at Rotterdam Centraal. They then marched in a procession to the city hall on the Coolsingel, where they made themselves heard. 'Behind the geraniums' "Years ago they wanted all the elderly out of the house, and now they send the elderly back to stay at home," says a woman fiercely. The seniors use public transport to go to their clubs, to do something with their grandchildren or to do volunteer work. "If this really goes ahead, we will be housebound. Then we'll soon be sitting behind the geraniums," says Nelly. 'All about the money' Nilva sees the abolition of free public transport for seniors as the straw that breaks the camel's back. She also criticizes the introduction of paid parking in all neighborhoods in Rotterdam. "All about the money," she says. "Taxis, door-to-door transport, they've cut those too, so people may only travel a certain number of kilometres. Public transport is now being taken away. What do they want to do with the elderly?" The woman is visibly emotional. "Rotterdam doesn't want to invest in the elderly. Not in activities for the elderly either. And now taking away public transport, it's only getting worse. I feel this in my wallet too." The Rotterdam city council will deal with the proposed decision this week.

title: D66 council member Sohib H. of Boxtel, suspected of electoral fraud, resigns
lead: Sohib H., the D66 council member from Boxtel who was arrested at the end of October on suspicion of electoral fraud, has submitted his resignation as a municipal councillor. The party's local faction leader announced this during the council meeting . The 38-year-old H. was arrested on 27 October on suspicion of, among other things, corruption and electoral fraud. Besides his council work, H. is an employee of the Parket Centrale Verwerking <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> (CVOM). After his arrest, D66 suspended him for three months. A criminal investigation into H. for money laundering was already under way. Because of that investigation, the OM placed him on non-active status. Empty chair. H.'s council seat remained empty this evening during the council meeting in Boxtel. The mayor, <entity id="person:ronald-van-meygaarden">Ronald van Meygaarden</entity>, initially said that H. was "absent", after which faction leader Wiebe de Leijer was given the floor. "The seat next to me will remain empty this evening," said De Leijer. "Yesterday you (the council, red.) were informed that my faction colleague has submitted his resignation to the chair of the municipal council. We of course respect that decision." D66 wants to install a replacement at the next council meeting on 15 December. Since he became a council member in 2018, H. entered the <entity id="org:gemeenteraad-boxtel">gemeenteraad van Boxtel</entity> twice with a large number of preference votes.

title: Heineken Netherlands director Maarten Schuurman (57) has died
lead: The managing director of Heineken Nederland, Maarten Schuurman, died on Friday from the effects of a brain haemorrhage. The brewer reports this in a message on its website. Schuurman was 57 years old. Schuurman started in 1996 as a trainee at the company. In the years that followed, he held various other positions. For example, he worked for a few years at soft drinks producer Vrumona, which was part of Heineken until three years ago. Afterwards Schuurman worked in Suriname, Ireland and Africa, among other places. In 2023 he became managing director of the Dutch branch of Heineken. In addition, he was vice-chair of employers' organisation VNO-NCW. The employers' organisation is deeply shocked by Schuurman's death. "With his unstoppable optimism, pragmatic attitude and warm personality, Maarten was a pillar of support", says chair Coen van Oostrom. Heineken writes that it will greatly miss Schuurman's "energy, involvement, warmth and sincere attention for others".

title: Pressure mounts after espionage scandal, can the chip giant do without 'Mister Nvidia'?
lead: Jensen Huang, CEO of the American chip company Nvidia, faces one of the biggest challenges in his more than three decades long career as head of the company. The CEO allegedly had an intimate relationship with a Chinese spy, according to American intelligence services. Trump announced that the FBI is investigating him, after the company itself had already started an independent investigation. In addition, shareholders have filed a lawsuit against the company and the CEO. They say they were misled because Huang kept the relationship with the alleged Chinese spy hidden. Still, Huang remains the head of the second most valuable company in the world. Affairs and relationships that were not reported to the board of directors cost other top executives their jobs, such as at McDonald's , Boeing or Intel . No successor Huang is often seen by investors as the brain and driving force of the company. "They see him as irreplaceable for that reason", says investment expert Corné van Zeijl. "He is 'Mister Nvidia', he is in every vein of the company and he sits on Trump's lap." Over thirty years he built it into a company worth nearly 4000 billion euros. "All these factors contribute to investors seeing him that way", says Van Zeijl. Company reports do not specifically state how Huang's succession is arranged, not even in an emergency. Nvidia does write: "We are heavily dependent on our experienced management team", but about succession it only says: "Careless succession plans for executives and key figures could hinder our success in the long term". In recent years Huang has given his daughter and son a senior role within the company. It is not clear whether they are meant to take over the leadership of the company. Also, it is a listed company in which ultimately the supervisory board decides who succeeds him. That board is full of people who have worked with him for a long time. Key-man risk Although dependence on one person is not common in other sectors, it does occur more often at American tech companies. "You see that tech bros try to draw all power to themselves there", says Van Zeijl. When the top executive becomes the embodiment of a company, this is also called key-man risk in business jargon. "You see that more often with these types", says investment strategist at ABN Amro Ralph Wessels. Listed companies usually have two important functions: the CEO and the chair of the board of directors, who must supervise the CEO. Of the largest companies in the United States, Nvidia is the only one without a chair of the board of directors. "That is why the key-man risk at Nvidia is so great", says Wessels. Executives in top positions are permanently under a magnifying glass. "You live, as it were, in a glass house", says emeritus professor of strategy and transformation management at Nyenrode University, Annemieke Roobeek. "It therefore requires that you operate carefully and are always transparent." Based on research by the American government and the photos that circulated, she thinks Nvidia's board must have been aware. "If Huang did not listen to that, then that says something about his management style, and that is a major risk for the company", says Roobeek. Replaceable The Nvidia CEO has no shares with special voting rights, which do occur with other top executives in Silicon Valley. "Huang holds only 3.6 percent of the company's shares, so in theory they could replace him, but investors vote with their wallets and see that this would hurt the company even more", says Van Zeijl. At 3.6 percent, Huang is nevertheless the largest shareholder. In the end Van Zeijl thinks Huang is also replaceable. "We have seen that at Apple too. That company also survived Steve Jobs' departure." Although there was a clear succession plan, with Tim Cook standing ready in the wings at the time.

title: Spaniard speaks of torture in Rotterdam and Utrecht by criminals
lead: A Spanish criminal made an extensive statement to the Spanish police about torture he reportedly underwent earlier this year in Rotterdam and Utrecht. His statement largely matches a witness appeal by the Dutch police in the same case and a report from regional broadcaster Rijnmond about five arrests in the Netherlands in February and June. Thanks to the man's statements, writes the Spanish newspaper El Periódico , the Spanish police, with help from Belgian and Dutch colleagues, were able to dismantle a drug organisation. It was also involved in kidnappings on behalf of other groups, including some linked to the drug war in the underworld. Kidnapped El Periódico spoke with the head of the serious crime unit of the Spanish police. He says the family of the 37-year-old man reported to the police in February that their relative had been kidnapped. The family had also received a video. It showed the man lying naked on the ground somewhere with his hands tied behind his back, being beaten and sexually abused. The kidnappers demanded 600,000 euros in ransom, as compensation for the loss of half a tonne of cocaine. That was reportedly lost during a transport from Spain to the Netherlands, in which the kidnapped man had been involved. Jumped out of car The police opened an investigation, but according to El Periódico the man managed about a week and a half later to jump out of a car in the Belgian town of Lokeren and seek help at a petrol station. When the police arrived, he reported what he had gone through in the preceding days. He told them he had been taken by the kidnappers to a warehouse in Rotterdam, where a torture centre had been set up. Other hostages were also there. They were guarded by men with heavy weapons. One fellow hostage had three finger segments of a hand amputated, another lay unconscious on the ground. He himself was also severely mistreated. After two days he was moved to a house in Utrecht where another victim was also being held. He says he was also mistreated there. When the kidnappers transported him to Belgium, the escape in Lokeren followed. Dismantled The man told the police who he believed was responsible for the kidnapping. People from his own organisation were among them. Thanks to his statements, ten people could be arrested. The ringleaders were arrested in Spain, the rest in the Netherlands, the newspaper reports.

title: Former president Biden (83) pelted during surprise visit to Ireland
lead: Joe Biden, former president of the United States, was assaulted and pelted during a surprise visit to Ireland. At least two people have been detained. The 83-year-old Biden was in the capital Dublin for a visit to Trinity College. There, his son Hunter was awarded a gold medal by student debating society The Hist "for his exceptional contribution to public debate". Father Biden entered the hall unannounced. From the front row, with his wife and former first lady Jill Biden beside him, he watched the ceremony. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators During the ceremony, a group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators gathered outside, and it kept growing. Chants included "Genocide Joe", "Blood, blood on your hands" and "Shame on you". Ireland is considered the most pro-Palestinian country within the EU. During his presidential term, Biden, who likes to boast of his Irish roots, supported Israel and said, for example, that he had no confidence in the death toll published by the Gaza Ministry of Health. In his speech during the ceremony, Hunter described the Israeli bombings of Gaza as "mass murder". "I completely agree that what is happening in Gaza is absolutely and completely wrong. There is no excuse for it." Hunter also believed that his father, during his time as president, "tried to make the best possible decisions based on the information he had at the time". Cartons of milk When Biden and his family left the building after the ceremony, demonstrators pushed forward and threw objects at them, including cartons of milk. Footage shows a police officer using a baton against one of the demonstrators who is being arrested. Two people were arrested. According to the university paper University Times, police used pepper spray in the process. Biden was then escorted to a car by his security guards, who shielded him with umbrellas. Prostate cancer Last year it became known that former president Biden has an aggressive form of prostate cancer, which has spread to other parts of his body and to his bones. Ahead of the release of his memoir, Promise Me, America, on 17 November, Biden said that his illness means he can make fewer public appearances than he had hoped. "Some days are better than others," Biden wrote on X. "That hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it does slow me down." Biden's son Hunter was convicted in 2024 of weapons and tax offences. He committed these while he was addicted to drugs. His father Joe pardoned him at the end of his presidential term.

title: Coalition and House still no further along with tax plan
lead: After another evening of debate, it is still unclear how the tax plan will move forward. An agreement on majorities in the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity> is still not in sight. The political parties are negotiating further today. "Let's look at what is then on the table with a new day and fresh courage," said <entity id="person:eelco-eerenberg">staatssecretaris Eerenberg</entity> (Taxation) in the debate. The tax plan as it now stands appears to be able to count on a majority in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> thanks to the support of Groep Markuszower, ChristenUnie and 50Plus. However, parties can still submit changes, also known as amendments, until 14.00 this afternoon. This could lead to other parties withdrawing their support again, so that there is no majority after all. Tax on wealth Opposition parties Pro and Volt still hope that <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> will choose the 'via links' route. In exchange for their support, the parties want to take 1.5 billion euros from people with a lot of wealth, in order to lower the tax on labour. To pay for this, Pro and Volt want, among other things, to end the tax-advantaged transfer of family businesses. There is no majority for the proposal: both coalition parties VVD, D66 and CDA and several opposition parties are against it. Pro may submit an adjusted plan today, in an attempt to still obtain a majority in the Tweede Kamer. Tight timeframe During the debate, members of parliament complained that the time to make a decision on the tax plan is too tight. They have one day to review all submitted amendments, because they must vote on them on Thursday. On that day, the entire tax plan will also be voted on a few hours later. "There is all sorts hanging over the market, we are all in limbo," says MP Mona Keijzer. The very experienced MP Pieter Grinwis (ChristenUnie) considers it "the most uncertain treatment of a tax plan I have experienced". This is because everything about the tax plan can still change until Thursday. It is therefore also unclear which tax plan the Eerste Kamer will then have to judge. Without an agreement in advance, there appears to be no majority for this. If the Eerste Kamer votes against the tax plan, chaos could arise for millions of taxpayers. The Tweede Kamer may therefore still decide to look for a solution for longer. To that end, the vote on Thursday could be postponed until next week. Motion of no confidence Gidi Markuszower, who forms the Groep Markuszower with six other PVV splinter members, still submitted a motion of no confidence against the cabinet. It did not pass. This motion did raise eyebrows among other members of parliament, because Markuszower was cooperating with the cabinet just last week. "Just shoot me" and "I have lost track" were heard from several members of parliament.

title: Sports club data on the street due to data leak at management system
lead: There has been a data leak at a system that manages the data of members of sports clubs and federations. Personal data was stolen in the process. RTL Nieuws reported the leak first. It concerns the system of All United. Among others, the Dutch cricket federation KNCB reports the leak. The federation says the data of all players has been stolen. It concerns names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and account numbers. Football clubs are also victims of the leak, such as VV Katwijk . The club writes that data from the database has been copied. The total extent of the data leak is not yet clear. Fake messages Both VV Katwijk and the cricket federation warn of fake messages that criminals could send. In them they could, for example, ask for membership fees or a fine to be paid via a link in a payment request. The KNCB advises changing your password for other accounts if it is the same as the password at All United. The federation says AllUnited has closed the leak and that a report has been made to the <entity id="org:zbo-autoriteit-persoonsgegevens">Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens</entity>.

title: No impeachment procedure against US Defense Secretary Hegseth for now
lead: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will stay in office for now. Republicans in the House of Representatives have blocked an attempt to start impeachment proceedings. Hegseth is under fire after the Republicans lost the midterm elections last week. Under his leadership, the United States began a war against Iran. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie had taken the initiative to start impeachment proceedings and was supported by the Democrats. He argued that the war against Iran and the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro should not have been carried out without the consent of Congress. However, Massie's proposal stalled. Republicans gained a majority in the House with 211 votes to 204. As a result, Massie's proposal is being referred to the Republican-led Judiciary Committee of the House. In effect, this means no impeachment procedure will follow. Trump jeers at Massie President Trump is pleased that Hegseth is staying on and speaks of a "failure" by the Democrats. He also calls Thomas Massie "a big loser". A forced departure of Hegseth may still come early next year. Then the Democrats will have a majority in both the House of Representatives and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>.

title: Shooting in Amsterdam, bullet ends up in moving bus
lead: In Amsterdam, a bullet may have flown through the window of a moving bus during a shooting last night. As far as is known, no one was injured. Around 22.30 hours shots were fired on the Slotermeerlaan in district Nieuw-West. At city broadcaster AT5, footage can be seen of a hole at the bottom of a bus door and an object that looks like a bullet on the floor. A passenger on the bus says the bullet came in where people check in and out. A spokesperson for the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> tells AT5 that an investigation is being carried out into the possible bullet impact. It is not clear who fired or what the motive was. No suspects have been arrested yet. The police are also still looking for witnesses.

title: Unemployment among migrants rises, especially young people more often unemployed
lead: In the first three quarters of this year, unemployment among migrants has risen. Unemployment among people born outside the Netherlands rose from 5.8 percent in 2024 to almost 7 percent, according to figures from the Central Bureau of Statistics. Among people born in the Netherlands who have one or two parents born abroad, also called the second generation, unemployment also went up. "We see that over the past year unemployment has risen slightly across the Netherlands, but there are differences", says <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">CBS</entity> economist Peter Hein van Mulligen. "If you look at people of Dutch origin, so those who were born in the Netherlands and whose parents were too, then that increase is only very small." That percentage went from 2.9 to 3 percent. Starting qualification Unemployment has therefore risen mainly among migrants, but the CBS does not yet know exactly why. "It may have to do with their level of education", says Van Mulligen. The Statistics Bureau also looks at the so-called starting qualification, which makes the chance of a job greater. This concerns a diploma of havo, vwo or mbo level 2 or higher. "Without that foundation you see that your chances on the labour market become smaller." The CBS economist indicates that age also plays a role. "Migrants are generally younger, and young people are generally more often unemployed." Tight labour market Van Mulligen also notes that the Dutch labour market is still fairly tight. "Unemployment has grown, mainly because more people have started looking for work", he explains. This may also be the case among the migrant groups. Because they saw that the labour market was doing well, they too started looking for work.

title: Wake-up call 11/11: Elfde van de Elfde and Sint-Maarten celebrated • Online abuse case goes to court
lead: Good morning! It is the Elfde van de Elfde, the traditional opening of the carnival season. In parts of the Netherlands, Sint-Maarten is also being celebrated. In Spain, strikes are taking place across the whole country. Demonstrations have been announced in almost all major cities. First, the weather. This morning it is cloudy, with periods of rain in the southern half. Fog is expected in the Wadden region. This afternoon the sun will shine now and then in the north, but in the south it will remain rainy for quite some time, with highs between 6 and 9 degrees. For the coming days and more weather news, see the NOS Weather: Are you going out today? Here you can find an overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here you can see the situation on the railways. What can you expect today? What did you miss? After another evening of debate, it is still not clear how the tax plan will proceed. A deal on majorities in the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity> is still not in sight. The political parties are continuing negotiations today. Tomorrow the Eerste Kamer is due to vote on the tax plan, but the vote may be postponed. Other news from the night: And one more thing: the Netherlands is gaining a swimming champion. Tatjana Smith has so far swum for South Africa, but is switching to the Netherlands with immediate effect. For South Africa she won gold twice and silver twice at the Olympic Games in Tokyo and Paris. She then stopped swimming for two years. At the WK kortebaan in Beijing, from 1 to 6 December, Smith will make her debut as a Dutch swimmer. Have a great day!

title: Four bears killed in Canada after fatal 'predatory' attack on hikers
lead: In Canada a mother bear and her three cubs have been killed because they are held responsible for a recent fatal attack on two women. The bears were captured last weekend in the Canadian province of British Columbia. Forensic investigation, including DNA analysis of the animals, showed that they were responsible for the attack, local nature authorities reported. The investigation also revealed that the bears had shown "predatory behaviour". To protect public safety, the bears were put down. Along a walking path. The remains of the women, a mother (48) and daughter (20), were found along a walking path near Bella Coola, a small coastal town northwest of Vancouver. According to a family member, the women had walked the route before and saw it as a simple "recreational" walk. The two went walking on Saturday 31 October and were reported missing a day later. Authorities found the remains of the first victim on Monday and those of the second on Tuesday. The discovery led to an investigation lasting several days into the cause of their deaths. Evidence was gathered, and the bears had to be tracked in difficult terrain under severe weather conditions. Although a large population of grizzly bears lives in the area, fatal attacks involving predatory behaviour are rare according to the authorities. This means bears deliberately hunt humans for food. A sign that this was the case here is that the daughter was found in a place where bears store food. Earlier attack nearby. The site of the attack on the mother and daughter is about 3 kilometres from an attack that took place a year ago. Three children and a teacher were seriously injured then during a school outing, when they were attacked by a grizzly bear. That bear was not captured at the time, but researchers were able to collect DNA. Tests showed that the four bears now captured and put down were not involved in that earlier attack. Curfew introduced. After the recent fatal attack, the Nuxalk Nation, the Indigenous government of Bella Coola, introduced a curfew for residents last week. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police also carry out night patrols, and officers escort schoolchildren to and from the school bus. The curfew has now been lifted after the four bears were captured, said chief Samuel Schooner. The night patrols will continue for the time being and will be evaluated in the coming days. Schooner urged residents to remain alert and to report any bear sightings directly to the authorities. Further investigation must establish which circumstances led to the fatal attack.

title: Strong figures again for ABN Amro, staff want to share in the profits
lead: ABN Amro made almost one billion euros in profit last quarter. That is well over half more than the same period last year, according to the figures for the third quarter. Important benchmarks for banks, such as return on investments and costs incurred, are all much better than a year earlier. It shows that CEO Marguerite Bérard, who has been in charge for about a year and a half now, is succeeding in making the bank more profitable. The half-year figures showed the same picture. At the same time, trade unions say staff are dissatisfied about the absence of a new collective labour agreement. Analysts now see the bank as one of the best-performing in Europe. Only a few years ago that was certainly not the case. Due to lagging performance there were rumours of takeovers. 5000 jobs gone. A key reason for the rising profitability is a major reorganisation, in which around 5000 jobs will disappear over a number of years. Almost half of that has already gone, so the bank says it is on track to reach that goal by 2028. However, after an earlier hiring freeze, vacancies are open again, confirms CEO Bérard. "We look first at talent within the bank and only then at specific positions outside it." Some of the staff protested today during the presentation of the quarterly figures outside the head office. Trade unions are very disappointed with the bank's latest wage offer and are using the rising profits to make their point. The collective labour agreement expired last summer. According to union FNV, the wage demand would cost the bank 160 million euros. Bérard does not want to go into that. "That is part of the negotiations and we are not conducting those through the media." Half the time in the office. Talks on a new collective labour agreement resume next week. As part of that new agreement, ABN also wants staff to be in the office at least half of the time. That is a sensitive issue, FD wrote earlier. Some staff now live far away. At the same time, ABN sees that it is difficult for new employees, especially young ones, to settle in properly in an empty office. The state is increasingly withdrawing as a shareholder. Its stake will be reduced from around 20 percent to about 10 percent over the coming period. This is happening at a share price that is rising quickly. ABN Amro shares are almost half higher than at the start of this year. Since Bérard took office, the share price has more than doubled.

title: Rozendaal, the smallest municipality on the Dutch mainland, wants to merge
lead: If it is up to the <entity id="org:gemeenteraad-rozendaal">gemeenteraad van Rozendaal</entity>, the Gelderland municipality will soon join the nearby municipalities <entity id="org:gemeente-rheden">Rheden</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-brummen">Brummen</entity>. According to the nine-member council, continuing independently is no longer financially and organisationally responsible. Rozendaal, near Velp, with 1800 residents is the smallest municipality on the Dutch mainland. Only <entity id="org:gemeente-schiermonnikoog">Schiermonnikoog</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-vlieland">Vlieland</entity> have fewer residents. On election nights the municipality is often one of the first to count all votes and announce the result. This year the future viability of Rozendaal was examined. It turned out that the municipality, located at Veluwezoom National Park, will face a structural budget deficit from next year. Also, the administrative organisation - about fifteen people work at the municipality - does not seem sufficiently equipped for the increasingly extensive statutory tasks imposed on it. "Continuing independently requires substantial, lasting investments in people, knowledge and systems", said mayor Timmer. "We do not have that financial room." 'Difficult, but responsible' Merging was therefore the logical choice. Initially, <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity> was also considered, but according to the board, joining the municipalities of Rheden (around 44,000 residents) and Brummen (around 22,000 residents) is the best option for the future of the municipality. Those two municipalities are in the middle of a reorganisation process. Rheden and Brummen want to have a plan next summer for what a new municipality should look like. Rozendaal can therefore take part early in those talks. "Rozendaal can participate as an equal third partner", according to the municipality. The municipal councils of Rheden and Brummen still have to agree to this. They will probably discuss this topic again this year, writes Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> . If all councils agree, the three municipalities will work together on a reorganisation design. And so, after 200 years of independence, an end may come to the municipality of Rozendaal, a municipality with relatively many homes worth millions according to appraisal company Calcasa. Mayor Timmer calls the decision a difficult but responsible choice. "This is not the outcome we hoped for at the start of this process", she says. But in her view, by joining the talks on reorganisation now, Rozendaal can still influence the future of the village. Rozendaal Blijft Not all residents of Rozendaal are happy with the merger process. Some think it is going too fast and started a petition asking the council to carefully weigh the matter again. The petition was signed more than 500 times. According to citizens' initiative Rozendaal Blijft, it has not been sufficiently substantiated that the board would be unable to balance the budget next year. Alternative scenarios, moreover, have not been seriously examined according to the initiative. "There is no clear indication why a decision is necessary today, and cannot be taken in a few months." The council acknowledges that the process is moving quickly, but also says it is necessary to join Rheden and Brummen as an equal third partner. In addition, the research was carefully carried out, says mayor Timmer. "The steps we have taken each followed from new insights. During the first phase it already became clear that we had to look more broadly than only at independent survival." Should the merger go ahead, Rozendaal will no longer be the smallest municipality on the Dutch mainland. Apart from the Wadden Islands, excluding Texel, the Utrecht municipality of <entity id="org:gemeente-renswoude">Renswoude</entity> with about 5900 residents would then be the smallest municipality in the country.

title: Podcast De Dag: If you swap your well-paid job for... something more fun
lead: Swapping a complex and demanding job for one that requires less specialist knowledge or involves less pressure. Irreverently this is also called 'downshifting', because it often pays less. Yet over the past ten years more people have taken that step, according to figures from the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">CBS</entity>. Why? And how does it change your life? Listen here: This episode of De Dag you can listen to via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. In this podcast three 'downshifters' tell why less money actually gives them more. Okke Amerongen happily went to his jobs as an e-commerce specialist, but one day decided to change course. He is now a baker, working from home. Nikki van Zunderd was a trainer for works councils and is now a hiking coach in the Austrian mountains. And Tobias Molenaar swapped his work as a sustainability consultant for the bicycle: he became a bike courier. None of them regrets it. Feedback? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation and editing: Elisabeth Steinz Editorial team: Max Smedes Final editing: Rosanne Sies
