title: Russia and Ukraine strike each other while negotiations take place in Abu Dhabi
lead: Russia and Ukraine carried out air attacks on each other overnight and this morning. The Russian army bombed, among other things, energy plants, and Ukrainian drones hit a Russian port on the Baltic Sea. Air raid sirens briefly sounded in the Baltic states. Meanwhile, negotiations on an end to the Russian invasion of Ukraine continue today in Abu Dhabi. The first day of talks between American, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators was described as positive and constructive by the parties themselves. However, the chance of a diplomatic breakthrough in the protracted conflict appears small. Moscow, for example, insists on occupying the entire Donbas region, including the areas Ukraine still defends. Kyiv calls this non-negotiable. A new exchange of prisoners of war is, however, in the works. Diplomats from EU countries are also present in Abu Dhabi. They are not at the negotiating table, but do speak with American and Ukrainian officials on the spot. European countries have not been directly involved in negotiations between Russia and Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022. Power outages due to Russian attacks Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continue meanwhile. At least eight regions are now dealing with large-scale power outages, the ministry of Energy reports. Capital Kyiv in particular has been hit hard. The Russian ministry of Defence says it has bombed transformer stations in three regions. In the southern port city of Odesa, a cargo ship was attacked. Russia claims the ship was transporting weapons for the Ukrainian army. Correspondent Christiaan Paauwe showed at the end of last month what Russia's attacks mean for residents of Kyiv: The Ukrainian army carried out long-range drone attacks again overnight. Among other places, the Russian port city of Oest-Loega, about 25 kilometres from the border with Estonia, was hit. The city's governor speaks of a fire in the port, but does not say exactly what was hit. Oest-Loega is an important hub for the Russian oil and gas trade and was therefore already a target of Ukrainian attacks earlier. Air raid alarm in Baltic states The Russian army says it shot down more than 600 Ukrainian drones overnight, spread across the country. In Smolensk, near Belarus, two deaths were reported. According to the regional governor, they died from debris of a drone. In Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, air raid alarms sounded due to the series of air attacks. In a number of border areas, residents had to take cover because of the possibility that drones were on their way from Belarus and Russia. It is unclear whether unmanned aircraft actually entered the airspace of the Baltic states. There are no reports of injuries or damage. The warning was lifted after a short time.

title: 'Cabinet shows little interest in managing the Dutch gold reserve'
lead: The <entity id="pos:minister-van-financien">minister van Financiën</entity> has little insight into the Dutch gold reserve. That is what the <entity id="org:algemene-rekenkamer">Algemene Rekenkamer</entity> writes in a report. He may gather information from <entity id="org:zbo-de-nederlandsche-bank">De Nederlandsche Bank</entity> (DNB), but hardly makes use of that option. DNB manages over 600 tonnes of gold worth over 72 billion euros. It is located in New York, Ottawa, London and Zeist. It is a kind of "piggy bank for emergencies" and DNB is solely responsible for how it is handled. "At the same time, the question is whether the minister does not want to know, in broad outline, how DNB manages the gold reserve", states the Algemene Rekenkamer. The independent body that oversees government spending calls this management one of the "vital interests of the state". "Then you would also expect him to want to know how these vital interests of the state are secured and what risks there are." But there are, for example, no agreements between DNB and the minister of Finance about what happens to the gold in times of crisis. DNB states that the gold belongs to the central bank and remains so, also in times of a financial crisis or war. Relocation this summer The minister of Finance has appointed an external accountant to audit DNB's annual accounts, but the report shows that this accountant does not take part in physical checks in foreign vaults. The minister is not informed about how the checks by DNB and the external accountant work. For example, DNB moved part of the gold reserve from New York to the Netherlands in 2014. The operation was prepared and carried out in secret. It is not certain whether the minister of Finance was informed in advance at the time. In the summer of 2026, when a large amount of gold went from New York and Ottawa to London, current <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> was informed by DNB shortly beforehand. Minister Heinen says he is convinced that the management of the gold reserve by DNB "contributes to the resilience of the Dutch economy, especially in times of geopolitical tensions". 'No reason for concern' He is not worried about the exchange of information. "In normal times there is little reason for that", he responds to the report. The minister also states that Finance and DNB have drawn up internal guidelines, which mean that "the gold reserve is managed passively". He also says he always attends DNB's annual meeting and receives information (un)solicited. The report on the management of the gold reserve concerns the function of the minister of Finance in general and not Heinen personally. The Algemene Rekenkamer writes that oversight of the management of the Dutch gold reserve was also not great under his predecessors.

title: Council of State: asylum minister must reassess security in Syria
lead: Asylum minister Van den Brink must reassess the security situation in Syria. That is what the Council of State, the highest administrative court in the country, has ruled. It writes that the policy on the security situation in Syria is now insufficiently substantiated. The ruling follows a lawsuit that a Syrian asylum seeker had brought after his asylum application was rejected under then asylum minister Van Weel. The man was captured and tortured in 2014 by the Assad regime in Syria, because he allegedly took part in a demonstration. If he were to return to Syria, he fears facing violence again. Voluntary return <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> said after the fall of the Syrian regime of dictator Assad, at the end of 2024, that parts of the country were safe again, and that Syrians from the Netherlands should therefore be able to return . Groups of Syrians then also left, flying back to Syria voluntarily on charter flights organised by the Dutch government. In 2025, 945 Syrians returned with financial support from the government. To encourage voluntary return, the then caretaker cabinet-Schoof temporarily raised that allowance from 2800 to 5000 euros per adult, and from 1650 to 2500 euros per minor family member. After almost two months, as of 1 January of this year, the allowance was reduced again to the earlier amounts. It is unclear to what extent the temporary increase contributed to voluntary return to Syria. Substantiation falls short But according to the highest administrative court, the substantiation of the current Syria policy of the cabinet falls short. The minister should have weighed the humanitarian circumstances and the aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime alongside the security situation. Therefore the current country policy offers an insufficient basis for rejecting the asylum application. Asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom writes in a response that the <entity id="org:immigratie-en-naturalisatiedienst">IND</entity> could have saved time by immediately giving the "correct assessment". By this he refers to weighing the humanitarian situation that still stems from policy of the Assad regime. Vluchtelingenwerk says the ruling acknowledges that reality in Syria is more complex than just the number of violent incidents. "The humanitarian circumstances also determine whether people can return safely." Minister Van den Brink says in response that he is studying the ruling.

title: Historic victory in Mississippi beckons, a Black senator for the first time in 145 years
lead: For the first time in 145 years, the southern American state of Mississippi looks set to get a Black senator again. Scott Colom has not yet won, the last votes are still being counted. But some residents of the state where Donald Trump won six out of ten votes in 2024 are already breathing a sigh of relief. "This was a great week", says Annette Hollowell. A week after the midterm elections, a neck-and-neck race is still underway in the states of Alaska and Mississippi in the battle for a Senate seat. Both states went convincingly for Trump in recent elections. But what was deep red Republican territory now seems to be turning Democratic blue. Counting the decisive votes The doors of the election committee office in DeSoto County in North Mississippi are locked. Onlookers are not welcome for now. Counting will take place here over the coming day. "Until then nothing happens here, we don't touch anything and we give no interviews", one of the polling station staff shouts outside. Inside are boxes of postal votes still to be counted. There are also ballot papers whose validity still needs to be determined. These are votes that could make the difference in a breathtaking battle. After counting 98 percent of the votes, Democrat Scott Colom now leads Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2990 votes, a difference of 0.3 percentage points. Clarity must come by Friday at the latest. Check our results tool for the latest situation: Hollowell is already taking a head start on that. "I am extremely happy that he will become our next senator", she says. Hollowell was a lawyer at the civil rights organisation where Colom also took his first political steps. "He is the kind of leader Mississippi needs. I think he will really commit to bringing people together." Hollowell runs Foxfire Ranch, an estate her family bought over a hundred years ago. It is a place where African American heritage, such as hill country blues, is celebrated. The likely election of Colom did not come out of nowhere, she says. "This struggle has a very long history here." Nearly 40 percent of Mississippi's residents are Black, the highest percentage of all states in the US. But for <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> white politicians were systematically chosen: the last Black senator from Mississippi left Washington in 1881. A long road to equal rights Discriminatory rules long kept Black voters from access to the ballot box. The Freedom Summer of 1964 gave new momentum to the fight for voting rights and the struggle against discrimination and oppression of Black voters. Young people, Black and white Americans from across the country, travelled to Mississippi. Together they fought for voting rights and civil rights, and battled the intimidation and terror of the Ku Klux Klan. "For things that ultimately benefit everyone, not just one particular group", says Hollowell. In 1965 the Voting Rights Act followed, the law that was meant to better protect voting rights. It did not stop there. "This is the result of years of organising", she says. "Many people worked hard to get voters to the ballot box, to mobilise communities and to stand up for their interests." Not everyone here is happy with the Democratic advance. "I'm disgusted by it", says an older white woman who introduces herself as Vicky. "Because I don't want to live under Islamic rule. And I don't want communism", she says when asked how the town of Hernando woke up after the elections. She refers to Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, against whom the Republicans ran a campaign full of Islamophobia. He was portrayed, among other things, as a "terrorist". El-Sayed himself said: "I am not running to become a Muslim senator; I am running for the US Senate and happen to be Muslim." A 30 percentage point difference in two years In the last presidential elections, the difference between Trump and his Democratic rival Kamala Harris in North Mississippi was over 24 percentage points. In the Senate elections, Democrat Colom now has a lead of 6: a difference of 30 percentage points. "A shock, they are bad for America", says a visitor to one of the cowboy churches, where faith is brought to the rodeo arena. He himself says he has remained loyal to the Republican party. "But with high petrol prices it's hard not to vote for the other side." Back at Hollowell's ranch, the cradle of the blues, the tones of Trenton Ayers ring loudly through the hills. His father was bassist for the well-known blues musician Junior Kimbrough. Today there is dancing here, and the Democrats' blue wave is being celebrated. "We're right in the middle of the blues wave", jokes Hollowell. "But there's still a lot of work to do, a lot of repair work to be done."

title: Brief outage at government websites caused 'by human error'
lead: Several government websites were briefly unreachable. This included the website of the national government, the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> and the Royal House. Anyone trying to reach one of the government websites saw a white screen with the text ' Access Denied' . There appears to be no intent involved. In a statement, the national government says the outages arose when an update was being rolled out. The national government speaks of a 'human error' . The website of the Dutch emergency alert system, NL-Alert, was also down for a while. Because NL-Alert warnings are sent via mobile networks, the system itself was not affected by the unreachable website. The current notices were still readable, and warnings could have continued during the outage, according to the spokesperson. Access blocked That error message came from Akamai, a so-called content delivery network that organisations hire to make websites quickly reachable anywhere in the world. That error indicated that Akamai was blocking access to the websites for all visitors.

title: German suspect in abduction and murder of 13-year-old Lisa dies
lead: The 22-year-old German man suspected of abducting and murdering 13-year-old Lisa from Berlin has died of injuries sustained around his arrest. This is reported by the Berlin Public Prosecution Service. The girl was reported missing on Tuesday of last week. She had left home early in the morning for school. On the way, according to her sister, she was still texting a friend, after which contact suddenly stopped. Germany was gripped for days by the disappearance. Last Sunday, the lifeless body of the 13-year-old girl was found in a house in Altglietzen, close to the Polish border, a good hour's drive from Berlin. According to German media, the 22-year-old suspect tried to take his own life when police arrived. He sustained life-threatening head injuries in the process and was taken to hospital. 113 Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking helps, and you can do so anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113. Both the suspect and the 13-year-old girl came from the Berlin district of Marzahn-Hellersdorf. The Public Prosecution Service reported yesterday that there are still no indications that the suspect and the girl knew each other. According to the German newspaper Tagesspiegel, the man was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for just over two months in November 2025. How Lisa died is still being investigated. So far, no clear cause of death has been established.

title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland evacuated over bomb threats
lead: In Italy, Northern Ireland and Scotland, schools have been evacuated due to a bomb threat. Countless educational institutions have been threatened by email. Authorities say it is very likely that these are false alarms. As far as is known, no explosive has been found anywhere. According to Italian Education Minister Valditara, at least 300 schools have been evacuated across the country. This number could be higher. Nothing suggests the threat is serious, the minister told Italian media. The false alarms seem intended to spread fear, says Prime Minister Meloni on social media. The threatening email to schools also claimed that a bomb had been placed in the prime minister's car. Meloni urges people to keep calm. 'Michail Antropov' As a precaution, police in several cities had turned out because of the false bomb threats. In some cases dogs were used to search school buildings for bombs in vain. The email threatened a "genocide of Italians". The message was signed by someone named Michail Antropov, reports news agency Ansa. Recently, various bomb threats under this name have been made in Europe. Who is actually responsible for these threatening texts remains unclear. 'Keep schools open' Authorities in Scotland and Northern Ireland also say that a large number of schools were threatened by email today. Schools are advised to remain open, as police do not consider the threat realistic. A primary school in Newtownards in Northern Ireland was evacuated, the Belfast Telegraph reports. Evacuations have also been reported in Scotland, but it is unclear how many educational institutions have been evacuated as a precaution. Recently, countless false bomb threats have been made, including in European aviation. Several media outlets in Ireland and the United Kingdom have also been threatened.

title: Arrests, fines and blockades: press freedom in Egypt under further pressure
lead: The free press in Egypt is under heavy pressure. Within a month, the entire six-person editorial team of investigative platform Matsaddash has been arrested, and a judge has ruled that the independent news site Mada Masr must be shut down. Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was held for a short time and had to pay a fine of roughly 50,000 euros. Attalah was also told that two years earlier she had been sentenced in absentia to one year in prison for running a website without a licence and publishing fake news. That case is being heard again today. Intimidation and threats Egypt is one of the countries where many journalists are imprisoned. There are currently eighteen of them, and on the Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index the country ranks 169th out of 180. Even so, this government campaign is of a different level, says senior editor Mohamed Hamama of news site Mada Masr. "It hangs over us like a sword of Damocles. And it works, because we are worried and tired." In Egypt, journalists regularly face intimidation and threats from the authorities, in addition to prison sentences. For example, at the beginning of October the prominent journalist and human rights defender Rasha Azab was questioned by the authorities about her posts on social media. Thanks to a patchwork of vague legislation, the authorities can tightly control and restrict the digital space, the human rights organisation The Egyptian Human Rights Forum warned this year. Since 2017, more than a hundred news sites have been blocked in Egypt. This often happens without a legal basis or a transparent process. Accusations such as spreading fake news, running a website without a licence and membership of a terrorist organisation are catch-all terms that the Egyptian state uses against political prisoners. The journalists of Matsaddash and Mada Masr are also accused of these. Legal limbo According to the Egyptian media law of 2018, journalistic websites must have a licence to exist. Since then, several independent news media have been in a legal limbo: they have submitted an application and paid the fees, but they hear nothing back from the authorities. Mada Masr also made several applications for a licence, in 2018 and again in 2020, when the statutes of the media law were published. Officially, the state must respond after three months, but it did not. Only in 2022 did editor-in-chief Attalah receive a rejection letter. She submitted a new application, but that too went unanswered. According to the head of the journalists' union, 95 website applications are still awaiting assessment by the regulator, and journalists are paying the price for this licensing crisis, writes the news site Al Manassa. The <entity id="org:hoge-raad">hoge raad</entity> voor mediatoezicht defended the policy and said that channels that still do not have a licence form only a small minority. 'Institutional panic' Mada Masr is the best-known independent news medium in Egypt, one of the few that still exist. For the editorial team, this new intimidation campaign is not the first: as early as 2019, security services raided the office in Cairo. According to editor Hamama, the harder intervention by the government is related to domestic and foreign problems. Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi announced in October that he would step down in 2030, which led to "institutional panic" in the army and other bodies, says Hamama. Moreover, Egypt has for years been struggling with a severe economic crisis and with several wars on its borders. Sisi is also considering becoming more directly involved in the war in Yemen by sending military aid to Saudi Arabia. 'Fighting hard' According to Hamama, the government's message to journalists is not aimed only at Mada Masr. "All journalists are terrified, because they know: if they manage to shut down Mada Masr, they are next. That is also why everyone is fighting hard to prevent that; their own survival depends on it." On 25 November, Mada Masr will appeal against the judge's closure order. "But even if they do not shut us down now, there is no guarantee for the future," says Hamama.

title: Closure looms for outdated RIVM laboratories, but relocation is not yet possible
lead: Laboratories of the RIVM at the Science Park in Bilthoven may have to close soon because of the risk of virus outbreaks. That is what the manager writes in a letter seen by the Financieele Dagblad. The laboratories are said to be so outdated that the manager of the complex no longer considers it responsible to use them. Research into contagious pathogens is carried out in the laboratory. 'The chance of an outbreak arising there is real,' says investigative journalist Johan Leupen of the FD to the NOS. 'They are very dangerous organic substances and viruses.' The manager of the laboratories, Stichting-ALt, must ensure that institutions on the site enforce the environmental permit. According to the manager, it is not responsible to keep the buildings open. 'Everything safe' A spokesperson for the RIVM tells the NOS that there is no risk of an outbreak. The National Institute for Public Health and the Environment says it received the letter a week and a half ago. 'It is now up to us to make clear that everything is safe,' the spokesperson said. 'It concerns the safety of employees and residents, and we are giving it all our attention and care.' According to the FD, 4000 people work on the whole park, of whom more than 3000 for the RIVM. Tolerated situation According to chairman Nico Oudendijk of Stichting ALt, there is already a tolerated situation at the moment, he tells the FD. The intention was for the RIVM to move earlier to a new location in Utrecht that does meet the requirements, but that move has been delayed. The buildings in which the current RIVM laboratories are housed date from 1953 and were built with 3,5 miljoen gulden in Marshall aid. With that American aid plan from after the Second World War, money, goods, raw materials and foodstuffs went to European countries in the form of loans and gifts. Meanwhile the buildings no longer meet the requirements. Among other things, the lock on the site where people have to disinfect themselves would not function properly, says Leupen. New office delayed again The new RIVM building was supposed to be ready in 2018, but the institute still has not moved. First there were problems with vibrations from the tram line near the building, which had not been sufficiently taken into account. Those vibrations could affect the sensitive equipment in the laboratories. Last year the security installation also did not function properly. Leupen of the FD calls this 'painful'. 'They have been working on a new head office for twelve years,' he says. 'But the RIVM cannot move because the building does not yet meet the requirements.' Last September it turned out that the move had to be postponed again. This was because gas generators still had to be installed. According to Leupen, the manager would consider pulling the plug as of January. The RIVM spokesperson says the organisation is in talks with the manager and that 'safety comes first'. 'Moving a laboratory is complicated, and an extensive planning precedes it.'

title: State secretary after U-turn Moerdijk: 'Task to win back trust'
lead: How can plans change so quickly in such a short time? Will we be standing here again next year, and will the residents of Moerdijk once again be promised a different future? State secretary De Bat (<entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity>) received these questions today at a press conference in the North Brabant village where he explained the revised plans. A year ago the municipality announced that the North Brabant village in the municipality of the same name must make way for the expansion of the nearby port and industrial area. Yesterday De Bat reported in a letter to the House of Representatives that the expansion can be limited, from 450 hectares to 200 hectares, so that Moerdijk can nonetheless continue to exist. The change of course raises the question of how that expectation could change so drastically in a year. "There is a new file on the table, you look at it and ask questions about it," said De Bat. "One of those questions was: how hard is that national task really?" Research showed that the expansion could be scaled down. According to De Bat, the difference mainly lies in changed expectations about the future of hydrogen and the circular economy. "We have now made the choice that Moerdijk is preserved and the surrounding area remains liveable. That is the direction we are now taking." Asked why the government could not think of this a year ago, he said: "It was not thought of, but it is now on the table." De Bat does not see the course looking different again in a year. Alderman Dingemans of Moerdijk emphasised today that the earlier decision to dissolve the village was also based on the 450-hectare expansion. Even so, he said he was also worried about the smaller expansion. "People cannot live in an unliveable environment. That is and will remain the starting point." At the same time he said that the plans for 200 hectares will also have their effects. "It is not only about people who live in the village of Moerdijk. The task spreads over a larger area. As a result the impact may be less concentrated, but people live in all those areas. That calls for an even broader look at what that impact will be." Plaything of policy. In the coming period, central government (Rijk), the province and the municipality will look at whether the new plans can succeed without the liveability of Moerdijk and the surrounding villages coming under pressure. De Bat said he could not say when new developments are expected in the file. "We did not expect to be standing here today either, but we are, because we have worked hard." The state secretary said he could well imagine that residents of Moerdijk feel like a plaything of policy. "But this is the situation as it is now. Now it is our task to win back trust."

title: OM suspects care worker under investigation may have claimed more victims
lead: The 26-year-old care worker who is in custody on suspicion of involvement in the deaths of two patients at a care home in Oirschot has probably claimed more victims, according to the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> (OM). Jelle D. denies that he has anything to do with the deaths of the patients. D. was a nurse at the Sint Joris care home of Joris Zorg. He was arrested last summer after the unnatural death of one of the residents of the centre. The OM started an investigation, which revealed a second death. The 26-year-old man is also suspected of involvement in the death of this person. The two deaths mentioned above took place on 15 and 19 August, but several residents also died in the weeks before. The OM calls this "highly suspicious". Jelle D. was the only employee who was working each time someone died, Omroep Brabant heard during the first public hearing. Insulin overdose The two residents who died on 15 and 19 August were, according to the OM, two men with advanced dementia. Puncture marks from insulin injections were found in their bodies. High concentrations of insulin were also measured in both of them. Both men did not have diabetes. According to the OM, the men were given an overdose of insulin by the suspect, which proved fatal. Footage shows, according to prosecutors, that on the evening of 14 August D. entered <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de kamer</entity> of the man who died on 15 August. This happened after the resident had been put to bed and staff therefore no longer had to enter the room. The footage shows that D. leaned over the man up to three times and pulled the blanket aside. Similar footage was found a few days later of the other man who died, the OM says. Tunnel vision D. believes that the OM has tunnel vision. According to him, he was not the last person to have been with the men on the evenings in question. "Something is being pinned on me that I did not do", he said. "There is no evidence and in half a year there still won't be. I beg you to release me until the substantive hearing." D. was seen a few years ago in the SBS programme De Bondgenoten. All episodes in which he appeared on streaming services have been removed.

title: Missing baby found alive in dog cage buried in US forest
lead: In the American state of South Carolina, officers have found a missing baby. The eleven-month-old boy was in a dog cage wrapped in a towel. Koah Sharpe, as the child is called, was still alive. According to the local sheriff, the baby has probably spent a full day in that condition. The father has been arrested. Koah went missing on Monday after the mother left him with his father. A babysitter was later supposed to take over but found no one there, after which an alarm was raised. A large search was then launched. More than a hundred officers and others searched for Koah. The child was finally found on Tuesday afternoon local time, after officers saw at the house of the suspect's father that earth had been removed from one spot. After they began digging, they heard the baby crying. Burglary Koah has been admitted to hospital. It is unclear how he is doing. The sheriff expressed hope that the child will fully recover. The father of the boy was arrested on the evening of the day he went missing. He was reportedly engaged in a burglary and resisted his arrest. The man has not yet been charged with abducting Koah or burying the child, but prosecutors are still working intensively on the case.

title: Wouter and Mart want a child, but the law makes it difficult
lead: Just like <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> and his fiancée, Wouter and Mart would dearly love to have a child. But the legislation does not make it any easier. Wouter hopes that Jetten's baby news will draw more attention to this problem in the Netherlands, he tells RTL Nieuws.

title: D66 and CDA strike deal with Pro and Volt on tax plan, no response from VVD yet
lead: Coalition parties D66 and CDA have concluded a deal with opposition parties Pro and Volt on a tax increase for the wealthy and a tax cut on wages. This was done without the consent of coalition partner VVD. "This is a breakthrough", says Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity>. "Over the past few days we have sought a compromise in good consultation to make the Netherlands fairer. If this proposal is adopted, the Netherlands will get a millionaires tax." Now we are waiting for a judgement from the VVD. The VVD has consistently opposed raising tax on wealth because the party considers it bad for the economy and the business climate. Millionaires tax The deal concerns an adjusted version of what Pro and Volt call the 'millionaires tax'. It is an amendment to the Tax Plan 2027 of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. In the version on which the deal has now been concluded, 1 billion more is taxed from wealthy people, and the same amount is subtracted from income tax. Previously it was 1.5 billion. The financial basis has also changed. It is now based on an increase in the wealth tax in box 3, the 'approach' to paper gifts, an increase in inheritance and gift tax, and a 'budget target' for tackling financial constructions designed to avoid tax. It appears that a majority in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> may support this amendment. But whether this will break the coalition out of its impasse, and whether the tax plan as a whole will win a majority in both the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity>, is not yet clear. Major objections The VVD has also expressed major objections during the debate on the tax plan to Pro's original proposal. According to the VVD, it goes against the coalition agreements and against the financial basis of the box 3 amendment. The VVD called it "unthinkable that this proposal in this form will be supported by one of the coalition parties". In its original proposal, Pro wanted, among other things, to raise the top rates in box 2 and box 3; with the money this brings in, workers would receive a higher general tax credit. In total this involved a shift of 1.5 billion euros. The amended plan has a different financial basis, but that has not yet been discussed with the VVD. "We have spoken with D66 and CDA. Whether the VVD supports it, you will have to ask the VVD", says Klaver. Votes Tomorrow the votes on the tax plan and all proposed amendments are scheduled. They are expected after an added debate with <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> about the situation. For this reason Jetten will not attend an EU meeting in Dublin. It is in principle possible that the coalition of D66, VVD and CDA will vote for the tax plan, but that the VVD will vote against Pro's amendment. The parties have agreed that in the extreme case they may let each other go during the votes. Political discussion is about the portion of tax revenue to be collected With the Tax Plan 2027, central government collects money from citizens and businesses. This is then used to pay for expenditure for citizens and businesses, such as care, social security, roads, public transport and schools. Most taxes are fixed, because most political parties agree with them. Central government expects to collect 480 billion euros in taxes in 2027. Most of this comes from wage and income tax, value added tax (btw), health insurance premiums, corporation tax, AOW premiums and employee insurance premiums such as WW, WIA and sick pay. The political discussion is about relatively small shifts and changes, which can nonetheless be very principled. For example, a plan that involves only 1.5 billion of the 480 billion euros, such as Pro's 'millionaires tax', can still lead to political discussion.

title: Nationwide strike in Spain shuts down parts of the country
lead: An adjusted public transport timetable, closed petrol stations, and schools with a minimum number of teachers in the classroom. Few Spaniards will be unaware of today's general strike. A strike that was already announced in the summer, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen . With the housing crisis as the main issue, it is the first general strike in fourteen years. Last month the government already took measures on the subject, but that was not enough for the trade unions. There had been talk on Sol for a while now, the Madrid square where hundreds of people camped out last month in protest against the housing crisis. But the day after the announcement of early elections, the trade unions announced the date of the general strike. The trade unions saw a momentum to keep attention on the issue. Wages, housing and prices With the motto 'wages, housing and prices', they called on Spaniards not to go to work today. The 24-hour general strike began at midnight, with road blockades and a limited public transport timetable. While the strike began as a protest against the housing crisis, the trade unions are concerned with much more than that. At la Plaza de Cibeles in Madrid, the two largest trade unions are already coming together during the day. It is raining hard, but many people have still turned up. Care workers, public transport staff and even lifeguards. A group of firefighters is there with a large banner. They are not satisfied with the working conditions the municipality offers them. But they are not only there for that. "The most important thing is that there is social justice, that there are decent wages, that people have the right to access decent housing", says firefighter José. "And that not all the money goes to those at the top. Wealth must be shared", he believes. Commissioned by the Spanish media El País and Cadena <entity id="org:sociaal-economische-raad">SER</entity>, research agency 40dB asked Spaniards about their support for the strike. According to the results, 46 percent of people support the strike and 49 percent do not. Not all of those people want or are able to lay down their work. According to the same research, about 23 percent would want to or be able to. But that percentage will differ greatly between sectors and regions. The police took a hard line against demonstrators in Madrid: In a café around the corner sit the friends Alice and Maddelena, tourists from Italy. This morning they stood at a closed door at the Reina Sofía museum. "There was a long queue and we had no idea why the door was not opening. Then the people there told us there was a strike", the friends say. They are not angry. "We are on holiday and have nothing to complain about", laughs Maddelena. They understand that people want to protest. "You see it all over Europe. People are frustrated about their livelihoods and take to the streets. We have these problems in Italy too." In most large cities, trains, metros and buses are running on an adjusted timetable. In Madrid, for example, this means that during rush hour about 80 percent of metros are running. Outside rush hour, half of the metros will run. Different percentages apply to city buses. Effects felt Many schools have fewer teachers present, so education is only partly going ahead. Some petrol stations are closed and markets expect to receive fewer deliveries. Even health centres and hospitals are on strike. In many places a weekend or holiday schedule is being followed. Regional broadcaster Canal Sur did not broadcast a news bulletin this morning. At 8.30, when the broadcast was due to start, viewers saw a black screen with the words: 'Not broadcasting due to the general strike.' The two large political parties have each responded to the strike in their own way. The socialist party has expressed its support for the strike. In contrast, the right-conservative Partido Popular accuses the trade unions UGT and CCOO of a political strike. They would want to serve the interests of the left and thereby undermine the credibility of the trade unions. Possible disturbances Large demonstrations are planned in almost all large cities for this evening. In Catalonia, 9000 officers are being deployed, 3000 more than on a regular day. The intelligence service of the Catalan police has assessed the risk of disturbances during the demonstrations as maximal. Disturbances are expected especially after the demonstration in Barcelona. Elsewhere, no major disturbances are expected.

title: Young people take matters into their own hands: working on future homes with their own tractors
lead: A group of future residents of new-build houses in Creil, in Flevoland, is doing the preparatory groundwork on the land themselves. This saves them thousands of euros. Seven terraced houses are being built on the Kiekendiefstraat in the Flevoland village. They have mostly been bought by young people, writes Omroep Flevoland . Normally the ground is prepared for construction by the contractor, but now the prospective residents have joined forces. One neighbour has a large crane, another a tractor and yet another a tipper. They normally use these agricultural machines to harvest potatoes and onions from the land, but now they are saving quite a bit of money on their new homes. In total, the seven new households save over 11,000 euros. "We have our own crane, and all the guys who are moving here have arranged a tractor", says new resident Jan-Hendrik Geschiere. "We have arranged with the building company that we do the groundwork nicely. So we're all happily getting on with it." Developing it themselves. The homes on the Kiekendiefstraat are being built through the Collectief Particulier Opdrachtgeverschap (CPO). That means a group of private individuals develops a home themselves, without a project developer. Residents then choose the architect and a contractor themselves, for example. "You go out and determine the balance between price and quality yourself", says project supervisor Wina Tiesinga. This can save a lot of money, she stresses. "You cut out a number of layers." By Friday the groundwork must be completed and construction can really begin. The houses must be ready in a year. Several parents of the residents are also present at the work. They are providing sausage rolls, coffee and cookies, the regional broadcaster reported.

title: Owner of bridal fashion shop and target of Tarwekamp to suspects: 'Shame on you'
lead: In their mother tongue, the owner of the bridal fashion shop addressed the men suspected of the explosion on the Tarwekamp. "Shame on you, shame on you deeply", the woman said in her pre-recorded statement on the fourth day of the criminal case. Her ex-boyfriend is the main suspect in the case in which four men are suspected of causing the explosion in December 2024, in which six people lost their lives. Shortly before the attack she had ended the relationship with Moshtag B. He felt his honour had been damaged and "wanted to make her pay for it". One by one, the owner of the bridal fashion shop addressed the suspects about their deeds. "When you say that you no longer wanted to take part in the explosion because the amount you would be paid was too low, that hurts me", she said to Adil A., who is suspected of less serious offences because he withdrew while planning the attack. "You withdrew because you thought the money was too little, not because you got a guilty conscience." She then addressed the cousins Mourad B. and Ilias B., who caused the explosion in the shop. "I cannot imagine that money was the motivation to take part in this", she said. "I want you to realise how much grief you have caused." Finally, she addressed Moshtag B., her ex-boyfriend, who is said to have hired the others. "From the beginning you have lied about everything. Was this worth it, are you satisfied with the outcome?" She calls it shameful that he committed an attack because a girl broke up with him, and reminds him that he comforted her after the attack. "You caught me and pretended to grieve. It is too sick for words." She suffers greatly from the explosion and its aftermath. For example, she lives at a secret address and is severely depressed. Others, and she herself too, blamed her for being the cause of the attack. She is grateful that she is now also seen as a victim. But she stressed that those who died and those who were injured or lost relatives are the greatest victims. The Chinese boy whose parents and sister died in the explosion says he misses his family very much. In a video message recorded in advance, he says that he grieves the loss greatly. "Often I cry in a corner of my room." The boy was 8 years old when the attack took place on 7 December 2024. Since the death of his 41-year-old mother, father (45) and 17-year-old sister, he has lived with his aunt. "However well she takes care of me, it can never replace my own home and family." He cannot forgive the four suspects of the attack. "I can never accept that bad people have taken away the innocent lives of my dad, mum and sister." Other relatives of the Chinese family also made use of their right to speak, through an interpreter or others who speak Dutch. For example, the mother of the father who died from the family from China said that since the attack she has been tormented by grief day and night. The consequences for her now 10-year-old grandson in particular are great. "He saw the total destruction of his family and has an irreparable psychological trauma for the rest of his life." Victims demand nearly 10 million euros. The court has received 68 claims for damages from, among others, individuals, companies and the municipality of <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity>, in total. In total, nearly 10 million euros is being claimed. This concerns 7.5 million euros in material costs such as medical costs or lost income of entrepreneurs. 2.3 million euros is claimed for immaterial damage, such as the emotional shock caused by the death of a relative. In total, fifteen people spoke today. A woman who had a studio in the building said she wonders how the Afghan main suspect Moshtag B. can act "in a way that strongly resembles the Taliban", the Islamic fundamentalists who are in power in Afghanistan. Both the family of the deceased Chinese victims and other residents of the building asked the court to impose appropriate sentences. "We want those responsible to be held to account."

title: 11/11 on Nieuwsuur: Deal on tax plan, what next? • How (un)safe is Syria? • Companies want fewer home workers
lead: Deal with Pro and Volt on tax plan. Coalition parties D66 and CDA have struck a deal with opposition parties Pro and Volt on a tax increase for the wealthy and a tax cut on wages. "This is a breakthrough," says Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity>. It is not yet clear whether this will get the coalition out of the impasse and whether the tax plan will win a majority in both the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity>. The VVD, for its part, has major objections to Pro's original proposal. We discuss the latest news with political reporter Arjan Noorlander, who has been following the Hague negotiations closely for months. How (un)safe is Syria? Is Syria safe enough to send refugees from that country back? That question has kept Hague politics busy for some time. Asylum minister Van den Brink thinks it is, but the <entity id="org:raad-van-state">Raad van State</entity> ruled today that he must reassess the security situation in Syria. That ruling follows a legal case brought by a Syrian asylum seeker after his asylum application was rejected. What does this court ruling mean for our asylum policy and for Syrians in the Netherlands?

title: Podcast De Dag: Tarwekamp victims and bereaved have their say
lead: Victims and bereaved relatives of the explosion on Tarwekamp in The Hague have had their say in the courtroom in recent days. They are using their right to speak to let the suspects know how deep the scars are and the pain they feel every day. Six people died in the Tarwekamp explosion. A gaping hole can still be seen in the middle of the apartment complex. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps . Like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. Court reporter Mattijs van de Wiel was in the courtroom yesterday and tells in the podcast De Dag how deep the feelings of insecurity are among the speakers. 30 people spoke about how the explosion affects them every day, including the owner of the bridal fashion shop that the explosion was aimed at. She told her story for the first time. What does that right to speak mean for them? And do these accounts influence the sentence? Respond? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial team: Judith van de Hulsbeek Final editing: Rosanne Sies

title: Researchers sound alarm over critical leaks in cooling systems: 'This is serious'
lead: Cooling systems in supermarkets, butcher shops and even blood banks across Europe must be disconnected from the internet as soon as possible if they are controlled with systems from the Danish company Danfoss. Dutch security researchers are calling on companies to do so. Danfoss came under scrutiny earlier this month when cooling systems across Europe were hacked and sabotaged. These involved companies that were still using older cooling systems or older versions of the software. The attackers raised the temperature, so the stock in supermarkets, for example, spoiled. The researchers from security company Midnight Blue, which specialises in research into devices with a built-in computer, however also found problems in newer versions of the software. Devices running Danfoss's very latest software are therefore also affected. "On a scale of 1 to 10, I am heading towards 10," says Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue. "This is very serious. Within an hour I found several serious problems, which I don't often encounter." Among other things, it is possible to gain full access to the device and therefore also, for example, to raise the temperature. The devices could also be sabotaged, making them permanently unusable. The researchers have confidentially informed Danfoss about the problems to give the company time to fix them. That is why they are not yet giving details about the problems they found. "But we want to bring it out into the open now, because people need to take measures," said Meijer. In a response, Danfoss says that a software update will be released later today to fix two problems, although it is not clear whether these are the problems the Dutch researchers found. The company did not go into substance on questions from NOS about the new problems. Inherently flawed Updating to the latest version is not enough, however, say the Dutch researchers: the quality of the software is simply too poor for that. The program code is so "inherently flawed" that installing updates yields little gain in security. Basic precautions are lacking, they write. Users must ensure as soon as possible that the devices are not directly connected to the internet, because otherwise the chance that malicious actors will gain access again is "very considerable". "In this case it is not enough to wait for updates from the supplier." Smaller companies In the Netherlands mainly smaller companies have been affected by the earlier Danfoss hacks, the supplier itself also indicates. In other countries the problems were bigger, especially in France, where thousands of systems were affected. The cooling systems are connected to the internet so that the installer can look on when there are problems. "Installers sometimes also force this," says Meijer. That can be done in a safe way, but in practice it is by no means always done. "Because it is easier to connect them directly to the internet," Meijer thinks. The downside is therefore that malicious actors can also easily get access when there are problems.

title: EU wants mandatory button to switch off addictive social media features
lead: Endless scrolling through your social media timeline. Or that online offer where the seller pretends there are only a few tickets, rooms or products left. More and more consumers are encountering unfair or addictive practices online. The European Commission wants to tackle this. The European Commission wants to make it easier for social media users to break free from addictive series of videos on their timeline. Anyone who endlessly watches videos that play automatically on TikTok, Instagram or Facebook finds it hard to put the phone down. It leads to addiction and sometimes to psychological problems. The Commission now wants a mandatory button that lets you switch off these most addictive features. Letting consumers choose themselves The Commission is not opting for a ban on the addictive design of social media, as the EU does want for children under 15. For adults it is different: apps retain the ability to keep their users endlessly addicted to their product. Consumers must have the choice themselves, reasons EU Commissioner Virkkunnen: "It is partly also the business model of those companies, to make their services addictive. Many users also like it. That is why we are making it transparent, and it is up to the user to choose whether to keep these features or switch them off." MEP Kim van Sparrentak of Pro calls this a wrong trade-off: "With this proposal the Commission is making a historic mistake, for both our health and our democracy. The Commission could have chosen to protect people, but they have chosen the tech bros. They have caved in and by doing so they legitimise the addictive business models of Big Tech." CDA MEP Jeroen Lenaers joins this criticism: "Not only children, but adults too are influenced online by misleading and manipulative design choices. Just as with the EU KIDS Act, we believe responsibility for a fair and safe digital environment should lie with the platforms themselves, and not with the user." Unfair practices Besides a mandatory button to switch off addictive features, the European Commission also wants to put an end to unfair marketing tricks that online sellers use to separate customers from their money. For example, influencers, who are paid by companies to promote their products, must also clearly disclose this. An end must also come to the automatic renewal of online subscriptions. After a free trial period, companies must explicitly ask for consent to renew a subscription. According to the Commission, the new rules are urgently needed to ensure that the online consumer is just as well protected as the customer in the physical shop. Around 60 percent of purchases in the EU are made online. And so the legislation must adapt to that, says EU Commissioner McGrath, responsible for consumer protection. "Our economy has changed. Our rules must provide more freedom of choice, more control, simple rules and strict supervision of them." According to MEP Lenaers of the CDA, it is very necessary for better rules to come for the online market. "Consumers must be able to trust that they can make a fair choice online. Without manipulation or deception. A strong digital economy requires not only innovation, but also trust, transparency and fairness." Both left and right in the European Parliament believe that the Commission's proposals could still be somewhat stricter. The 27 EU countries will also still have to agree to the plans. As a result, it will take more than a year before the new rules take effect.

title: Ukraine and Russia agree on prisoner exchange, but no breakthrough
lead: After the second day of negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on ending the war, there appears to be no breakthrough. Only on the exchange of prisoners does there seem to be agreement. The talks began yesterday in Abu Dhabi and were led by the United States. Beforehand, expectations of achieving concrete results were not very high anyway. It is the first time in nine months that Russia and Ukraine have spoken at this level. Further talks. It is telling that the negotiators first chose their own channels after the meeting to announce the results. For Russian television, chief negotiator Vladimir Medinski said there is more mutual understanding on some points, without becoming specific. That would mean peace has come closer. But, he added: "At this moment, a lot depends on all those involved in the process. A lot depends on Ukraine, on the stance of the United States and on whether Europe comes to its senses." About Europe, Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arachamia said right after the meeting that the talks must be multilateral. By this he means that Ukraine believes Europe should also take a seat at the table. Arachamia added that he thinks a basis was laid in Abu Dhabi to reach a solution before the end of this year. He did not say how. From Europe there is cautious optimism about the preliminary results. The German government assumes that Europe will be directly represented at the next round of talks. US negotiator Kushner said about this: "We need to have the Europeans at the table." According to Germany, there is partial agreement with the US on a future "security structure". Working groups should now work out sub-aspects. 1000 to 1500 prisoners of war This negotiating round did not pass without any concrete results. Ukraine and Russia have agreed to exchange prisoners of war again. "One of the positive results is that we have reached agreement on the largest exchange of prisoners so far. Tomorrow we will finalise the numbers", said American Jared Kushner, who led the talks. The exchange would involve 1000 to 1500 prisoners on each side. The last major exchange of prisoners of war was this spring. In May both countries each exchanged 1000 prisoners. The American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet President Putin in Moscow tomorrow. Afterwards they travel on to Dublin, where they will meet Ukrainian President Zelensky. While both countries were talking, the war continued unabated. Both countries attacked each other from the air. Ukrainian energy plants bore the brunt of this. Ukraine hit a Russian refinery.

title: Bulletproof briefcases and bodyguards on skis: this is how you protect the king
lead: How do you protect a king who wants to be accessible and mix with the people? At major events, but also during working visits, we see <entity id="person:willem-alexander">koning Willem-Alexander</entity> close to the public. Recently it caused a moment of alarm when a confused person approached him during a working visit in the North Holland village of Ursem. "You take on an accepted risk", says personal security expert Mark de West, who in the past also protected members of the Royal House. In the NOS podcast De Monarchie he explains that the largest part of security is invisible. "Most of what we see, for example at events on TV, is the last 10-20 percent of security. Those are the men and women in suits who walk around them. People think that is personal security, but it is much broader." In Ursem it ended with a fright. The king himself spoke briefly with the man, who was then taken away by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. "You can set all kinds of what-if scenarios against that", says De West. "Nobody will be happy that he got so close, but I dare to say in general: you do not just stand within a meter of the king without already having been seen. The bodyguards make an assessment in advance." "You can imagine that wherever a person to be protected goes, there are many people who may display deviant behaviour. And if we intervene immediately every time, then a King's Day, for example, also becomes a very different ritual." Want to know more? Listen to episode 5 of the NOS podcast De Monarchie via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Listen and all other podcast apps. In it, presenter Fleur Wallenburg talks at length with Mark de West about the security of the Royal House, and royal affairs reporter Beau Heimensen fills you in on the choice of the upcoming state visit to Qatar. All kinds of steps are taken to reduce the risk of an unsafe situation. A hundred percent security at a major event such as King's Day cannot be guaranteed, De West explains, but significantly reducing the risk is what it is all about. "As security, we are there to make this possible. On King's Day it would, for example, be remarkable to ride in a little car like a kind of Pope. That is not something we are used to in the Netherlands either." To make it possible anyway, there is security along the route and reconnaissance is carried out weeks in advance. 'Spontaneity you can forget' Apart from the major events and working visits, the ten members of the Royal House are protected 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "And 24/7 really is 24/7", De West says. The impact on someone's life is very great. "Spontaneity you can largely forget, that is the practice. Many people do not realise that." A lot of preparation is involved. For example, all locations where the Oranjes go are examined in advance. "What approach routes are there, but also what is the nearest hospital?", De West says. How visible the security is at the location depends on the visit. "Think of ADE, where the queen and the princess went dancing. If you put eight men in suits around them, the atmosphere is quickly gone, that does not work." To blend in with the surroundings, a bodyguard sometimes has to learn new skills. Think of skiing. "Then we do not say: on the slope you are responsible for your own safety. Blending in is basically what you try to do."

title: Tension in coalition over tax plan: 'This leaves scars'
lead: Relations in the coalition of D66, VVD and CDA are under strain after the deal between two of the three parties and the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt. Negotiations took place until 3 a.m. between D66, CDA and Pro about an amendment to the tax plan, without the media being informed. This morning the talks continued and a deal appeared possible: 1 billion euros in tax increases for the wealthy and 1 billion euros in reductions for ordinary incomes. Only when the three parties were done were VVD leader Yesilgöz and the VVD's <entity id="person:ruben-pieter-brekelmans">fractievoorzitter Brekelmans</entity> informed. "No, they were not happy when they heard that", says one of those involved. VVD top gathers Meanwhile the VVD leadership has been together for hours to consider how to proceed. This evening a broader consultation is planned. House members of D66 and CDA have no idea how coalition partner VVD will react. They hope the VVD realises that this proposal can well be supported, they say. During the lengthy negotiations, part of the original plan of what Pro calls a 'millionaires' tax' has been struck out. But it is the question whether the sharp edges are thereby removed for the VVD. Live blog Follow the latest developments from The Hague in our live blog. They have a knot in their stomach, say CDA and D66. It had to happen to prevent the tax plan from failing. But for the relationship this is of course not good, they realise. 'This leaves scars', says one involved. 'However it ends.' D66 and CDA anxiously await in their parliamentary groups how their own coalition partner will respond. 'At the VVD they knew talks were going on, but they never thought it would succeed to make a deal with Pro.' The cabinet is also in a tense spot. Besides the parliamentary groups, the situation is also tense for the <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity>. In it, VVD <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> may have to judge the deal together with D66 state secretary Eerenberg. Heinen as <entity id="pos:minister-van-financien">minister van Financiën</entity> and Eerenberg as state secretary for tax affairs. Tomorrow's debate will also be tense for <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, as he can expect many questions about the future of his cabinet. The House debate on the tax plan can be followed live tomorrow at the NOS on nos.nl, <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> 1 and on NPO Politiek en Nieuws. Updates can regularly be heard on NPO Radio 1.

title: Woman (58) dies after garden wall collapses in Vlaardingen
lead: A 58-year-old woman who ended up under a collapsed wall in Vlaardingen this morning has died. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> confirmed this to regional broadcaster Rijnmond. The garden wall collapsed this morning at around 09.00 in an alley in the centre of Vlaardingen. Bystanders then tried to pull the victim out from under the rubble. The fire brigade eventually managed to free her. The victim was resuscitated and taken to hospital, where she died of her injuries. It is not known what caused the wall to collapse. The police examined the incident and assume a fatal accident. The wall stood on private land along a back garden and served as a kind of fence. Residents previously told Rijnmond that the wall was already leaning a little. The woman had just picked up her bicycle to go exercise with a friend when it went wrong.

title: World leaders unanimously concerned, but conflicts cast a shadow over climate summit
lead: At the climate summit in Turkey there was a constant coming and going of world leaders. Calls to honour climate agreements, the disaster in Nepal, weather extremes, El Niño and geopolitical tensions as well left their mark on their speeches. In the case of <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, it was national politics that coloured his contribution to the summit: he stayed away from Antalya entirely because of the problems he has at home with the tax plan . At the start of the major international climate summit, heads of state, prime ministers and senior representatives from all corners of the world traditionally travelled to the conference to speak on behalf of their countries. Major absentees, apart from Jetten, were US President Trump, Indian Prime Minister Modi and Chinese President Xi, although the latter did send a representative. Of the world leaders who did attend, Brazilian President Lula drew a lot of attention. His presence is for many attendees at the climate summit an unspoken relief. Two weeks ago he won the Brazilian presidential election against his opponent, the radical-right Flavio Bolsonaro, who has no time for climate policy. Lula, under whom the climate summit was organised last year, cares all the more. Geopolitical power struggle Even before many other world leaders got the floor, he expressed his annoyance that a number of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases had not come to the summit. "Climate change has disappeared from the speeches and policy documents of world leaders," said Lula. "We talk more about weapons and trade tariffs than about the survival prospects of future generations." "War and inflation are on our doorstep today, and as a result it is becoming ever harder for us to focus on the future climate catastrophe," Lula said. "But the planet cannot be left to the whims of geopolitical power struggles." Gaza Still, it proved difficult to stay away from such geopolitical tensions, as became clear already in the speech of the president of the new host country, Turkey. Erdogan devoted part of his speech in particular to the war in Gaza, which according to the Turkish president is the victim of both genocide and ecocide. "Centuries-old olive trees have been destroyed, soil and water have been polluted and cities have been levelled." This part of the speech earned applause from some of the leaders present, although some of them were less able to appreciate the detour. Among others, the President of the European Commission, Ursula Von der Leyen, did not clap. Iran But Von der Leyen also did not keep geopolitics out. She spoke of a "summer of truth", referring to the many heatwaves and severe drought Europe has experienced, before immediately moving on to the Iran war. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, she recalled, has pushed energy prices up enormously. President Pezeshkian of Iran spoke about nothing other than the conflict in his country at all, and lashed out at Israel and the United States. "The environment is the silent victim of wars. The devastating impact will remain long after the conflict has ended." Peace, he said, is a prerequisite for environmental protection. As President Stubb of Finland explains it: while the 1.5-degree target hangs by a thread, climate change threatens to be buried under the international agenda. "We cannot solve the climate crisis without multilateralism," he said, referring to the need to tackle a major problem like climate change jointly. Drought and floods That appeal resonated mainly with the poorest countries, which voiced their concerns about drought and floods caused by climate change and El Niño. Almost none of them dwelt long on geopolitics. They demanded fair climate policy and the honouring of all agreements already made. "For the record, the climate does not negotiate with geopolitics," summarised Prime Minister Mottley of Barbados on their position.

title: Landslides and floods in Portugal caused by Charles, flights cancelled
lead: In the south of Portugal and in the Lisbon region, storm Charles has caused problems. Heavy rainfall and strong gusts of wind are reported. The Portuguese public broadcaster RTP reports that hundreds of incidents have been reported, including landslides, floods and fallen trees. So far there are no reports of victims or missing persons. The weather has also disrupted air traffic. The Portuguese air navigation authority ANA reports that by midday 360 flights had already been cancelled nationwide. Lisbon airport was hit hardest: more than half of the arriving and departing flights there did not go ahead. Flights from the Netherlands were also cancelled. The Schiphol website shows that one flight to Lisbon has been cancelled and that three flights from the Portuguese capital to Schiphol have been dropped. Ahead of the storm, the Portuguese government called for vigilance. Several schools, supermarkets and other public facilities were closed as a precaution. Residents were urged to stay at home if possible. Because of the storm, six national roads in the districts of Setúbal, Portalegre and Guarda were partially closed this afternoon. Not only on the Portuguese mainland but also on the Portuguese island of Madeira, incidents related to the storm are being reported. Last night the storm already peaked there. Wind gusts of up to 130 kilometres per hour were measured. The Madeira authorities reported 78 landslides overnight. There were also 72 floods and dozens of fallen trees. A man was rescued after being swept away by water when a stream overflowed its banks. Code orange: Storm Charles is turning out less severe than expected despite the problems it caused. For four districts where code red had been issued, the weather warning has been downgraded to code orange, reports the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Code orange now applies to the districts of Leiria, Castelo Branco, Beja and Portalegre. The weather warnings are in effect until midnight. Spain: Storm Charles is also affecting the southwest of Spain. In Piedralaves (in the western province of Ávila), around 2,200 residents were evacuated as a precaution. Extreme wind gusts were measured on the Canary Islands, with speeds of up to 148 kilometres per hour.

title: El Salvador allegedly bombs gang headquarters in Haiti, prime minister thanks Bukele
lead:
"We have kept our promise". With those words, Salvadoran president Bukele announced that he had destroyed the alleged headquarters of one of the largest criminal gangs in Haiti. It is said to be the house of Wilson Joseph, also known as Lanmò San Jou, the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. "Most of them ran away without even fighting back," Bukele writes on X. "What cowards!". Footage shows helicopters opening fire on the compound. As black plumes of smoke rise above the buildings, dozens of people can be seen running away from them. Bukele, who is not averse to media spectacle, shared the video on social media. It is a tool the authoritarian leader often uses to amplify his own successes.

Prime minister praises president. Two days before the attack, which took place on Sunday, Bukele had already made his aim clear. "Give us the exact address, and we will destroy it," he wrote on X. Joseph was not killed in the attack, which was carried out in cooperation with the Haitian <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. No information has been released about casualties. Haitian prime minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé has responded enthusiastically to the attack in his country. "Hats off to President Nayib Bukele," he writes. "For your support and commitment in the national fight against the gangs," said the prime minister.

Offensive stepped up. With the attack, Bukele has significantly stepped up his offensive in Haiti. Last month El Salvador sent at least 2,000 soldiers to the country following the disappearance of four Salvadoran members of an international security mission. The four soldiers were ambushed, but what happened to them afterwards is still unclear. Initially it was reported that their bodies had been found, but Bukele quickly stated that the remains were not those of the soldiers. Since then Bukele has been constantly posting about the military operation in the Caribbean country, mainly in Haitian Creole. For example, last week he shared footage of soldiers being cheered by civilians as they march through the streets. "It seems the gangs do not want to fight us," the president wrote. With these posts Bukele appears to want to position himself as the saviour of the country torn apart by violence. But further information on how long the soldiers will remain in the country, or who is directing the troops, remains unclear.

Letter to UN chief. The Salvadoran presence in the country therefore raises question marks and is attracting increasing criticism. Gang leader Joseph is among the critics; last week, in an interview with news agency AP, he stated that he had serious concerns about the troops. He has written a letter to UN chief António Guterres requesting that he send a delegation for dialogue and mediation. He would be willing to lay down his weapons. He also said he had a message for Bukele: "Given the vindictive remarks, expectations and threats of Mr Nayib Bukele, I fear this situation will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people will be the first victims," Joseph said. He also stated that the four Salvadoran soldiers are dead and that they were in the territory of another gang. No evidence was provided for this. Bukele's response, however, did come, as he appears to answer those words with the attack on the residential compound.

title: Young people still celebrate Elfde van de Elfde in Tilburg: 'We know our limits'
lead: In the sprinter from Den Bosch to Tilburg sits a group of girls, dressed as bees and ladybirds. They are on their way to the Elfde van de Elfde in Tilburg, the traditional opening of the carnival season. The girls cram themselves all together into the toilet on the train. When they come out again, it is time for new alcoholic drinks. One ladybird is hanging limp against another ladybird. The girls discuss what they will do with this ladybird, because the party has yet to begin. How do you deal with young people at the festival grounds? That question hung over the Elfde van de Elfde in Tilburg in recent months. The municipality wanted free access for minors, because carnival is a party for everyone. But the hospitality industry wanted to be able to refuse minors at certain times. Partly because they often drink heavily, Alex Boonmann said earlier on behalf of the Tilburg hospitality sector to the NOS. 'Equally strong' After several talks, the municipality, hospitality sector and carnival foundation agreed that anyone who causes nuisance or is noticeably under the influence of alcohol or drugs can be refused. The number of NIX18 teams has also been increased; they address minors who are drinking alcohol. And on the festival grounds so-called buddies walk around to support security. Security guard Joshua has worked at carnival and the Elfde van de Elfde many times before. Today he is stationed at the start of the Stadhuisstraat, where the party traditionally began at 11:11. In the eighteen years he has been a security guard, alcohol use among young people has changed, says Joshua. "The trend is that they drink younger and younger. And they often drink strong stuff right away." For minors, Joshua and his colleagues always check the ID card. If they have not drunk too much, they may go inside. If that is the case, he calls the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. It also happens that Joshua gets into a discussion with a parent. "During carnival some parents tolerate their children drinking." But such a discussion is quickly over, he says. "We then point them to the house rules." Celebrating together On the Stadhuisstraat stands Leandra (40) with her sons Tijs (12) and Pim (7). She is glad they were allowed onto the festival grounds. "We had to check first whether it would work out, but it's nice that we can celebrate together now." On the Heuvel, the central square in Tilburg, Koen (17) and Nienke (17) are out with a few more friends. They drank at home, with their parents' permission. "As long as it doesn't get silly", says Koen. "We do behave", Nienke adds. "We know our limits." They have heard the discussion about minors at the party. "I do understand it from cafés, because if they serve alcohol to minors they get a fine", says Koen. "But well, I just think it's fun." Job (15) and Matthijs (14) are also celebrating Elf-Elf today. They are glad they may go onto the festival grounds as long as they behave. "We belong here too", says Job. "And otherwise people all over town will be messing around." At the first-aid tent in front of the town hall it is still very quiet early in the afternoon. Around 4 p.m. the first drunk young person is brought in. "He had signs of hypothermia", says first aider Ad van Laarhoven. "We're trying to get his temperature up. He'll be checked for a while and if all goes well, he'll go home with grandpa and grandma." Toward the end of the afternoon it gets busier at the first-aid post. Three tipsy teenagers are brought into the town hall by someone from the municipality. There they get a glass of water and the advice to go home. Otherwise the first aiders are mostly busy with other incidents. "We treated a man and a woman who had been beaten up", Van Laarhoven says. "Also people who had fallen off their bikes, someone who had tripped and someone who had fallen and then landed with a hand in glass." Still, it is still manageable, says Van Laarhoven. Security guard Joshua also has everything under control. He has had to refuse two people "because they were too drunk". "But those were adults." Boonmann, the hospitality entrepreneur, also says there have been no "noteworthy incidents" yet. "But Brabant nights are long, so we will all have to remain alert."

title: Member of Italian terrorist group (74) escapes by rope from fifth-floor balcony
lead: The 74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, former member of the Italian terrorist group Red Brigades, escaped while he was under house arrest. The man managed for years to stay out of the hands of the authorities, while a prison sentence of 27 years awaited him in Italy. When he was nevertheless arrested in Argentina and extradition to Italy threatened, he decided to set up an escape by rope.
